C orrected oral evidence: Dynamic alignment
Tuesday 16 June 2026
Watch the meeting

Members present: Lord Stirrup (The Chair); Baroness Ashton of Upholland; Lord Barrow; Baroness Brown of Silvertown; Lord Elliott of Mickle Fell; Lord Jackson of Peterborough; Lord Moynihan of Chelsea; Baroness Smith of Newnham; Lord Tugendhat.
Evidence Session No. 13 Heard in Public Questions 127 - 136
Witnesses

Dr Silke Goldberg, Partner and Global Head of Environmental, Social and Governance (ESG)/Sustainability, Herbert Smith Freehills Kramer, and Professor of Energy Law in the North Sea, Faculty of Law, University of Groningen; Kathryn Porter, Energy Consultant, Watt-Logic.
USE OF THE TRANSCRIPT
Examination of witnesses
Dr Silke Goldberg and Kathryn Porter.

Q127 The Chair: Good afternoon and welcome back to this public evidence session of the House of Lords Select Committee on European Affairs, where we are looking into the issue of dynamic alignment. We are delighted to welcome to the second half of the session Dr Silke Goldberg, who is partner and global head of environmental, social and governance/sustainability at Herbert Smith Freehills Kramer, and professor of energy law in the North Sea in the faculty of law at the University of Groningen.

We are hoping also to be joined by Kathryn Porter, who is an energy consultant with Watt-Logic. She is participating remotely, but we are having a few technical difficulties at the moment, so we hope that she will join us as we proceed through the session.

It is a public session. It is being broadcast. There will be a transcript provided. You will see a draft to check for errors and omissions. We will finish by 1 pm because I know that is when you have to go. Thank you very much for being with us.

Without more ado, let us crack on. I will ask you a general question, if I may. Is UK participation in the EU’s internal electricity market the only way of overcoming the difficulties that we have experienced in trying to implement the TCA arrangements for electricity trading, or are there alternatives?

Let us put it this way. As part of the TCA implementation, the specialised committee on energy has tried quite a number of things, particularly in relation to multi-region loose volume coupling, which is the key instrument that was put forward as part of the TCA for trading. In addition, companies operating interconnectors have tried to do direct access agreements in relation to those interconnectors.

Within the framework of the TCA, the possibilities have been exhausted. In order to improve trading across all timeframes, in particular SDAC—the single day ahead market, which is the largest volume market in the EU—there is no alternative but to have an agreement to join the internal energy market and, therefore, to return to price coupling rather than multi-region loose volume coupling, which all participating TSOs—transmission system operators—had concluded was not workable.
The Chair: So rejoining the internal market is the only way of going back to price coupling.
Yes.
The Chair: That is very clear. Thank you very much indeed.

Q128 One question we asked in the previous panel, but we would very much welcome your expert view on, is whether a prospective electricity agreement should be seen mainly as technical to address electricity trading arrangements, or whether it could have rather more significant and wide-ranging policy implications for the UK. For this committee, that matters quite a lot in terms of the way we might want to report to our parliamentary colleagues.

Thank you very much for the question. When looking at what such an agreement might contain, it is instructive to look at similar agreements that the European Union has concluded. The most recent, comprehensive and comparable one is likely that between the European Union and Switzerland. If you look at the agreement between the European Union and Switzerland, there are a number of articles that are purely technical, in my view.
The Chair: I am so sorry. Can I pause you for one second? We have just been joined by your fellow witness. Kathryn Porter, thank you very much for joining us. We have just got started.
I will just ask Dr Goldberg to finish her answer. Then we will come back to you and reframe the question for you.

If I look at the Swiss agreement, there are numerous articles in the agreement that will say, “This is the way that transmission system operators participate in European Union decision-making. This is how the co-operation will work. This is how the parties will consult one another”. By and large, it is technical.

However, it is also, by implication, a political or policy agreement in the sense that there will be dynamic alignment. In relation to the Swiss agreement, this was done in the first instance by having an annex that said, “The Swiss Confederation will comply with” or “implement the following directives and regulations from day one”, as it were, and then there was a phased discussion in relation to that.

Overall, it has both very technical aspects and policy implications in relation to, for instance, dynamic alignment. It is perhaps quite natural, if you set up and integrate a market, that there are policy correlations that will need to be taken into account.
The Chair: Baroness Smith, do you want to reiterate your question for Ms Porter?

I will do, and then I have a supplementary, if I may. I am delighted that you are finally with us, Ms Porter. The question that I framed originally was to what extent a prospective electricity agreement might be mostly technical, and how far there might be wider policy or political ramifications. You heard Dr Goldberg’s answer.

To add to that, we took evidence a few weeks ago from the Swiss ambassador. At various levels, Swiss citizens, as well as Swiss parliamentarians, might choose to try to block things that could be subject to dynamic alignment. How significant might the amount of legislation that we are talking about be if we are looking at a new agreement?

In terms of the significance of the legislation, that is going to be quite lumpy. In some years, you could see very little change. In other years, you could have a whole load of change all in one go because the EU comes up with a major policy shift that has quite a lot of associated implications. That would then lead to quite a large amount of activity in that sense. You could not really pin it down and say, “On average, it is going to be this much per year”. Some years, it will be very quiet, and then, other years, it will be quite significant.

I am in complete agreement. The European Union likes to adopt, in particular in the energy sector, directives and regulations by package. It is, therefore, quite likely that, if there is a new package, there might be five to 10 directives and regulations, and there might be years where nothing at all is happening.

You were previously asking about the political implications should Swiss citizens not agree to go along with a particular part of dynamic alignment. Article 28 in the Swiss agreement addresses that by saying that certain constitutional obligations within Switzerland need to be fulfilled, and there is a timeframe to set out how that works in detail.

Q129 I have a question for both of you, but maybe we will start with Ms Porter and then Dr Goldberg. What are likely to be the most difficult or contentious issues in the negotiation of an electricity agreement? Are any of them, in your view, potentially deal breakers?

The most difficult elements are likely to be ones that potentially do not even surface in the negotiation. Across Europe, we are having various instabilities in the power grid that the EU regulators are dealing with at the moment. We saw this with the Spanish blackout. If you look at the report into that, they mentioned these oscillations that were becoming normal in the power grid, and this had been tolerated.

We now have a similar situation in Scotland. Those types of situations can be fine for a period and then can quite rapidly degenerate into not being fine. Retaining flexibility to address those types of situations is quite important. Typically, the EU allows system operators and market participants to respond to emergency situations with temporary measures, but some of these situations will require something not temporary. They will require longer-term solutions potentially outside of normal market frameworks, and Scotland is a very good example of this.

We have only two conventional power stations left in Scotland. The National Electricity System Operator is, in essence, experimenting with untested solutions to how that grid can operate when those two power stations close, which is likely to happen in a five to seven-year horizon. The solutions that it may end up having to adopt if these experimental technologies do not work would have to be implemented rapidly and potentially sustained over, potentially, a long period because we have big bottlenecks in supply chains for getting generating equipment. They are likely to require extra-market actions, which the EU might find difficult to sanction.

We really need to make sure that we retain the flexibility to manage our grid security, not just in short-term emergency situations, but where these issues can persist. It could be the case that we encounter those challenges in advance of other parts of the EU, in which case the normal regulatory frameworks just will not catch up. The key negotiating point should be to make sure that we have sufficient flexibility to maintain our stability under scenarios that, potentially, are not considered mainstream at the moment.

Looking at the potential issues of contention or friction, where the TCA—trade and cooperation agreement—has, in effect, invited or manages divergence, I can see some issues. Divergence since the TCA coming into force has happened in particular in relation to state aid, where the rules are different, so they would need to be reviewed.

Grid planning is something that could take place as part of ENTSO-E, the 10-year network development plan, of which GB would need to become a member again in the fullest sense. It is about scrutinising the areas, and perhaps a bit of work would need to be done in relation to where that divergence has crystallised.

Ultimately, the British market design was, let us face it, adopted by the European Union prior to Brexit. I do not foresee any particular deal breakers, because Britain was such an influence in the European Union when it came to liberalisation and design of the markets. Bar some technical areas, which Ms Porter has just pointed out, related to perhaps what I would call the regulatory sandbox, where GB has taken a particular innovative approach outside the EU framework, all of these things could be addressed. Ultimately, we would be coming to a market design that is not foreign or strange. It is one that was invented here.

Q130 The question we are really interested in is whether it is possible to say at this stage whether the electricity agreement would have an effect on UK energy markets. Do you think domestic energy costs are going to go up or down?

I am not an economist, so please take what I am about to say with a pinch of salt. I think costs overall would go down. If you look at the costs that have arisen since Brexit and the non-price coupling, Matthew Hinde from National Grid spoke in front of this committee some time ago and estimated a cost of between £200 million and £300 million per year that has just been lost to ineffective interconnector trading, so that cost would not be incurred.

In addition, if you look at power price developments across the European Union, one of the founding principles of price coupling is that the electricity migrates to where the power price is the highest. On average, Britain is a higher price zone. Therefore, I would expect power prices at wholesale level to go down.

It is right to say that removing inefficiencies from interconnection trading will lower prices in the wholesale market. However, the extent to which that feeds through into bills will be limited because of the mechanism by which the subsidies are paid.

Under contracts for difference, which is the dominant subsidy mechanism, there is an explicit independence from the market, so generators are given a fixed price, which is and always has been higher than the wholesale price. With contracts for difference, if you lower the wholesale price, you have a corresponding one-for-one increase in the subsidy top-up that they receive, which is added to bills, separate to the wholesale price, so the wholesale component of the bill falls but the subsidy element goes up one for one, offsetting that reduction. There needs to be some caution around the assumption that a lower wholesale price translates into a lower bill. For a large part of the generation mix, that is not the case.

The other difficulty we have around interconnectors is that Ofgem published a report in 2021 where it said that, if Britain becomes a net exporter because of increased interconnection and increased domestic generation—primarily, renewables—that would create a disbenefit or financial disadvantage to consumers that would translate into higher bills. This was, in fact, the main driver for Ofgem declining many of the projects that came through in window 3 of the cap and floor mechanism. If we were to adopt dynamic alignment, that might restrict the ability of Ofgem to make these types of choices.

We would also, potentially, face restrictions if we wanted to introduce different types of support for different customer groups. For example, we currently provide, in effect, subsidies for energy-intensive users. We also provide subsidies through the warm homes discount for consumers. There have been debates from time to time about introducing a social tariff. These are things that would, potentially, come into conflict with increased alignment with the EU, particularly around state aid, and that might restrict our flexibility to lower bills in that way, so we need some caution around the assumption that we would see lower bills.

There are a couple of things in there. I agree that, in general, the European Union is not looking favourably at consumer price subsidies currently. There is a general principle that such subsidies should not happen. There have been ECJ judgments on the topic. However, in practice, a lot of jurisdictions have these. For instance, France definitely has a social tariff, and these are then cleared through state aid rules. The same is true for CfDs. Many European jurisdictions have subsidies for renewable energy. Some are CfDs and some are feed-in tariffs. In Germany, there is a direct market premium. There are many different models, so that would not be unique to the UK. The difficulty of maintaining or offsetting that against the power price would need to be looked at in the round.

I just want to come back to the point that Ms Porter made in relation to interconnectors and the possibility of Ofgem making certain policy choices. Europe is generally under-interconnected. At the political level, the European Union has reiterated a number of times that it wants more interconnectors, yet many national regulatory authorities, for instance the French, have made choices in relation to which interconnectors to build.

Rejoining the internal energy market would not make it more difficult for Ofgem to say, “We would be supportive of this interconnector rather than that one” or, “This is how much interconnection we want”. That, in fact, would make it easier for those interconnectors that are built, because they would be built on a foundation and framework of holistic decision-making.
The Chair: My understanding, particularly from what Ms Porter said, is that, although the price of electricity may come down, people are not going to see any real change in their bills.

Again, I am not an economist, but I do understand that, in Britain, wholesale market and consumer prices have been decoupled to some extent, so what happens on the wholesale market does not necessarily translate into all of our bills in our function as consumers.

The Chair: Would you agree that, if we wanted to see a significant reduction in bills, the solution lies in our own price structures and the way we do it, rather than participating in the EU’s internal electricity market? That may have other benefits as well, but, in terms of driving prices down, we have control of that.

Yes, absolutely. At the moment, I understand that Parliament and Ofgem are debating reformed national pricing, zonal pricing and all the different ways of structuring price zones in GB. Whether or not Britain is in the European Union, that [structing of electricity pricing] remains entirely in British hands, if you wish.

Q131 Building on what you have both been saying, something that is important as we think about dynamic alignment is the implication for what happens outside of the EU and whether, by moving in one direction, we, in a sense, cut off options or make changes that could have negative implications. When you think about participation in the internal energy market, are there implications for the UK’s energy relations outside of the EU, and, if so, what would they be?

I do not think that there are necessarily implications that would be difficult. The EU is importing energy from many countries across the world, such as Qatar, the United States, Algeria and Norway, and, indeed, from the UK at the moment. However, that is done regardless of whether there is an association agreement between that jurisdiction and the European Union. Likewise, the United Kingdom imports LNG from the United States, Qatar and Algeria. You get the idea that the countries from which the EU and the UK are importing are relatively aligned. There is nothing in there that would necessarily hinder those import arrangements, which, in any event, are done by individual companies rather than by countries.
Ms Porter, do you agree with that?
Yes, I do. I do not really have anything else I would add to that.
Thank you. That was straightforward.

Q132 The Chair: Could I turn now to the issue that is of most importance to this committee’s inquiry into dynamic alignment? That is the involvement of Parliament. The Government are planning to publish and have a Second Reading quite soon of their UK-EU partnership Bill, which will give Ministers the power to dynamically align sectors of UK law with certain sectors of EU law. That will be a power that applies to all agreements as they come down the road, not just the ones that they are currently trying to finalise.

In your view, what part does Parliament have to play in scrutinising the arrangements that are made and the decisions that are taken in subsequent agreements, such as internal electricity market participation, in terms of delineating which areas of EU law should be part of dynamic alignment, and scrutinising the changes that the EU subsequently makes to those areas of EU law?

This is a very difficult question that we are trying to get our minds around, because, clearly, once Parliament decides that it will dynamically align, it will dynamically align, but what are the boundaries of that dynamic alignment? How do you make sure that things do not creep into it that were not foreseen in the first place? How do you make sure that unintended consequences do not flow from that dynamic alignment?

What part do you think Parliament should play in scrutinising that? As part of that, is it important for the UK to retain the power, in essence, to say, “No, we are not going to align in this particular area”? Perhaps I will ask Ms Porter to have first stab at that.

I absolutely think that Parliament does need to retain the ability to say no. For me, this is a wider question about the sovereignty of the UK Parliament. If you are going to automatically align with regulations that are being created elsewhere, under the proposed dynamic alignment, the UK would have no vote in those changes. We may be able to influence certain things through negotiation, but we would have no power of veto and no ability to vote along with other EU member states when those decisions are being made at the EU level.

It is important that we do not find ourselves having to passively just accept anything that is decided by the EU and then adopt it without any ability to say no. It is very important that Parliament retains a veto, scrutinises proposals at the earliest possible opportunity and maintains things such as an ongoing, live alignment register so that these decisions and their potential impact on the British market are being tracked as early as possible. That would give Parliament the opportunity to have its say and to make sure that British consumers are not disadvantaged by changes proposed within the EU.

We have seen Norway, for example, being quite robust with the EU on certain proposals. It has neglected to implement some of the EU energy packages. It has pushed back very strongly around some of the cross-border interconnection arrangements. In fact, the Norwegians have twice amended their internal electricity Act to give themselves powers to restrict electricity exports to other countries because of the perceived risk of shortages that they face. There are some specifics in the Norwegian market that make them very vulnerable to that.

The EU has always said that it does not like this and has tried to push back, but the Norwegian Parliament has really insisted that it has the right to make these choices, and has been quite explicit that it will make choices for the benefit of the Norwegian people and not subordinate Norwegian interests to the wider EU context.

If I may direct you to Article 26 of the Swiss agreement, it acknowledges, first of all, that Parliament has an important role in scrutinising but also in shaping decisions, and that should not be forgotten. Article 26 of the EU-Swiss agreement sets out how experts and Parliament are consulted, and how decisions of the dynamic alignment committee are being influenced and shaped by those joint consultations.

Then there is the matter of politics, really, and the comments that UK representatives want to make in relation to decisions and Acts that are being brought forward in the joint committee between the EU and Switzerland. I imagine that there could be a similar joint committee between UK and EU representatives, who could then negotiate politically where they should and should not align. It is also a question of what form the dynamically aligned legislation would take. If it is a statutory instrument, it would be laid before Parliament, so there is an in-built scrutiny, if you wish.

Ms Porter referred to the Norwegian example. That is slightly different, because Norway is not an associated member of the European Union. Norway is part of the EEA agreement, so the negotiation powers are perhaps slightly differently distributed. Norway does not implement everything from the European Union, but it has also developed a certain muscle in relation to accompanying European Union policy.

If I may be permitted a 30-second anecdote, I went to an energy law conference many years ago in Norway. It was in the middle of the night and I had to take a long taxi ride to get to this place. The taxi driver goes to me, “Why are you in Norway?” I said, “Some conference”. I wanted to sleep and did not want to discuss it. “What sort of thing?” “An energy conference”. He looked at me and he goes, “So will you talk there about interconnectors? Let me talk about interconnectors”. This was a random taxi driver at Oslo airport.

The third energy package made the front page on all Norwegian newspapers. Dagens Næringsliv , which is like the Financial Times of Norway, if you wish, runs energy stories all the time, so they have a much bigger policy debate around that. They have, in effect, a muscle when it comes to European policy issues, which goes all the way from the Norwegian Parliament to the taxi drivers at Oslo airport.

What we need to do collectively in Britain is to rediscover our muscle memory. Britain influenced energy policy in the EU for so long. If we remember how we did that collectively, dynamic alignment might not be so bad.

Q133 I wanted to come back and pick up on the point that Ms Porter has made about Norway, then the Swiss points, and then back to Dr Goldberg’s points. In response to my earlier question, Dr Goldberg rightly pointed out that the EU likes to work in packages and to bring forward directives, regulations and so on. From the perspective of EU lawmaking, there is a difference between directives and regulations. Directives are very much about framework legislation.

How does it work with Switzerland? If the EU is bringing forward a directive, and if you are a member state, it is up to you and your Parliament to decide how you want to put that into your own national legislation. How does that work for an associated country? Clearly, there will be opportunities for us to shape whether we are using statutory instruments and so on if we are simply implementing EU law, but a directive might be a bit different.

It is fair to assume that the principles might be similar in the sense that, if a member state such as Germany or France implements a directive, the differentiating point is, of course, that directives first need to be transposed into national law. Here in Britain, everything would need to be transposed into national law, so there is a certain framework.

I do not see that you could necessarily have a directive apply directly, just in terms of the legal mechanics around that. I imagine that there would be a certain degree of latitude as to exactly how you implement that into UK law. Regulations, I imagine, would be rather word for word because that is the whole point of regulations. In particular, regulations tend to cover more technical things—for instance, the powers of ACER that there might be in a regulation, or how SDAC works, or, in relation to more subordinate legislation, EU network codes for SDAC trading or capacity allocations.

I would find it hard to see that there is leeway as to how regulations are being implemented because that is the nature of them. They are very technical. Again, in the Swiss agreement, which serves somewhat as the blueprint here for this comment, principles have been laid down on effective and harmonious application.

Much like the European Commission looks to member states to apply directives correctly and in line with EU law, the joint committee that I imagine might be established might have a look at how the UK is doing that.

Q134 We have had discussion in other bits of this inquiry about decision-shaping and how effective, realistically, that can be from outside. Do you have examples or instances of where you feel others have been effective in influencing and shaping decisions from the outside? You talked about the Norwegians, the Swiss and others. What, in your view, is the most effective way in which the UK could seek to rediscover that muscle memory and influence? Maybe it is slightly different in this area because of the package approach, but over to you.

Norway has certainly pushed back in relation to how the power market design in the European Union might affect Norway. I am sure that Ms Porter knows this in more detail, but Norway has five bidding zones, in effect. It has been very careful to make sure that whatever alignment it has with the European Union does not unduly impact that particular design, so that is an area where Norway is particularly active. It had a lot of public debate around exactly what the powers of ACER and of the European Commission are.

I would also say, in fairness, that sometimes Norway does not necessarily implement EU legislation. It does so in breach of the EEA agreement, but that then is a political decision and, presumably, if we were to be in that situation from a UK perspective, it would be up to the UK Parliament and Government to take such a political decision.

The strongest bit in terms of influencing really is in participating in that dialogue, being in the joint committee, participating in the policy debates, and having that muscle memory as to how European directives and European policy-making functions. I caught the very end of the last panel that you had, and a similar point was made there as well.
Presumably, it is as upstream as possible in the debate. The earlier you are trying to influence, the better.
Yes, absolutely. That means engaging very actively in Brussels in all the various policy fora that are available.

I would agree. The more we can be at the table putting forward our view on how things should be done, the more likely we are to get results that are not against our interests, although we have sometimes been confused around what we want to achieve.

I referenced earlier Ofgem’s analysis of interconnectors providing a consumer disbenefit if we are in a net export situation. I had some meetings with people in Ofgem, where they expressed the view that countries should not engage in energy nationalism and that decisions should be made in the collective benefit. I pointed out that this was the exact opposite of the position that it had taken on approving interconnectors in window 3 of the cap and floor mechanism. They were quite surprised and realised that that was, in fact, what they had done.

I do not think they were incorrect to do that, but you cannot simultaneously say that we are going to make decisions for the collective benefit of the European market as a whole and then implement decisions that are specifically in only your own national interest. We need to be clear about what our objectives are and where we are drawing those lines when we go into those discussions.

Q135 Can I just draw you back to the question that the Lord Chairman asked about a veto? It does seem to me, Ms Porter, that you are advocating for a veto, if I heard you correctly, but Dr Goldberg is talking more about scrutiny and oversight that stops short of a veto. Is it not the case that, once you have passed that European Partnership Act, you are in a position where you cannot really veto it, because it is a dynamic alignment Act? Therefore, unless you bring in primary legislation—with the exception that, in the Lords, we could, very unusually, vote down a statutory instrument or secondary legislation—you just have to accept that you have signed up to the whole package.

Yes, that is the intention. My understanding of the Government’s intention is to allow dynamic alignment. The entire concept of that is to subordinate the decision-making to the EU, where we will not have a vote. We will have the ability to have some influence, but we will have no vote in those decisions that are being made. We will be entirely passively accepting that.

I fundamentally disagree with that as a concept. The UK Parliament ought to have sovereignty over what happens within the UK and, if dynamic alignment prevents, waters down or removes that in any way, I would object to the entire concept.

I would perhaps frame it differently. If you sign up to dynamic alignment, you are signing up to a package, but you are also signing up to a process. Dynamic alignment works through mutual consultations to shaping of decisions, whereas the veto would only ever be the very last resort where somebody says, “We can’t do this”, for whatever political reason. You might be in a Norwegian situation where you do not adopt or implement a particular Act. That is then a political decision where you do not follow on. That is not really a veto. That is a choice not to implement something at a political level, and I am sure that would lead to further discussions between the two parties in more detail.

Fundamentally, the idea is that the UK and the European Union consult one another about the shaping of particular decisions. For me, the veto is perhaps quite harsh in the way that this is formulated, because the UK would, one would hope, have been involved in many joint consultations and decision-shaping meetings prior to that.

At the same time, I would point out that, to some extent, the TCA has ultimately foreseen some level of divergence management. In the TCA, there are areas where, if the UK wants to have a relationship with the European Union, the European Union, de facto, sets certain rules, so joint decision-making or decision-shaping under dynamic alignment, from a co-operation perspective, seems to be preferable.

I have a brief technical question. We are talking about joint consultative bodies, arbitration panels and, eventually, adjudication on EU law by the European Court of Justice. Has that happened very much in the case of Switzerland or Norway in this or other sectors?

Norway is subject to the EEA court, which is slightly different, so the ECJ does not come into that. In Switzerland, the agreement is fairly new. I am not aware of any particular decision of the joint arbitration panel that would have an impact here.

I would say that there are two levels here as well. First of all, the ECJ, from the European Union’s perspective, is the court that interprets and has the sole interpretation rights in relation to definitive interpretation of what constitutes European Union law. You then have the agreement between the UK and Switzerland, which is a different level. There is an arbitration panel, so any conflicts between Switzerland and the EU, or the UK and the European Union, would be settled under that arbitration panel. That is different.

Q136 The Chair: So far we have talked about the benefits and costs to the UK of participating in the internal electricity market. Could I turn it around and ask for your view on the nature and scale of the benefits to the EU of us participating in its internal electricity market?

First of all, trading would be more efficient also from the European Union’s perspective. Yes, it has been inefficient on our side, but it has also been inefficient on the side of the European Union. On a more idealistic level, British ideas about how to run and influence the energy market have been lost to the European Union and would come back into the EU.

On a more practical level, from a supply security perspective, when we talk about the European Union, we also need to talk about our nearest neighbour, meaning Ireland. The island of Ireland is, for electricity purposes, a single island market. The supply security of Ireland would improve because, at the moment, Ireland is entirely dependent on the UK for supply security in terms of gas imports. The UK is the transit country. Well above 80% of Ireland’s supply security depends on the UK. If the Kinsale gas fields deplete over time, it would be even higher, so there is, first of all, an Irish supply security issue.

Secondly, European Union member states provide or lend each other solidarity in case of energy penuries. Using the N-1 standard, if there is an incident and the biggest energy facility in a country goes down, EU member states can call on one another to help with that. At the moment, Ireland is disconnected from that because the UK is in the middle, so Ireland would benefit from the UK being part of the internal energy market again and, therefore, also being able to call on solidarity in those circumstances.

Likewise, the UK could, of course, call on the same solidarity mechanism. Given where we are geopolitically, with lots of uncertainty globally, and having seen the impact of various wars on the energy market, proximity does matter. Therefore, having that mutual solidarity mechanism is helpful.
The Chair: So a significant benefit.
Yes.

I am afraid I disagree with that. In practical terms, very little would change from the EU side. The trading that the EU has with the UK is not material versus all of the cross-border trading within the EU. While making it a bit more efficient would have some benefit at the margin, it is at the margin from the EU perspective.

When it comes to Ireland, it is completely dependent on GB, but, under the current arrangements, the island of Ireland is treated under our emergency rules in the electricity market as a region of GB. Under the demand control rules, if we have an electricity shortage in Britain that would lead to rotating blackouts, for example, Ireland is treated as a region of GB, pari passu with all the other regions of GB, so there is no reason that that would change. It is already at the highest level of support from GB that it could have.

There might be some political decision down the line to change that, but what we have seen since the Russian invasion of Ukraine is increasing energy nationalism from EU member states. I have been told by market participants, system operators and regulators that system operators within Europe have communicated to their peers that, in the event of a domestic shortage in their country, they do not care what the rules are. They will protect that domestic market, and it is highly unlikely in practice that any country would decide differently.

In some cases, shortages could be shared across countries simultaneously, due to geopolitical or weather-related factors. Bearing in mind that we share very highly correlated weather patterns with all our connected countries, except for Norway, and almost all of them, with the exception of Norway and France, have a very wind-heavy transition strategy, we could all experience low wind conditions simultaneously. The idea that countries will sacrifice their domestic security for the benefit of their neighbour is deeply unlikely.

In practical terms, I do not see that this alignment will make any of those improvements that were just mentioned in terms of energy security and co-operation. That is quite idealistic and does not translate in practice. In practice, we are likely to continue to see what we have seen to date. It is unlikely, in fact, that Britain would cut Ireland off, so Ireland would retain its position as having its security guaranteed by Britain.

We would continue to see countries suspending electricity exports when they experience domestic shortages. We will continue to see a situation where there is no mechanism to compel a neighbouring country to import. We have interconnectors within our capacity market, which is a deeply risky approach because imports cannot be compelled—we can only restrict exports—so the situation would broadly continue as it is at the moment. There might be some window dressing around it, but, if push comes to shove and we are facing shortages, it will be each country acting in its own best interests.

The Chair: That is an interesting divergence of views, not the first and nor, dare I say, the last we will hear in this particular inquiry. We did promise that we would finish in time for Dr Goldberg to depart at 1.00 pm, and we have achieved that. I want to thank you both very much indeed for contributing to the evidence on this most important issue. Ms Porter, apologies for the technical difficulties at the beginning, but we are very grateful to both of you for coming and for sparing us so much of your time. With that, I draw the public session to a close .

sessions.iT: Written Parliamentary Questions: Departmental performance in Session 2024-26
sessions.w: Department for Education; Department for Education

segs.tx: Procedure Committee
Oral evidence: Written Parliamentary Questions : Departmental performance in Session 2024-26 , HC 48 (828)
Wednesday 17 June 2026
Ordered by the House of Commons to be published on 17 June 2026 .
Watch the meeting
Members present: Cat Smith (Chair); Bambos Charalambous; Sir Christopher Chope; Mary Kelly Foy; Gurinder Singh Josan; John Lamont; Mr Tom Morrison; Lee Pitcher; Kenneth Stevenson.
Education Committee Chair present: Helen Hayes.
Questions 48- 78
Witnesses
I : Josh MacAlister OBE MP, Minister for Children and Families, and Tony Foot, Chief Operating Officer and Director General of Strategy and Operations Group at the Department for Education .
Examination of Witnesses
Witnesses: Josh MacAlister and Tony Foot.

Welcome to this afternoon’s public session of the Procedure Committee. Written parliamentary questions, WPQs for short, are an important tool for MPs in raising public interest and dealing with much of their constituency work, and our Committee routinely monitors the performance of Whitehall Departments in responding to WPQs in a timely manner. Where performance dips below a certain threshold, we ask Government Ministers and officials to come before us to explain any issues and set out their plans to resolve them.

This afternoon, we are joined by Josh MacAlister, the Minister for Children and Families, and Tony Foot, the chief operating officer from the Department for Education, to discuss the Department’s WPQ performance over the last Session of Parliament. Good afternoon to you both. Before we begin questions, please will you formally introduce yourselves for the record, starting with Minister MacAlister?
I am Josh MacAlister, the Minister for Children and Families, and the Member of Parliament for Whitehaven and Workington.
Hello, I am Tony Foot, the chief operating officer for the Department for Education.

Q48 Thank you both so much for your time this afternoon. As is traditional, the first question comes from me. In the last Session of Parliament, there was a significant drop in the DFE’s performance in responding to WPQs in a timely manner. Could you shed some light on the factors underpinning that drop?

Thank you to the Committee for the opportunity to come before you and explain a bit about the Department’s performance. As a Minister, I recognise the importance of the parliamentary questions process and the need for replies to be accurate, detailed and timely. The Department for Education’s performance is poor, and I am not coming to you today to make any defence of it. It is not good enough, and the whole ministerial team are determined to get it back up to where it needs to be.

There are a number of causes of the deterioration in the response rate; some—volumes and the changing policy and legislative landscape—are contextual factors, and I will not spend any time talking about them, because you will have heard about them from other Departments. However, there are particular process challenges in the Department for Education, and I will briefly set out the changes we are making to get back up to timeliness. Essentially, those challenges bottlenecks in the process that mean that too many responses are not coming through when they should.

There are four key areas of action and, with Tony, I am happy to elaborate on them in more detail. First, we are streamlining the process. Some of those changes have already come into effect, which has allowed us to stop the deterioration of the response rate and achieve a slight improvement in recent weeks. That is welcome, but it is nowhere near where it needs to be, so further streamlining of the process needs to be done.

Secondly, we want to increase the visibility of teams’ performance and have greater accountability across the Department for resolving the bottlenecks and ensuring the quality of answers is where it needs to be. Thirdly, there is the introduction of a new case management system. The Department is using an older system than other Departments, and we are going through the process of putting a new one in place. That will be in place by September this year, which will improve the system.

Finally, there is temporary additional resource to ensure that we get back up to responding in the expected time. Although the Department’s view is that the situation is not the result of resource constraint per se, we do need additional resource in the next couple of months to get this issue fixed.

The commitment I am making on behalf of the Department is that we will be back up to 85% by the end of November. I will be in touch with the Committee between now and then with updates on the progress we are making.

Q49 You mentioned the increased volume, which we have seen across the board for all Government Departments. Is there anything specific to your Department that means you have particularly struggled, whereas other Departments have managed the increased volume and still met expectations? Other than what you have set out already, is there anything specific to your Department that means that that been particularly challenging?

There is nothing specific to the Department. I have seen the evidence given to your Committee by Department of Health Ministers, and there were very similar issues about new policy and policies on fairly controversial areas, where there is a lot of constituency contact with MPs offices, which cascades through into lots of written parliamentary questions being asked.

To take just one example, the SEND policy landscape, and adoption, which is my field, there have been considerable spikes in volumes. New policies have been adopted, which has required quite a lot of back and forth and, in some cases, rewrites. The rewrites rate has gone down, which is good. The proportion of answers provided by officials to spads and Ministers that are being redrafted has reduced, but it is still too high. Building confidence in the system for giving accurate responses within the narrow timeframe we have requires a system that is really slick, so that questions can move through and be answered quickly. That is what we need to address.

Q50 On the transition to the new casework system, you said you would like to get back to target performance by November. That system is coming in up until September. In the scenario planning, have you thought through the risks associated with bringing in a new system? If any of those risks were to materialise, would it detrimentally impact the November target?

Tony will come in on this, but the system is being used by other Government Departments, so it is not novel. I am confident we can make good progress between now and September on improving timeliness. The Department used to be high performing on response rates using the current system. There is now a higher volume, but we should be able to make progress even without the new system.

We are working with other Departments to learn from systems that they have introduced. We have seen Departments get some real benefits—about 20% in terms of processing efficiency—from automated downloads of PQs and automated grouping of PQs. We are following and learning from other Departments that have done this and done this well. As the Minister says, the plan does not solely rely on that element; there is a series of other elements that really matter. We know we can do it even without the system, but the system will really help.

Q51 Good afternoon, Minister, and Mr Foot. I was going to ask about when you expect to get back to the 85% level, but you have confirmed that, hopefully, it is going to be in November. Can you explain what the process is within the Department? The question comes in and it goes to the policy people in the Department to draft a response; it then goes to spads before it gets to the Minister. Can you talk us through the process, please?

I will go through the key stages of the process and then talk about the challenges and timeliness of each of those. Broadly, we look at four key blocks. There is an allocation process out to policy teams. It is important that that happens quickly so that the PQs get through to the drafting teams. The second part of the process is securing responses from those teams on time. It is quicker for named day PQs than it is for ordinary PQs, but we have clear deadlines for both of those processes. There is then a spad and ministerial clearance process. Across the whole of the cycle we look carefully at redraft rates, because redrafts add time to the process and, as the Minister says, it can undermine confidence in quality, which makes it harder for cases to flow through seamlessly.
Q52 Can you identify the bottleneck that has been causing the drop in performance? Are the rewrites that you mentioned the main issue?

I can go through the different stages of that. In the allocation process, we are relatively rapid, with 95% of cases allocated to teams on time. We still have challenges with cases that are particularly cross-cutting, and we are taking further action on those, but at that stage of the process, we are relatively strong.

We have made progress on policy teams drafting responses on time, but we want to go further on that. There are some bottlenecks at the spad and ministerial stage that we will go through. The redrafts are critical. We were at around 19% redrafts in the second half of last year. We got that down to 12% at the beginning of this year, but we want that to drop further because, as I say, every one of those redrafts is additional time in the process and has an impact on confidence in the sequence overall.

Q53 Analysing what you just said and thinking back to my time in Government, sometimes there were issues with spads and the Minister sitting on responses and not signing them off quickly enough. Is that an issue?

From my own perspective, I have responses for colleagues who ask questions about my portfolio, which are in some senses slightly easier to move through quickly. The volume that I am responsible for is much lower than, for example, Minister Gould’s. She has responsibility for the curriculum and SEND, where the volumes are extremely high, particularly at certain times of the year. There is a need at the moment for spads to clear all PQs and for that then to go to Ministers. If there is a problem with the content that needs to go back and be rewritten, or a clarification question needs to be asked, or a spad is out of action for a few hours, you can quickly end up with responses arriving with Ministers on the day they are due. If, as I have today, there are commitments in the diary that mean you span the full day, you are basically timing out sign-off. So building in enough time earlier in the process to make sure that stuff moves through is important.

The other element is where the question relates to a Lords Minister’s portfolio. I cover Baroness Smith’s portfolio—I am answerable for it in the Commons. I clear all her PQ responses to MPs about higher and further education, which is not my portfolio area. They have been cleared already by spads and Minister Smith, and then by me. Actually it is quite hard to get allocation, policy response, spad clearance, Minister and Minister approved, with diaries as they are. We need to improve some of those processes. I alluded to this earlier: we need to improve confidence in the system, so that fewer people need to eyeball everything. That will be a big part of resolving some of the bottlenecks.

Q54 Will the new system address that? It will not create any new Ministers or new spads to help with that process. It just strikes me that, ultimately, there is only so much capacity at that bit of the process. I do not know whether the new system will address that.

The new system is just one of four things that we need to do. The system we are using at the moment is quite old. It has not been updated for a number of years. Other Departments use systems that are better at doing the allocation and the tracking—you can see the timeliness in a more transparent way, which helps the system to move through more quickly. All that is not an excuse. Our performance is nowhere near where it needs to be, but the volume of PQs with the Department has doubled from 2024 to 2025. The approach that we have at the moment cannot handle that volume. The bottlenecks have just grown, which is why the performance is on the floor and needs to be improved.
Q55 How will you ensure that efforts to improve the timeliness of responses do not lead to lower-quality answers?

That is a really important question. As the Minister said, quality and timeliness can and should go hand in hand. Ministers rightly have very high expectations of the quality of responses that go back to parliamentary colleagues, and the higher the quality, the better able we are to secure timely responses.

The actions we are taking on quality specifically are in two main blocks. First, we have significantly strengthened and improved the guidance and the WPQ templates, so that they absolutely reflect the latest set of ministerial preferences and the best practice in other Departments. Then we work very closely to watch the redraft rate to make sure that we target teams that have high levels of redrafting with training and support, so that they are able to improve. Alongside the system, that is one of the key things that will improve the pace of cases moving through the whole chain.

I relate this back to engineering, and I think that the modern methodology is to make sure that the quality is inbuilt all the way through and is not just inspected right at the end. You seem to be doing that, and you have that iterative cycle, where you look at it again. Good, thank you.
We are delighted that Helen Hayes, the Chair of the Education Committee, is guesting on the Procedure Committee this afternoon. Helen, I think you have some questions.

Q56 Thank you very much for having me, Chair. I am glad to be here. Minister, you have mentioned a couple of times the role of automation in improving the Department’s response rate. Can you tell us a bit more about what automation looks like in this context?

Yes. The new system offers an opportunity to build in some AI functionality. Tony will come in on the potential of the new system coming in in September, but it is very limited, if of any use, at the moment in either the WPQ process or the Department’s correspondence process. In my view, where we have a clear repository of information and of policy positions that the Department has taken, directing large language models at that content in order to generate first drafts and accurate information—if it can speed things up—I would be personally very supportive of. The use of that could allow for us to have highly accurate information on the table to be looked at by people, and to be cleared much more quickly and in a less resource-intensive way. Tony, do you want to say anything more?

Absolutely, yes. On automation opportunities, the biggest gains for other Departments have been the automated download and the automated grouping and processing at the first stage of the process. We have seen other Departments secure much better information on the challenges and blockages at each stage of the system, so again we can take that information and feed it back into the process engineering that colleagues have described.

Looking ahead, AI definitely has significant potential to source data more quickly and effectively, albeit it is always a really important principle that answers are human-driven and human-owned for accountability.

Q57 There is a huge debate within the Department’s remit of responsibility about the use of AI in the education system, and there are concerns about the potential that we end up with work that has been generated by AI being marked by applications that use AI. We could cut out human interaction from much of the process of education if we do not get this right.

What principles are you applying to decision making in this process? We would all agree that our constituents expect to see bona fide responses from a Minister, reflecting the judgment of the Minister and the policy position of the Government—not something that a machine has spat out to meet a deadline and improve performance in the Department.

There are a couple of things to say. There is a functionality distinction between our use and the role that AI could and should play in the education system—I imagine that topic was discussed at the Education Committee meeting this morning. That goes beyond the brief of this session. There are really important factors around cognitive offloading, the challenge that you need in the system for children, the marking of children’s work, and the role that feedback can have for children through teacher-pupil interaction.

That is a completely different function to what a lot of PQs represent, which is an information trawl. Lots of PQs that I receive and sign off are specific questions about data points that are in files or links on other Government sources. AI could assist with identifying that and presenting it quickly, and then it would be approved and signed off by a series of human beings before it gets released.

My view is that, in time, the public would look increasingly dimly on Government Departments and agencies not making full use of technology where it can create more efficient processes that save them tax money—these processes are all expensive—and deliver more efficient, quick and transparent public services. The principle would be that where automation can speed up processes that humans would take longer to do, we will use it with human judgment and sign-off baked into it. That is the approach that I would expect the Department to take.

Q58 Thank you. Are you looking at any other measures that could help to streamline those processes? It would be helpful to hear a bit more about where the bottlenecks are. Is it Ministers signing off? Is it the drafting capacity? What are the stages?

Tony can say a bit more about this, but across the four buckets of the process, there is an accumulation of delay that gathers through them—some more so than in other areas. With Ministers and spads, the accumulation is greater. They are at the end of the process, so to some extent you might expect that, but it accumulates through. Tony, do you want to say a bit more about the four areas where we are putting changes in place to meet the target?
Absolutely. We have talked about the system, and I will not repeat that. The Minister talked about two areas: streamlining processes and raising visibility and accountability.

On the streamlining processes part, we are doing three things. The first is improving the spad clearance process by more clearly marking cases that are particularly urgent and helping spads to triage more effectively so that cases can move automatically on to Ministers and we do not squeeze the ministerial clearance time. There will be more frequent meetings between the WPQ team and the private office so that we have a real-time feedback loop on process challenges and any quality issues, and then we will share a daily lates report. Every day, information is shared across the private office set for all PQs that are late and the reasons for that so that we are learning in real time about those areas.

On accountability and raising visibility within the Department, there are two further steps that we are taking. First, the permanent secretary holds regular accountability meetings with each of her directors general. Performance on WPQs will be a standing item in that until we are back up to 85%. We are also going to use S C S forums each month to call out and celebrate the teams that are doing this well and give them a chance to discuss and talk through the things that are working for them as well as to challenge and call out the teams that are performing poorly.

Q59 On occasion, my Committee has been frustrated at late responses we have received to our reports from the Department. We perceive a tendency for the Department to wait until it has got all the answers, or it is a convenient moment to respond to the Committee. That is not how accountability is supposed to work.

There are timescales attached to Committee responses regarding the accountability process and the role of Back-Bench MPs and Committees in bringing information into the public domain and holding the Department to account. It is not for the Department to hold on to those responses until it is ready to provide them. Within the process we are talking about for questions, I wonder whether some of the delay is about that tendency to hold on to things until you have an answer that you are ready and want to give rather than the more bureaucratic issues that you have discussed already?

In my experience, it definitely is not. The Department’s view is that we want to respond within the timeframe set and the expectation there. There are sometimes very inconvenient questions where you think that if the Committee had asked that next week, I would have been able to give them a fuller answer. However, we definitely do not hold them back. We are not in a good place on our performance with this, and we want to get it back up to the right place and would prioritise doing that over having the more convenient moment through which to answer. I will take on board your broader point about Select Committee responses; you make an entirely reasonable point.

Q60 In your view, what are the particular difficulties posed by named day questions compared to ordinary questions? Are there any suggestions around actions that could be taken to overcome those difficulties?

Our performance on named day questions is even worse than on normal written questions because it takes time away from the bottlenecks that we have in the standard process. It is a more acute issue. In answer to previous questions, Tony described how we have tried to compress those timescales for named day questions. All the four actions that have been set out will help with both types of questions being answered in a timely fashion.
Q61 Given that named day questions caused such difficulties, do you think that that distinction should be maintained?

As an MP, no, I do not think so. There are few and far between moments where you would need an answer at that pace. On balance, thinking about what matters most for the parliamentary process and Parliament undertaking its functions—for accuracy and speed and getting the balance right—my view is that one model with one set of expectations would be reasonable.

Q62 Our inquiry has found that some Departments are performing better than others, even with significant increases of volume. For instance, the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero has a near 100% on-time response rate across both categories. Have you worked with any other Departments to share best practice or do you know of any channels where Departments can share those kinds of things?

We have not done enough of that, otherwise we would be in a better place now. However, we are really alive to this. Neither myself as the Minister nor Tony as the official are here today to say that we have had it really tough and the volume means that it is not in a great place and then to make excuses. It is nowhere near where it needs to be, and we have it within our own powers between now and November to get it back to where it needs to be. Part of that is looking at Departments that are getting it right and duplicating what they are doing.

We are chairing a cross-Government WPQ network, so we are very well placed to learn and to collaborate with other Departments. We have done that very consciously. The system step we are taking is very much informed by lessons and learning from other Government Departments, and it is similar with the other steps I have described on clearances, raising visibility and accountability. We are, for example, talking closely with DESNZ.

Q63 You may be aware that we have a much broader inquiry under way on WPQs; we are seeing the Leader of the House next week to conclude it. There is a set of terms of reference for that, and I wonder whether you have any views on those.
I have not seen the terms of reference. Are there particular parts that you would be interested in?

We have asked a similar question to a number of people who have come to see us as part of the other inquiry. It would be good to get your feedback on them to see whether there is anything missing or anything you think would be particularly important. I assume, Chair, we might be able to get them sent out.

Q64 Absolutely. If it is easier, Minister, we could write to you and perhaps get something in writing. We are looking broadly at written parliamentary questions and how they are used, and we are interested in your experience as a Minister answering them in terms of volume. We are aware that Departments across the board, not just DFE, have seen an increase in volume. We know that a lot of them are struggling with maintaining timely responses and the power of Back Benchers to hold Government Ministers to account, but, at the same time, getting quality answers back. It is much broader than just the timescale thing; we are looking at how we can perhaps do things differently. We are happy to write to you about that.

That would be great. My perspective is only from the Department for Education, but the issues of written parliamentary questions and correspondence are often seen as one and the same. We manage and respond to them in a similar way, and some of the challenges we have with WPQs are similar to the challenges we have with correspondence in terms of bottlenecks, timeliness and quality. They are a really important mechanism where you can often elaborate more and ask more questions of Ministers, and the majority of that correspondence is from MPs. I am happy to share feedback, but it may well be worth widening the net to look at correspondence between parliamentarians and Ministers as well as the formal WPQ process.
Q65 If you could change one aspect of the WPQ system for the Commons, what would it be?

My answer to Mary’s question probably covers that. A simple thing would be to move to one model with one set of expectations. There are some characters who ask lots of questions. My one wish would probably be to see some of those volumes drop, but that may encourage the opposite effect.
Q66 When you say just one model, do you mean getting rid of the named day questions?
Yes.

Q67 Can I dig a bit further into the delays that are caused by Ministers and/or spads looking at these questions and then rejecting them? It is a very high figure—19%, although you said you got it down to 12%. Are those rejections being made by spads or by Ministers?
The 19%—which bit of the process does that sit in?
That is the spad stage of the process, and 12% go back at that stage.
Q68 What about the Minister stage of the process?
I do not have that statistic with me, but it is a significantly lower number than that.

Q69 Going back a few years, when I was a Minister, we did not have spads, so the Ministers took responsibility. Would it not improve the process, the timeliness and the accuracy if spads were not in the way? The Ministers decide the policy, they look at the answer that has been drafted by officials, and if they see an issue arising from it, they can refer it to a spad if need be. Why don’t you cut the spads out of the process and let Ministers take responsibility and control?
How many— Well, I am not here to ask you questions, Sir Christopher, but I would imagine that you had a considerably lower volume of questions being asked.
In answer to that: no, I did not, because I was the junior Minister for the poll tax, or community charge. I think I probably had more questions than any Minister in the Government at that time.
I can imagine your answers. [ Laughter. ]

Q70 One of the issues that caused a lot of the questions was that, because the policy was being developed, nobody knew the details of it. One of the problems that you will have in the next six or nine months is what exactly is involved in the social media ban. It seems to have been produced a bit off the hoof, so isn’t that going to generate an enormous number of additional questions? Will you need to bring in extra resources, or will you just need to be clearer about your policy?

The social media ban is a DSIT policy, but there may well be questions that drift into DFE’s policy responsibility space. Taking the substance of your question, the volumes mean that it is extremely difficult to have no special adviser process built into the response to WPQs. Officials overwhelmingly do a really efficient job of articulating, from their area of responsibility, the position of the Government at the time, but you will know that many policy areas go beyond the remit of the policy official who is responding.

Having somebody who has a wider departmental view and a view of the politics, which is what we are all engaged in here—I do not mean that in a glib way—of what the Department is trying to do and whether that is expressed in the answer that is being given is an important part of the process. Were that to rest simply with Ministers, they would be out of action for a considerably larger amount of time—which may well be something that Members are happy about.

Q71 Drilling into that, what do you mean they would be out of action for a considerable amount of time? All you mean is that they would have more stuff in their red box overnight and they would have to work a bit harder.
Correct; that is what I mean.
Q72 Yes, so you are ducking out of working as hard as you could.

I don’t accept that. There are finite hours in the week, even with colleagues who work 60 or 70-plus hours. The allocation of time is a reflection of the allocation of priority. WPQs are an important part of the priority of being a Minister, but they are not the only part, and it needs to be balanced in a measured and sensible way, as I think most Members would expect. The spad process is an important part of it.
Q73 Do you ever overrule the spad? Or does the spad tell you if he or she has rejected that question on your behalf and had it redrafted? I want to get a handle on it somehow.

Very rarely. I cannot think of questions where I have looked at the answer, not been happy with the feedback from the special adviser and gone back around the loop. Some of these questions drill into important parts of Government policy, which, if not totally clear, deserve some conversation and dialogue. That is no bad thing, and in many respects, it may well be what Members are seeking by putting a parliamentary question in.

On the process side, from an officials and process perspective, we are trying to make sure that the spad clearance process is as efficient as possible, so there is much greater marking and indication of what is most urgent, and an automatic progression point for cases to move on to Ministers so that we are not squeezing the ministerial time.

Sir Christopher, you made a point about the bulge of issues as they come through—for example, SEND reforms. There is an important role for—Tony referred to this—making sure that the policy teams are really well prepped for being super - clear on the evolving policy position of important , high - profile areas where the volume is high , b ecause otherwise we get swamped and responses are delayed.

Q74 Would it be unfair to characterise what you are saying as that, essentially , Ministers are delegating to their special advisers the role that they as Ministers should have , in a lot of the policymaking?
No.
Q75 In that case, why are n’t the questions coming direct ly from officials to Ministers?

In the same way as Ministers do not draft the first draft of an answer , there is a process that involves delegation , because Ministers do not do , end to end , the running of D epartments, as you well know.

Q76 But special advisers are not civil servants ; they are political appointees. What I am saying is : why can ’t you rely o n the civil servants to produce an answer and then you, as the Minister, look at it and see whether it is properly drafted and reflects your policy ? If you did away with the special advisers — you have said , in your evidence , that sometimes the special advisers are on sick leave or annual leave or whatever it is called , and that therefore that delays the process. Surely the absence of a special adviser should not delay the process in any circumstances.
I disagree. Tony, h ow many officials do we have in the DFE— 6 , 000 ?
About 7 , 000.

And we have four or five spads and five Ministers. The ratio of officials , who are not party political , to appointees , who are able to express the will of the Government , is very imbalanced . The resource allocation of th at time needs to be put into the things that are most important , and that is a combination of special advisers and Ministers working as part of a political team to pursue the agenda of the Government of the day. That is more than right and proper.

Q77 Just one final question : can you assure us that you as a Minister, when you answer a p arliamentary question, have read the question , read the answer and physically approved it yourself , rather than delegat ed that to a s pad ?
Correct.

Q78 I want to delve a bit more into planning ahead . Sorry, these figures might not be exact , but if you go back a couple of decades, we were talking about 30 letters per week for an MP , whereas we know we get about 200 emails per day now. T h e volume just at an MP’s office has substantially changed . If we look at the figures for what is coming to the D epartment, there was, from the 2023-24 Session to the ’ 24 - 26 Session, an 89% increase in volumes. So much more is coming in.

You talked about planning ahead. You wish you had talked to some of the other D epartments about some of the things they have put in place , in order to learn from that best practice. In terms of the exponential increase in numbers that we see nowadays, are you ready for the level coming in to be sustained? Basically, are you planning for that increase remaining the same now, because it becomes the new norm ?

Yes, and the actions that we are putting in place are designed to enable us to do that. The other thing I would say is that, alongside this , it is obviously really important that we are continuing to make publicly available information more accessible, more usable , and more possible for colleagues , p arliamentarians and citizens to download and use. To give one example of that , we have invested a lot in our E xplore e ducation statistics service, which now basically , for all DF E data, allows you to download tailored cuts of data , based on your own parameters. We continue to invest in those services that make it possible to access information directly , rather than people having to ask for it.
T hat brings us to the end of our questions. If you would like to add anything, please feel free to write to the Committee and we will make sure that we look at that promptly.
