Examination of witnesses
David Abraham, Jane Tranter and Nigel Warner.

Q22 I would like to welcome our second panel of witnesses. In this part of the session, we are interested in exploring some issues raised by the BBC charter Green Paper from the perspective of independent production companies. Could you please start by introducing yourselves and telling us a little about the organisations you represent?

Good afternoon, Chair. Thank you very much for inviting me to speak this afternoon. I am the chief executive of Pact, the Producers Alliance for Cinema and Television. We represent the independent production community all around the UK. I have been in the post for two months and am very pleased to be here.

I am the CEO and co-founder of an independent production company called Bad Wolf. Bad Wolf is notable for two things, not including its name; you can tell me later if you recognise where the name comes from. The first is that we are one of the UK’s leading independent drama producers and the second is that we are based in Wales. Bad Wolf has been in existence for nearly 11 years and our presence in the nation and regions—specifically Wales’s impact on Bad Wolf—is significant.

Good afternoon. I am the founder of a company called Wonderhood Studios. We operate in London, have about 100 employees and work at the intersection of the creation of premium content for channels, streamers and the advertising industry.
Q23 How would you describe the health of the UK independent production sector currently and what are the main pressures facing producers?

In my first couple of months, I have been travelling all around the country, meeting Pact members and independent producers based in the nations and regions of the UK. It is fairly safe to say that most are experiencing significant financial pressures at the moment . It is a tough time in the marketplace. There are some reasons for that. One is that there is a significant amount of uncertainty at senior levels in most of our main public service organisations at the moment and obviously over the longer-term future of the BBC.

The public service broadcasting world—ITV, Channel 4, Channel 5 and the BBC—accounts for about 80% of all the money that is spent on independent production and original content in the UK. It is a very important part of the market for my members, and all those organisations are in a state of flux at the moment for one reason or another. That creates quite a lot of uncertainty but there are also the longer-term trend s of the decline in advertising revenues for the main PSBs and that the BBC is about £1 billion worse off today than it was a decade ago.

The financial pressures are cascading down the marketplace and affecting commissions for all our members, which is raising significant challenges for them. They are a highly resourceful bunch and are looking at ways to address those pressures —i nnovating, raising finance and all the rest of it. But it is fair to say it is a tough climate out there at the moment .

It is an interesting one. If you were to ask what the health of the UK’s production economy is, you would say it is actually quite buoyant, but I agree with Nigel that the health of the UK’s independent production sector is suffering some significant challenges. According to some recent BFI statistics, there is increased investment year-on-year in high-end television—where I specialise in production in the UK—coming from big American shows that come over here to film. Money should be spent by genuinely UK-based independent producers who are making stories in the UK for every part of the UK , and they are very cash-strapped.

Remember that I am really looking at this through the lens of a drama producer. There are crises in three areas: funding, sustainability and creativity. The crisis in funding comes from the fact that the budgets for high-end television have more than doubled over the past few years and yet the public service broadcaster’s licence fees have roughly held the same. What this means for an independent production company is that , when you get a commission for a drama from, for example, the BBC, one thing you know right from the start is that the licence fee will not cover the entirety of your making of the show. You then have to go out and raise money elsewhere in order to put that together with the BBC’s licence fee, throw in the UK tax credit, and hope somehow that you will get to the figure that works.

Recently the opportunities for funding outside the UK have really narrowed —for two reasons. First, normally the greatest part of that money comes from America. Partly with the increasing merger and homogeneity of some companies, those opportunities for individual pieces of co-production funding have lessened. Secondly, those American companies that would and are still able to invest and partner with the BBC are not interested in UK content in the same way that they were. We are finding that America is beginning to look into itself culturally ; it is more interested in Americana than it is in our UK stories.

There are good news examples—one being “ The Other Bennet Sister ” —where you find a way of fighting your way through. It really is a battleground and means that every time you go to the BBC for funding, you know perfectly well that the BBC will green - light it and that that is the beginning, not the end of its journey. That is what we are paid to do; that is our task, but it is harder than it ever was and means that there are fewer opportunities for British indies to be able to find that funding.

The sustainability point is around rights. Increasingly for independent production companies, the old-fashioned way of doing things, if you like—where you would get a UK licence fee and hold on to and use those rights to go and raise the money around the rest of the world—does not happen anymore in the streaming economy. I am sure you will have questions about that so I will not go into too much detail. Suffice to say, it means that the Labour Party’s 2003 terms of trade , which the whole of the UK independent production sector was built from, is being eroded because independents no longer hold on to the rights in the same way. That means it is not sustainable as a business because you are not having any growth put into your business.

Inevitably the third outcome from those first two things is creativity because , when you are looking to develop a project and to tell stories about the way we live now, you have to look to develop them with an eye to how we are going to get this funded. That means that some stories that are really important to us to share as a nation are no longer getting told, either because producers feel, “Well, I’m never going to get it off the ground”, and a form of self-censorship happens or they simply cannot get it off the ground because there is no longer the market available that there once was.

Q24 I was going to ask a question about how global stream er s have changed the economies of independent production , but I will come to David first. You can start us off on that or answer the subsequent question.

Just building on what Jane and Nigel have said, in answering the health question there are three layers. The really vibrant , healthy part of the creative economy in video production—let us not talk about TV as a traditional subset but video—is the creator economy. The creator economy employs and generates wealth for far more people in this country today than the traditional TV industry, which is a good thing. It has been created by the availability of YouTube and social media platforms that have revolutionised the way that creative people reach an audience.

In our industry—I suppose the more conventional, linear part of the industry—we are looking to that community to contribute to the world we are in. One of the biggest cinema launches of the last few days is a movie that comes from a 19 year-old who was a star on YouTube. We are living in a very buoyant, interesting, creative era in terms of the creative economy. Clearly, the premium end of television production remains very buoyant because the tariffs are very high. If you are fortunate to be in a position to get those commissions—hard though they are to win—then there is revenue to be generated.

The collapse has been in the middle area of the industry where people could set up a business at relatively low barriers to entry, produce some maybe inexpensive programming in daytime or teatime, and then over the years build credibility and start doing bigger shows. That conveyor belt of creativity has been broken and has forced a lot of people out of the industry. The freelance community that relied on those types of programmes is now almost giving up and permanently out of work. There is a big structural change. The question for us all is perhaps not to look back but to build on the strengths of what we have, both as a country and in particular the strengths of the BBC and other public service broadcasters.
Jane and Nigel, do you want to add anything on that second point I raised about how the rise of global streamers has changed the economics of independent production?

I understand David’s point but there is the reality that the industry that I represent and the companies that are involved in that industry constitute something like around £3.5 billion a year. It is still a big industry and a very important part of the television and audiovisual industry. Many of those people are exploring all sorts of opportunities on new platforms, YouTube and other places, but most people are finding that the revenue opportunities there are quite limited at the moment , as your witnesses demonstrated to you in the previous session.

Jane made the point that the streamers are an important part of the inward investment that has come into the UK. Successive Governments have done significant things to attract investment from international players and that has become a very important part of the mix. As I said at the beginning, we must not get away from the fact that 80% of the money that is going into commissions in the UK for television and television content comes from the public service broadcasters. We cannot just abandon all that as if it is some part of the past and move into something that we think is the future because actually it is still and will continue to be very important. I hope one outcome of this charter review process is to give the BBC the strength to continue to be a very important part of that story.

Q25 Jane, you talked about the difficulty with funding. Probably the most critically acclaimed recent British independent production was “Adolescence”, which was made on a streamer by Jack Thorne, a collaborator of yours on “His Dark Materials”. Is that an example of British talent having to go to the streamers because they just have more funding?

I would say that is an example of how good the streamers can be. I agree with the last point that Nigel made : just because the streamers are growing and having a great deal of success—both creatively and economically—does not mean that we are all going in that direction. It simply means that public service broadcasting, in particular the BBC, needs to be protected. The world is changing and therefore the BBC needs to have change accompany it.

We are very fortunate in the UK because we have very strong UK commissioners in Netflix and Apple. While in the UK you have access to everything that, for example, Netflix and Apple have to offer, they have very strong teams. A lot of our best dramas—for example , “Slow Horses”, “Adolescence” and “Baby Reindeer”—have come from those places and are quintessential British pieces of drama. They are the minority and may have a public service value to them , but they are not made from that point and purpose of the public service; they are made for very different reasons.
Interestingly, they have employed writers, actors, producers and directors, all of whom—
They have grown through the BBC.

They have grown through the system —exactly. If you are thinking about the ecosystem of creativity that the country is nurturing 10 or 20 years in the future, I suspect it will come far more from the world of YouTube than the world of traditional television.
John McVay must be a hard act to follow.
Nigel Warner : I have been told that many times.
But you are still here after two months so you are doing well.
Nigel Warner : Exactly!

Q26 I am not trying to undermine that. I have said this before so there will probably be groans from the rest of the committee. I was on the Puttnam committee that looked at the 1983 Act and one of the most successful pieces of lobbying then was to extend the market for the independent producers, which Pact became very successful in representing. The only drawback is that although John’s strongest message to legislators was that he was working for people working in garrets in Glasgow and other places to produce this good work, the creatives were very quickly gobbled up by international companies and even the independent sector was very difficult to see as promoting British values.

At the moment , I am interested in the way the BBC is promoting itself, particularly with its drama productions, for example “Blue Lights” in Northern Ireland and the other regional-based drama productions, which are still part of the great strength of BBC drama. It is very difficult to see how it is able to sustain that, as you say, with it having to look for funding from a wide variety of sources, most of which will—one suspects—demand a watering - down of the distinctive regional contribution to the blander sell-it-in-any-market contribution.

How do you think the BBC is sustaining the UK’s independent production sector. Is it too big a burden for the BBC? Are there reasonably sensible changes in legislation that would help that independent sector as they did with the 1983 Act?

One thing I can reassure you on—having gone around the country and been at lots of members’ meetings—is that there are lots of substantial companies that have grown out of the very fertile environment that was created around independent production and that is the envy of the world, quite frankly. But t here are also still plenty of very small businesses: more than 80% of independent producers in the UK are SMEs where turnover is lower than £25 million a year. There are very small companies growing all the time. It is still a very mixed sector with some very big players but a very long tail. My job is to represent all those interests.

The role of the BBC in relation to the nations and regions’ production is particularly critical. More than a third of all the commissioning revenues outside London among independent producers comes from the BBC , so it is a very big player in that marketplace. The relationship between the BBC and the independent producers is very important. A message that I have had from members over these last couple of months is that they want to see that relationship improved. They would like—the BBC is minded or thinking in this direction—to see more power, authority and finance devolved down to local commissioning centres, which already exist in Northern Ireland, Wales, Scotland and elsewhere, to people on the ground who have close relationships with independent producers to be able to streamline the commissioning processes.

As Jane mentioned, one of the most difficult things for our members at the moment is partly a financing issue but also just the length of time that commissioning decisions are taking because the BBC’s processes are complex. That just causes huge cash flow issues for our companies. While they are going around raising money from whatever sources they can find to do so, they are having to pay their staff, run their offices and develop ideas, all of which cost money. The more streamlined we can make those processes, the better.

The other thing I would say is that it is not just the BBC; there are other players in the marketplace that are helping and supporting independent production. The screen agencies Creative Wales, Northern Ireland Screen and Screen Scotland are all putting money into helping to support local businesses, develop ideas and develop their local creative industries, particularly their screen sectors. They all see the opportunities that their local screen sectors provide in terms of jobs for local people , but it has to be on a sustainable basis. You need a good long-term relationship with the commissioning organisations and that is really the role that the BBC can crucially and increasingly play , in my view.

Q27 What about intellectual property? One of you—I cannot remember who—mentioned that in raising money for a project, the intellectual property has to be signed away if not given away by the original initiators to be able to raise—

It does not have to be with the BBC. With streamers, the rights situation is different. That is one way that the BBC has worked hard to support independent production companies: it has recognised that you need to hold on to the rights in order to be able to raise the rest of the money for you to make your show.
Is that the difference in how it works ? W ith the BBC you retain your rights; with the streamers you do not .
Yes.
With Channel 4 as well.

And ITV. Can I just return to your point about nations and regions? I have a slightly different view about the BBC and its relationship with the nations and regions. I am obviously not Welsh , but I have a very long association with Wales that started in 2003 when I was controller of drama commissioning at the BBC and I made the decision to make “Doctor Who” from Cardiff.

What I discovered then was the importance of doing one thing of great strength. For example , rather than try to grow lots of small flowers and hope you are going to have a big impact, you actually keep those flowers growing but do not put too much pressure on them and allow something bigger to blossom there. During the period of time that I was at the BBC, drama in Wales grew and grew. One of the last things I did as controller of drama commissioning was to move “Casualty” from Bristol to Cardiff in order to ensure that that cluster in Cardiff was going to survive.

I then went to work in the US from 2009 to 2015. I worked a lot in New York , where I began to meet a lot of the crews and t eamsters who are based there. I discovered that their jobs—those local crew jobs—were generational jobs. They were passed down, normally from father to son; I would like to see mother to daughter. That really struck a chord with me. One of my grandfathers was a coal miner and the other was a mill worker. Both those jobs have been in their families for generations; it came to my parents’ generation and they were gone.

I began to look at New York and think, "Well, if you can do that in New York, why can’t you do that in Cardiff? If you come with a position of strength, why can you not grow a creative cluster just as an independent production company?” I started Bad Wolf in complete association with Creative Wales; you are right about how important those screen agencies are. We started strategic partnerships with people in the local community. With schools, we built a studio and we have a classroom in the studio. With universities, suppliers and all sorts of satellite business es around our business , the production started . Over the past 10 years, we have put hundreds of millions of pounds and the equivalent of 11,000 full-time employees into the Welsh economy. In so doing, it has just created a whole new way of doing things.

We all pretend we can , but we cannot get away from the fact that London is where the theatres are, therefore the actors are, therefore the agents are, and many—not all—writers are. It should not matter anymore where someone is placed. What matters is how much care and attention you are giving to the people, the creative industry and the stories that they are telling in that nation and region. I feel that it is not necessarily about devolving power to a Welsh-based commissioner but forming strategic partnerships with the independent production companies that are there, both the big ones such as Bad Wolf and the smaller ones, to work together with the universities, as your previous witnesses were talking about. It is about working together to strengthen on the ground, not from a grander, “Let me give you this money”, but actually from the practitioners from the grass roots up.

In fairness to the BBC, I have always had to get co-production money but have made “His Dark Materials” with the BBC and HBO, “Industry” with the BBC and HBO, “Dope Girls” with the BBC and Hulu, and recently “The Other Bennet Sister” with the BBC and BritBox. It has really supported us in that area along with Creative Wales and , in so doing , has enabled us to help grow that area. There is no one-size-fits-all answer of, “We’ll build a new block in Salford and everyone will come”; they will come only if you have the right people there.
Do you think the BBC gets enough credit for that?
Tom, we need to move on. We have three more questions. Could I come to you, Baroness Caine?

Q28 Yes , and it is linked actually; you have already started to talk about issues that my question relates to. Basically we are just talking now about whether the BBC should have a new public purpose to support growth and the broader creative economy. Within that, what should it actually encourage ? It is interesting that you were just talking about the drama situation and linking it to the questions earlier, which you were here for. I am also interested in some narrow er genres that we were talking about: the diversity of genre and smaller companies that are producing around things such as arts, daytime et cetera. David, could you perhaps start on that? Jane has already given a fantastic illustration of Wales. Then , Nigel, could you finish up ?

I will be brief in my answer because I know that there are a couple of other points to cover. I am a little sceptical about broad-brush ambitions around growth , because it is such a large and amorphous concept. What Jane has shared is very impactful and I reflect on the contrast between that and the interventions of putting offices and buildings of broadcasters around the country, particularly more recently at Channel 4. It is not that many good things have not come from that , because they have, but is perhaps about the sustainability of the ecosystem , where you have clustered all those trades, crafts and specialisms . This is much more how the American model works.

We need to recognise the position of London in the global industry. We are now in a global industry, supplying content to global players that exist on a scale that has never occurred before and we therefore have to ask ourselves how many of those clusters we can actually create as a country.

I guess where it works best is where there is good collaboration between the different partners, whether they are commercial, public sector or public authorities. Often it relies heavily on strong local leadership, good local leaders and the relationships with those people. The message that I have taken from the last few weeks of travelling is that , without collaboration between the different players, we will not be able to sustain the level of production investment that this country has seen over the last couple of decades.

Last year , the independent production community contributed more than £650 million into the overall costs of PSB production. Our members are big players in that mix now. If you put together the commercial contribution from those, the screen agencies and the support that they provide , and public service broadcasters and the critical role that anchor tenants such as the BBC can play in certain places — particularly the West Midlands and the north-east —you will have something that works together . You can bring other partners into that as well.

If you look at what is happening in the West Midlands at the moment , you can see the growth potential there. Part of that is to do with independent production, part is to do with the BBC, and part is to do with strong local leadership there and the resources that people are prepared to dedicate to it. It really needs people to come together with resources who are prepared to work together on a long-term, sustainable basis. I go back to my point that , unless the BBC is given some longer-term certainty and sustainability—particularly over its future funding— it will be really difficult to sustain that .

Q29 I would just like to press you on one more issue that Jane alluded to, which is that talent is the lifeblood of all these industries and the development of that talent is really important . The whole skills - training area was identified by both the Green Paper and the BBC as being a key contribution to growth. Do you have views on what the role should be and how it should sit alongside current arrangements within the industry?

It works in a number of different ways. The BBC is a very important player when it comes to bringing new, young talent into the marketplace. BBC apprenticeships and all the training programmes that the BBC has in place are very important to that. Something that we have seen in the sector in recent years has been the loss of people in the middle tier of the industry and the BBC has an important role to play there. Part of that is actually through its commissioning structures , because those are people who will work if there is work to do ; they learn as they are working and will improve their skills during the course of that. That may well be something that we need to look at focusing on more as an industry. ScreenSkills is doing it and Pact as an organisation is doing it to help our members learn new skills —how to reach out into some new platforms and how to take advantage of the opportunities that exist out there . That is something that the BBC can also continue to play an important role in.

An ecdotally , our industry is quite a mobile industry , so it normally tends to be that you follow where your production needs to be filmed. In moving to Wales, I made a commitment that we would immobilise ourselves and try to look for employment for people 52 weeks a year. In so doing, I also had to accept the quid pro quo, which is that I might not have all the people I need 52 weeks of the year. I had two things to look at ; one was that the cost of my productions is going to be slightly higher sometimes because I might have to bring people outside Wales into Wales.

While I was doing that, I did the second thing, which was to start a training programme at Bad Wolf with Creative Wales and Screen Alliance Wales. We have people in our classroom from age eight onwards , but one of the last people we trained who went on to take a job with us was in their 60s , so it is a range across the piece. It has meant that I am able to target where we have a shortage—for example grips or editors—so you can really begin to focus. The focus normally tends to be on writers or actors , but it is actually everything so you can target it.

I am going to keep going back to the same thing about having these clusters of people. We are in a world where there are some players who want to sit there and do it all on their own. Maybe they have the ability to do that; maybe that is just the way they are driven. But the rest of us have to share, which is not a bad thing. It is not a bad thing for an independent production company to take its responsibility of training, but the BBC needs to take its responsibility too.

Over the years, it always has. I did my training at the BBC ; most of the big drama players across the piece started at the BBC , in one way or another. Long may that continue because , if it does not, David is right: they will come from other places as well. They should not be mutually exclusive; there should be room for us all if we arrange ourselves properly to include everyone.
The next question takes us back to something we started with Jane on regions.

Q30 You have answered part of the question I want to ask , but I want to turn on its head what you were talking about—the support for nations and regions from the BBC . You can tell from my accent that I am very much from the regions. The Government have said that they will explore a “ range of interventions” that could help the BBC better support the production sector in the nations and regions in the next charter period. I am very interested to know what interventions you think the Government should prioritise to actually do that. What would work?

I will just say very quickly what worked for Bad Wolf. When I started, instead of taking start-up money from a broadcaster, studio or distributor, I wanted to be truly independent and make my productions in Wales. I knew perfectly well that , if I took money from elsewhere, they would say, “Well, come and work in our studio that we own rather than be in Wales” or “It will be cheaper if you move this particular production to X part of England or somewhere else or go to Europe to film it”. Stubbornly, I did not want to do that; it was non-negotiable that I wanted filming to be in our studio in Wales so I could grow this community.

So we entered a public-private partnership with the Welsh Government and I took a commercial loan, which was repayable and has been repaid , so I could start . It was offset against the slate of programming that I had so that when I said, “Okay, we are now going to make ‘ His Dark Materials ’ ”, no one could say, “Could you please go to our studio in Leavesden?” It had to be in Wales. I am not saying that Bad Wolf is one-size-fits-all but public /private partnerships are really important . Incentivising people to go and set their productions up and form these kinds of clusters that Bad Wolf has managed to form around itself is one way that I strongly urge the Government to look at.

Physical production around the world is about to go through the biggest revolution it has ever experienced with AI. It is now possible to shoot a movie in a box with actors and then add all the sets and external experiences that the viewer normally would only—up until now—see through physical filming. If we had a strategic focus through the BBC and into the industry over the next decade, it would be to make sure that the next generation of talent coming through understands how to use those tools really effectively to continue the brilliant storytelling that we will always have as a country.

We are currently at the very start of this. I am in the middle of a production for the BBC at the moment , where we are taking some scenes that would normally be done as a documentary and which are going to be dramatised . We have gone out to different groups, individuals and companies to see what is now possible in the world of elevating what a documentary can be through AI. I can tell you that what is happening in that space almost on a weekly basis is utterly extraordinary. It is going to be possible to do things in hours on a computer that up until now were only possible with hundreds of people and millions of pounds.
I quite like the employment of hundreds of people though .

I do not defend this other than to say that we also cannot be Luddites; it is coming. It is also going to create a lot of career opportunities for the next generation of young people who are currently in their bedrooms creating this content, which is already achieving a level of visual finish that is indiscernible from something that is shot using physical production. We need a national plan for this , and it goes back to something that was said earlier around where the horsepower for all this AI is really based . Do we have a sovereign strategy with regard to that component of it? A subsequent question is around the distribution of the content and the extent to which we can have a strategy to control that better than we are at the moment .

I agree with the point that Jane made about public / private partnerships. Something that was interesting talking to the various screen agencies in different parts of the UK is that there is an increasing focus on linking the resources that they make available. Some give grants and some give recoupable loans to companies to help them support production. There is an increasing focus there on growing local companies as part of the requirements around that money.

That will potentially have an impact because , if you are having to put together a mix of funding, for example to commission at the BBC , and can only get 50% of the way and need 50% of the money to come from the producer, the relationship that they have with those local agencies is going to become important. That may well direct resources towards specific areas where those agencies are providing funds that are linked to local companies in that way . That could be a significant way to help to develop local sustainable businesses. We see that happening now.
Q31 What can the Government do to help the BBC?

The BBC is the only public service broadcaster that has obligations to make content in the nations — Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland. Maintaining those kinds of quotas and obligations is an important part of these charter discussions and we should not let that go.
Q32 Should they be increase d ?

They are a floor, not a ceiling; the BBC can spend more if it wants to. It comes to the point of how the local economy and the organisations there work , and the BBC’s ability to work with those organisations to develop the best ideas. What we are looking at here is creating these clusters or local economies where different players are all involved in making all this happen. The truth is that the BBC cannot do it all on its own.
Nor should it be expected to.

Exactly. We want a plural environment and commissioning. We want Channel 4 to be in a stronger place than it is today , because Channel 4 was originally designed to support the independent production sector. This is more of an operational thing to be honest, but we want to encourage the BBC to be more streamlined and efficient , and to reduce the levels of bureaucracy and the pressures that it puts on producers in terms of having cash flow over long periods of time while decisions are being made . Some of that stuff sounds quite dull and like business affairs , but it could actually make a significant difference to quite a lot of companies in terms of their sustainability locally.

Q33 To what extent do you agree that there is an “ u rgent need” for strategic partnerships between public service broadcasters to enable them to compete with the big technology companies? Could you discuss the opportunities and risks that this would present? After hearing about Jane’s work in Wales, I am particularly interested in how we ensure that these partnerships do not inadvertently squeeze out smaller producers.

David is probably going to have a much better answer about the strategic partnership in terms of the bigger picture across the broadcasters. My interpretation , in a smaller way , goes back to the thing I was saying that , actually , strength will come through partnerships. I have always taken this analogy with Bad Wolf : you know that thing on the aeroplane where you do not put an oxygen mask on anyone else’s face until you have put it on your own, and it seems like a terrible thing to do with your kids but, “All right, I am breathing. You breathe too”? Bad Wolf is a successful company , but it has taken us 10 years for me to think, “All right, I can now look around”. As Nigel talks about, we have weathered the enormous cash flow gaps that you get sometimes.

To be honest, the BBC is probably the least bad offender of all that. Sometimes you need cash flow to such an extent that any other company would be put out of business. We have finally got ourselves to a solid enough place to be able to look around and think, “All right, it’s not just about training crew or heads of departments and getting people’s careers up. It is not just about training school kids and giving college students their first jobs. It is not just about the writers or the directors. It is actually about other independent producers”.

That is a very good example of how the BBC could work with Bad Wolf to say, “All right, what can we all do together? Can you help with independent producers who are just starting out?” You can get knocked over very easily and times are such that we are not always very good at sharing or asking for help—I am terrible, let us be clear—or asking for partnerships. Everything will be better if we start doing that, not just in this industry but everywhere. A good place for the BBC to start is in the nations and regions ; go for the more solid people and ask them to help together.
Q34 Do you think there are risks involved as well?

There are huge risks involved in starting out as an independent production company in the year 2026. I am not saying that there was no risk in 2015; there was massive personal risk. The risk is strong and it is now very easy , if you start off small , to get hoovered up by someone bigger. That bit cannot be a hoovering up; it has to be a partnership.

We are all reliant upon a healthy ecosystem, both nationally and globally. There is no doubt that the global is winning out over the national, both in the UK and around the world. We have a decision to make as a country about whether we want to reset the level of collaboration that occurred in previous eras .

If you think back to the origination of the BBC as a radio technology and how it was an industry body that got together with the Government and licenced users, and then how television as a medium has evolved in subsequent developments, these were national strategic priorities and then systems and ecosystems were built to deliver on them. Everyone in the creative industries contributed to and benefited from those ecosystems.

As a country , we do not have a sufficient vision today as to what the future ecosystem of these media looks like. We are fooling ourselves to believe that the current line-up of technologies globally—let alone nationally—is the end state that our children and grandchildren will be consuming. I actually think that we have gone way backwards in terms of the consumer experience and the clarity and simplicity of how we find our media compared to where we were 15, 20 years ago. Just buy a new TV set, try to plug it in and work out what the hell you are meant to do in terms of the borders between free, pay and streaming; it is profoundly confusing. There is a huge amount of friction and then you layer AI on top of that.

We need a national strategy for our distribution that will then breathe new life into the ecosystem for the creative industries. Without that, I fear that there will be a small number of very significant winners because the excellent and best of the industry today will continue to get great commissions from these huge global companies. I fear for where the next generation will come from, albeit that the organic chaos of YouTube is going to generate a wave of creative voices that have yet to find their outlet in traditional media , but it is coming.
Q35 Do you believe that these partnerships will be enough to take on the global technology companies?

This country cannot take on a global media company that is in 200 countries , but it can set the parameters with Government for how we wish to operate as a country. We can remind ourselves that there are now bad actors everywhere in the online world that are trying to do the opposite of what public service broadcasting is there to do: they want to disinform, divide and disrupt among our young people and within our communities. This is a fight that has to be addressed slightly less politely than it is being at the moment . We have to deploy some of our best tech minds in the interest of defending the boundaries of our culture and media in a way that has hugely more force, resource and ambition than we currently have.

From the point of view of the independent production sector at least, it is important to maintain the plurality of different opportunities to go to in that environment. Some are growing organically. If we were having this conversation 10 years ago, we would not have been talking about UK commissions from international streaming companies , because it was just not happening. We would not be talking about opportunities to grow and monetise your IP on YouTube , because it just did not exist in the same way. There are new opportunities growing organically.

It is also important that we ensure that the diverse opportunities that exist at the moment for producers to bid for commissions for content continue to exist in this new world , because it is still a very important part of our broadcasting, content and IP creation. It is a world-class industry. If you talk to people in other European countries about this, they still look at the UK and what we have succeeded in doing here in the last 20 years with a degree of envy . We need to ensure that we preserve, maintain and build on that , at the same time as exploring all these new opportunities that are coming up.

A lot of the reason that people outside the UK look at us, admire what we do and follow their admiration is these huge productions that helicopter in because it is cheaper to film here, but they love our UK talent, both in front of and behind the camera. The irony is that the majority of the people they are helicoptering in to work will have started in the BBC , in some form or another.

While we exist in this system, we have to look to protect the BBC , because one thing that the BBC does best is to give people a first: a first job, a first taste, their first steps in whatever it might be. If we are looking at, “All right, let’s really drill down into what the point of the BBC is and what its public purpose should be”, one of those is to ensure that a healthy, creative economy is first off kick-started by the BBC. We should not forget that.

I know this is not necessarily the subject of your inquiry , but we need to be braver about the conversation we are having about the future funding of the BBC. Everybody accepts that the licence fee model is extremely challenged and that we need to have a public conversation about how it is actually going to be funded for the future.

To the question about whether we need a new public purpose, it is also brave to have those conversations about what the public purpose of the BBC is. It will be defined as much by what it does not do as by what it does. At some point, do we really throw some doors and windows open and say, “Okay, this is what you should be doing”, and close some others in order to ensure that? To be clear , I believe it tackles its public purpose really well , but it needs to future-proof itself.

Q36 We have just a couple of final questions on the BBC’s public purpose. David answered whether he thought the public purpose should be on growth and I think he said no. Do you believe that the public purpose should be stated in terms of driving growth?

I do not think it is about driving growth. I understand that I am a drama producer and that I am very touchy-feely, but , as David is talking about, in a world of confused truth, facts and alternate facts , storytelling has never been important . Storytelling is the way that we will communicate about our very humanity to each other, and you cannot argue with the truth of a writer’s story. The BBC tells stories as well as anybody in the entire world. Our cultural life should not be a luxury; it should be a necessity.

Again, the BBC broadcasting as it is—into living rooms, not in places that you have to pay hundreds and hundreds of pounds to get into—has never been more important. Really focusing down, I do not think that the BBC has to be any bigger; it has to be fit for purpose. The battleground is to find out what that size looks like and therefore what its purpose looks like.
It may not be able to do it on its own given the scale of this, so the national plan is really important .
I agree ; it does not have to do it on its own.

If there were alignment on the right issues among all the broadcasters—including those US-owned PSB owners , because there is a lot for them to gain from being in the tent , as well—that level of national co-ordination would have a chance. We need to rediscover our creativity and technological prowess at this moment , because we live in a world where we are being told that the resources of Silicon Valley and the scale of its investments in AI mean that we are basically not going to be invited to the party.

I challenge that because I see, for example, the impact of DeepMind on Google being very profound. What did the founders of DeepMind do in their childhood? They watched the BBC, they went to school, they benefited from the National Health Service and they have just made an extremely significant contribution to the future of Google, albeit they had to sell their company to make that happen. Nevertheless, what was the source code of that brilliance? It came from the UK . W e should not allow ourselves to be told that global distribution platforms are the end state forevermore to get our stories to our own audiences. That simply makes no sense , and it feels almost cultural suicide to accept that as an end state.
Q37 The final question—we put this to the first panel , when I think you were all here—is whether there is a case for restoring technology, R&D and innovation as a core part of the BBC’s remit .

Yes. L ook at what the BBC R&D department is doing currently ; it is doing very good work. For example , it often looks at how workflows and distribution technology are changing , but mostly using systems that are proprietary. Ultimately the source code comes from Silicon Valley and a lot of the storage is subject to kill switches that Silicon Valley will ultimately control at a sovereign level. Therefore, again, if we think about this far more—as we are beginning to do—around the defence of the country, we will go out there and build our own systems ourselves. We will be told by the Americans that we are idiots and that we should not be doing that , but we have to make a decision such that we can at least embark upon that as a national goal. Everything else we have been talking about this afternoon is down stream of that issue.
Growth should be part of the BBC’s charter mission; it always has been. My old boss, Tessa Jowell, called it the seed corn for the creative industries.
It is v enture capital.

Indeed —and we should recognise the whole value of the BBC. Of course it is a very important media institution , but it is also a £3.8 billion public investment in our creative economy. We need to make sure that we make the most of that without expecting the BBC to do absolutely everything , because clearly it cannot.
I agree with what everyone has said, really. We cannot say that the BBC should be a place of firsts if we are not asking it to make this a core ten et , because it is just going to get left behind.

The idea of sovereign developments will be music to Lord Tarassenko’s ear s because that is his big thing. Thank you very much indeed. We have covered a huge range of ground and I am really appreciative of your input. Thank you so much for coming.

segs.tx: Communications and Digital Committee
C orrected oral evidence: BBC charter renewal
Tuesday 2 June 2026
Watch the meeting

Members present: Baroness Keeley (The Chair) ; Baroness Caine of Kentish Town; Baroness Elliott of Whitburn Bay; Lord Kirkhope of Harrogate; Lord Knight of Weymouth; Lord McNally; Baroness Owen of Alderley Edge; Lord Storey; Lord Tarassenko.
Evidence Session No. 1 Heard in Public Questions 1 – 21
Witnesses

I : Professor Catherine Johnson, Professor of Media and Communication, University of Leeds; Gill Hind, Managing Director, Media, Enders Analysis; Chris Waiting, Steering Group Member, British Broadcasting Challenge.
USE OF THE TRANSCRIPT
This is a corrected transcript of evidence taken in public and webcast on www.parliamentlive.tv .
Examination of witnesses
Professor Catherine Johnson, Gill Hind and Chris Waiting.

Q1 Good afternoon and welcome to this meeting of the Communications and Digital Committee. Today we are holding the first of a short series of evidence sessions focused on the BBC charter review. The Government kicked off this review process by publishing a Green Paper in December setting out proposals for the BBC’s next royal charter. The public consultation on those proposals closed in March, and we are expecting a White Paper to follow later this year. In our work on this committee, we will be focusing particularly on the proposals put forward in Chapters 2 and 3 of the Green Paper. We will discuss these with a range of witnesses in the coming weeks. I am delighted to welcome our first panel in this short inquiry. Could I ask each of you to introduce yourselves, starting with Chris Waiting?
I am the chief executive of The Conversation and part of the British Broadcasting Challenge , a campaign group focused on the future of PSB in the UK.
I am the managing director of media at Enders Analysis. We are a research and advisory company that focuses on the TMT sector.

I am professor of media and communications at the University of Leeds. I have been doing research on public service media—particularly television—for the last 20 years, including a three-year project last year looking at the impact of platforms on public service broadcasters across seven markets.

Q2 Let me ask the first question, then. The BBC says that it is now “ a t risk like never before”, and that global streaming and social media platforms pose the “g reatest threat” to the UK’s broadcasting sector. How well do you think these statements capture the challenges currently faced by the BBC and other public sector broadcasters? I will start with you, Professor Johnson.

That is a fairly accurate picture. It is important to understand the nature of the threat. Where we once had public service broadcasters as the primary players in national markets, they are now in national markets that are much more open to global influence. They are facing competition from platforms and streamers for our time and attention, talent, production and revenues, but they are also increasingly having to deliver via the internet.

They are becoming dependent on tech and media infrastructure that is owned by US tech oligarchs. These companies increasingly set the terms and values that underpin the UK’s audiovisual media system. The risk is that those values are at odds with the public service broadcasters’ aims and remits, and it is a largely unregulated environment. I am happy to talk more about some of the challenges that we found in our research that public service broadcasters are facing as a consequence of that wider change, if that is of interest.

I agree with everything you said there, Cathy. I would just like to elaborate on a couple of points. If you go back to the time of the last charter, say 10 years ago, and you look at consumption of video, on the TV set 98% of everything viewed was from broadcasters and a tiny weeny bit from the likes of Netflix and YouTube.

If you fast forward to now, you will see that the picture is entirely different. In fact, YouTube was 10% of all viewing on the television set last year, which is quite phenomenal. Then you have the SVODs. The biggest service is actually Netflix ; it is bigger than the BBC. In terms of consumption, you can see that the British broadcasters—not just the BBC, but all the PSBs and indeed Sky—are facing much greater competition, which of course is impacting how much they can then invest back into the production sector and so on. We get this ever worse spiral.

I agree with the other two panellists that it is a uniquely challenging moment. There is a major shift in audience behaviour, as we have heard, as well as changes to the fundamental architecture under which public service broadcasting is delivered, moving away from over-the-air transmission towards IP delivery. Obviously, PSBs such as the BBC need to continue to distribute through those channels, but it means they have higher costs and are reliant on platforms and technologies over which they have little control.

I realise that this committee is focused on specific chapters of the Green Paper, but behind all these are obviously the questions of independence and funding, and the challenges the BBC faces if it is not independent. Its charter expiring every 10 years is a cut-off point beyond which it cannot necessarily operate. Then there is the question of funding: the BBC has to spend money to distribute content and to be present on these multiple platforms, at a time when its current funding model is in decline. It is really important that what comes out of the White Paper addresses both those threats, in order to explore these technological challenges.

Q3 Lord Kirkhope of Harrogate: Welcome. Can I just take you back? I do not want to go on about the history of the BBC, but it has always had what has been referred to more recently with the Green Paper as the “ BBC mission ” , and yet the whole world has moved on, of course. The original mission of speaking peace to nation s or whatever it was on the actual coat of arms of the BBC has long moved away, apart from perhaps with the World Service.

The Green Paper makes some suggestions about the use of third-party platforms. There is a reference here to Channel 4, which has a rather amorphous or middle-of-the-road approach to that. But of course here we have a suggestion that the BBC should allow its content to be more broadly seen through using platforms such as YouTube, for instance. The BBC wants to increase its visibility, although reference again to this business of the BBC’s mission includes this question of a “ c losed and safe ecosystem”, as it is referred to. In your eyes, what are the risks here of such a policy? What may be the opportunities of such a policy? To what extent should the charter, in being redrawn, have some specific mitigations in relation to that? It is a very wide question, but it impinges on the whole ethos and way in which the BBC looks at itself. Could you comment, please?

We will take this all together. The first thing to look at is what people are watching, especially younger people. For children, 32% of their viewing last year on the television was YouTube. Obviously, outside the TV, they are all basically sitting there on their phones. They are watching YouTube, TikTok, or whatever. Even with 30 to 34 year-olds, 15% of everything they watch on TV is video-sharing platforms: it is basically YouTube. There is a big issue when we see that broadcast viewing is declining and is going to continue to decline: if the BBC, with its mission, needs to hit younger people, it has to be broadcasting or be on the platforms where people are watching.

That is an opportunity, but obviously there are a lot of risks involved in that as well. There are various of those. Obviously, if you are on something such as YouTube, there is an algorithm that determines what you watch and what you have watched before, then you will watch more of that. There is a danger that there is just the BBC, or the other public service broadcasters, against the billions of hours of YouTube content that is up there. How do you make sure that content is viewable? That is one of the big issues that comes out of this charter. There have been discussions at Ofcom and the DCMS about making YouTube part of the prominence regime. Regulation should look at that quite seriously.

It is really important to recognise that the public service broadcasters are already doing this. Channel 4 started a deal with YouTube a few years ago, ITV has a deal with YouTube, and the BBC now has a deal with YouTube, for all the reasons that Gill gave . With the research that we did, we looked at 10 public service broadcasters across seven media markets. A few of them are saying, “We’re not really using social media at all”, but the vast majority are. They talked to us about significant risks that they faced in doing that. They felt they had to, but they were very anxious about it.

One of the risks, as Gill said, is around content visibility and the transparency around that. We had public service broadcasters talking about what is referred to as shadow banning: suddenly their content disappears and they do not know why, and there is no way to find out. That links to accountability. We heard about content being taken down that was compliant with the watershed in the UK, and then by the time you go to a moderator it is completely out of date, especially if it is news content.

Then there is reduced access to data. Data is increasingly the engine that drives today’s contemporary media industries; it helps to inform user engagement, editorial strategies, decision-making , and so on, and it demonstrates fulfilment of remit. But the data that public service broadcasters get from the social media platforms is much less than they would get from their own services.

Then there is just the platform architecture itself, which has been shown to amplify harmful and misleading content, potentially encourag ing addictive user behaviour. There are concerns from public service broadcasters that just putting their content on these platforms lends them legitimacy, or that they are going to have to adjust their editorial strategies to align with the values of the video - sharing platform’s algorithms. So t here are a number of risks there.

My take on this is that we need some kind of regulation. There is prominence regulation, and there are a few different ways that you could do that, but there also needs to be greater accountability for video-sharing platforms. Ofcom needs to be able to verify the reach of content from public service broadcasters on those platforms. There is also an argument for looking at the terms of trade in terms of requiring greater data sharing and , for the commercial public service broadcasters, looking at revenue shares.

Again, I would agree with all that. The BBC , in particular, is defined by universality. It is something that is available to all of us and that all of us are paying for, and so it is right for it to be available on those platforms where audiences are. Looking at the report that came out over the weekend on young people not in education, employment or training, there is a risk that the BBC loses that generation if it is not present on those platforms. Professor Johnson is absolutely right that there need to be some conditions in return for the BBC being there around data sharing, prominence and so on.

Q4 Lord Kirkhope of Harrogate: This, in fact, does not retain the BBC’s particular difference, as it were. You are equating it almost with the Channel 4 approach. Currently, as far as I am aware, the BBC will allow third-party platforms only to carry trailers to bring people back into the BBC sphere, as opposed to pushing them out to the other platforms to have the full experience of the programming.
That was its strategy, but it has announced a new deal with YouTube. There is a shift in strategy at the BBC just recently.
Yes, in January. Now the BBC is actually making bespoke content for YouTube. It has not aired yet, but it is starting to make bespoke content.

Q5 Lord Kirkhope of Harrogate: Finally, the risks, then : I asked you for the opportunities and risks. It sounds like there are a load of opportunities here, but what about risks? Are there no risks at all in terms of the personification of the BBC, its constitution and nature, as opposed to any other risks? Are there no risks?

No, there are multiple risks , indeed. One is about a value misalignment. The values of public service media and public service remits are not aligned with the values of those social media platforms, which is why there is an argument for regulation of those social media platforms.

I teach public service media to students. A couple of years ago, one of my students said, “This is so interesting, this public service media thing. Why isn’t our media like that?” What she meant was, “I don’t really use the BBC, I don’t watch a lot of television, I’m on social media all the time. Why doesn’t my media have those kinds of positive benefits that you older people are getting with your media?” That is a question we should be asking.

The question of risks is absolutely right . The BBC should want its viewers and listeners to be consuming content primarily on the platforms it owns. That way, that is the safe environment. It can make sure that all the content is compliant and that it is a safe space for younger audiences, for example. Whatever strategy it can have to bring them in, it also needs to be realistic. It cannot just tell young people that they need to come over here. It needs to find them where they are and have a strategy that allows for that. The point about legitimacy of those platforms and whether that dilutes the BBC’s direct connection is absolutely a risk.

Finally, there is a risk strategically to us as a country of being reliant on these platforms, which are almost entirely foreign-owned and foreign-controlled. My colleague Pat Younge talks about the six richest men in America , who increasingly control the platforms and technologies on which a lot of this content is distributed. We as a country need to recognise that the BBC, and the PSB ecosystem more generally , needs to ensure that it has a direct relationship with the people of the UK, whether that is in moments of crisis, for the provision of high-quality news, or for all the other content people can find elsewhere.
I am just going to add one comment in there, which relates to the commercial broadcasters , not the BBC: the revenue that they get from their YouTube content is very small in comparison to broadcast.
That is worth noting, thank you. Let us move on to questions on partnerships.

Q6 In the Government’s Green Paper, they said that they thought there was an “ u rgent need” for ambitious strategic partnerships between the public service broadcasters to enable them to compete with the global technology companies, or the oligarchs, as Professor Johnson described them. Do you agree with that statement? If so, what lessons can we draw from Project Kangaroo and Freely, or from some other attempted collaborations between the PSBs? Let us start with Chris and then go along.

There are not too many barriers in the charter to the BBC doing more partnerships with other PSB organisations as well as other bits of civic infrastructure, such as the British Library, National Archives, museums and galleries. That is something we should expect the BBC to do, as indeed it has always done.

Looking back at what happened with Project Kangaroo, it was in the early days of iPlayer and was a proposed sharing of that technology across PSBs. In hindsight, most people recognised that that was a missed opportunity. It was in the market long before Netflix was streaming and would have given the UK PSB ecosystem a real step up. Part of the problem when that was reviewed was that it was looked at through a very narrow definition of what broadcasting was and could be.

Certainly, looking ahead, we have talked about prominence, and the prominence regime is struggling to keep up —i t is still talking about icons on smart TVs rather than algorithms — but I suspect over the next 10 years there may need to be discussions about prominence within AI. If YouTube is recommending content based on a chatbot, or indeed a ChatGPT or a Claude is increasingly drawing on content from PSBs, what do we need to be thinking of in that space? How should we therefore be evaluating proposed collaboration? But the BBC has always been an organisation built on partnerships. Certainly, the more it can do and the fewer hurdles there are, whether that is removing formal trials or doing competition assessments, the more that would help it to do that.

Q7 Just before Gill responds, you said that there was not much that needed to be changed, in essence, around the charter or the framework agreement. A change to the competition authority’s stance would be necessary, though.

I agree. To go back slightly to the previous question about the challenges from streaming platforms, the answer is probably not in the charter. It is in some regulation of the platforms, rather than itself. The review of the charter is an important moment to look at the regulations and legislation more generally. You would want a charter to support that, but ultimately, the BBC should be set tasks that are defined by the ends, not the means, and that recognise how rapidly this space is moving.

I am going to agree with everything you said there, Chris. You mentioned Kangaroo and Freely. I would like to talk about the success stories there. Freely is a success story. It is new, but behind that, if you think about Freeview and Freeview HD, that is where the PSBs were collaborating and it has proved hugely successful. Freeview has been the largest TV platform for years now. Freely is the next generation of that. Where the PSBs work well together is when it is about things such as distribution. You always have to consider that every single broadcaster will have different strategies and objectives. It is always going to be very difficult to come up with one path through, as you can imagine, especially if the others are funded by advertising and the BBC is not.

Where the PSBs have worked well is on distribution. Something that they should really be looking to collaborate on is the technical investments they have. At the moment they all have their own individual iPlayer — ITVX , et cetera. You can see there is a very strong argument for pooling those resources. Even if you do not have one player that they all use, you have the same tech stack underneath it , with their own portals , et cetera. That would make a huge difference because they are competing with the likes of Netflix, which has an incredible user interface. They will n ever have the money to spend against that but , put together, collaboration on that would be very productive.
I am going to do some agreeing, and then I am going to do some other stuff, so it is not just all agreeing.
We love a bit of other stuff.

Yes. I completely agree on competition regulation. The key thing there is recognising the nature of the market the BBC is operating in, how you define that market, and recognising that there are these players that the BBC is competing with that are operating in this multi-market way. That is one of the natures of platforms. That is the key thing around competition.

In terms of collaboration, I would agree around tech innovation. One of the things to recognise is that public service broadcasters cannot simply copy what the likes of Netflix are doing — say , around algorithm innovation and what their interfaces look like — because they need to be bound by public service values. Those public service values are different. What you have at the moment is the BBC creating its own algorithms, and you have Channel 4 and ITV buying them off the shelf and then adapting them. There is a lot that could be done from sharing innovation around technology —algorithms, AI and son— in the public interest.

However, there is a real risk in thinking that this is the silver bullet that is going to solve everything: if only we just get the public service broadcasters to work together, then there is more scale, and then that addresses the fact that they are dealing with these larger competitors. The scale of the competitors is just not replicable by national broadcasters because they are operating at a global scale. We want our public service broadcasters to serve the UK; we want them to serve the UK market principally. I worry a little that there is this approach of, “Oh, we’ll look at that because it’s an easy regulatory thing to do. It doesn’t involve any changes to the charter”, rather than looking at the wider infrastructure and addressing some of those challenges.

We have multiple public service broadcasters because back in the day we thought it was good to have competition for public service broadcasting; that that would keep our public service broadcasters honest. We might want to have a conversation about whether that is actually still happening. Is that still possible with the commercial public service broadcasters’ remits going less and less ? The fact that they are in competition makes it harder—in the way that Gill was talking about—for them to come together and have one on-demand player or whatever.

Q8 I will come back to that, but I will ask just a small thing before I do. If I choose to access public service broadcasting through my Sky box thing, I get recommendations of public service content. Are you saying that I cannot do that if I go through a public service app; I can do that only if I go through an independent app?

It depends on what the terms of agreement are between the broadcasters when they are making those deals about going on different platforms because it all depends on what metadata you are sharing. They operate in different ways.
It could be done, they just have to agree.

Freely basically does that. Freely creates this environment where you go into this public service broadcaster environment, you can watch live TV, and you can get recommendations from the different broadcasters all in one place. Freely is the epitome of that.

Q9 Finally, I would like to come back to what you were saying about the silver bullet thing. Clearly, you are bound to be right, but I just have a question about whether we are being ambitious enough when we are thinking about this. Why should we not think about a single platform for all the glorious, rich content that our public service broadcasters collectively produce and look for it to compete against HBO Max, Netflix, Prime, Disney, Paramount, and all those others that we are shelling out on subscriptions for? The list is endless. Why could we here in the UK not be in the mix? You say it is because they are big global players and they have that reach. Is it possible to argue that in the English-speaking world—certainly the BBC has a good brand, it has reach—we could behave like a platform, rather than a public service broadcaster that does a bit of video on demand on the side?

There are lots of things there. Absolutely, for all our public service broadcasters, their strategy is digital first. That is their ambition. Obviously, t hey still have to provide linear television—broadcast television—to those people who are still dependent on it. There are about 4 million people in the UK solely dependent on watching linear broadcast television. That is still a requirement for them, and that can have an impact on their tech innovation.

I would recommend going and having a look at a Freely telly because that is exactly what you are asking for. It is not available on all TV sets because these things are down to commercial agreements. Gill could certainly go into this in more detail for you if you wanted. Freely is exactly that one-stop shop space for public service broadcast ing that also does a really interesting thing of providing linear alongside on demand, so that those audiences who are much more comfortable in a linear environment are not going to lose that. There is quite a lot of evidence that this on - demand environment is really difficult for some people.

That call for ambition is good. It may be that something such as that is necessary but not sufficient , because if you pool all that content together you have a degree of archive content but how much of that gets consumed at any one moment in time? As Gill was saying earlier, the needs of the broadcasters are different: iPlayer at the moment does not have the functionality to deliver ads, for example.

It is not a straightforward project, but the ambition of creating some sort of sovereign digital platform is an interesting idea to explore. It could go beyond PSBs. As I mentioned earlier, there is the role of other civic institutions — universities, libraries, museums, galleries and indeed the work of the Government Digital Service. There could be something really bold that you look at in that space. As well as focusing on the content, you could look at some architecture that underpins it.

Q10 You have just started to illuminate something I was going to ask. The Green Paper talks about partnerships with public service broadcasters and others. It is the “a nd others” in a digital AI age that I was interested in exploring, as well as the other players that you just mentioned. Happily, you have just touched on and answered my question. I do not know whether you might want to amplify that. The other thing I wanted to touch on was whether you have any international examples. Is there anything that we can look at from outside the UK that would be useful for us to consider within the UK when addressing this question?

The biggest international example would be Project PEACH. That was a project led by the EBU—European Broadcasting Union—to create a public service broadcasting algorithm that public service broadcasters across Europe could just adopt. That has been adopted, but it is not nearly as widespread as it had hoped. That speaks to the fact that across Europe you have different broadcasters with very different business needs, funded in different ways, with different remits. A lot of those broadcasters said , “Well, we could take that, but we’d have to adapt it anyway. We’ve already started adapting this commercial algorithm, so we’re going to stick with that”. That speaks to the challenge of getting one piece of tech to work for businesses that have really different demands on them.

I am not sure there is a lot more I can add to that question because the others have actually said it all. It is incredibly complex, and many of the underlying issues are the different objectives of each individual party. Freely, if you have not seen it, is supposedly broadcast-like for the IP generation. On those Freely TVs, you are still going to have the likes of Netflix on there. In reality, I can imagine that in five years’ time there will be, say, two or three global streamers that everyone will watch, and you will have two or three, or maybe one or two, local players in each market. That therefore calls for those local players to be bigger together ; h ence the BBC’s call for iPlayer to open up a bit more.
Q11 Are there any other partners that have not already been mentioned that you would identify in the UK context?

Public libraries and institutions. In terms of AI, there is an argument about publishers as well because what we are seeing is large language models coming down and scraping video content, publishers’ content. There is an argument that the BBC should be at the centre of all that in terms of pulling it together.

We could also think about minority languages there. Could the BBC be a driver in terms of developing a large language model for Welsh, Gaelic , et cetera? That is not going to happen in the market, but it makes it very difficult because things such as voice recognition just do not work for those minority languages. If you are S4C, that is a significant challenge moving forward. There is some research that shows that voice recognition is much easier for older audiences, when they are shifting over to on - demand environments, than almost any other way of finding content, actually . Yes, that is something.

On the topic of AI, the BBC was one of the organisations that brought together this SPUR C oalition of news publishers. It has made a number of demands of major AI firms to ensure that content is accurately cited, that it receives some data, and those kinds of things. To go back to the previous question, it is an opportunity to think about what our civic technology needs are. That might be some sort of sovereign AI ; it might also be a way of bringing down some costs.

I was quite struck recently that if you were to replace the search bar on the BBC homepage with an AI overview the way that Google has, the cost in tokens—in computing power—of doing that for the 20 million readers that the BBC homepage gets each month, could be up to £500 million a year. This stuff is incredibly expensive. It is right for the BBC to have a role in AI. It is right for the British Library, the National Archives and universities to have a role . L ooking at some of these technology needs , t he BBC could absolutely be a partner in bringing together some of that AI work, but the BBC cannot do all the work itself.

Q12 I wanted to remind us that we talk about the PSBs, but of course Channel 5 is owned by Paramount, Sky is owned by Comcast, and Comcast is bidding for ITV and aims to create a British streaming powerhouse. That is going to have huge impacts on PSBs generally, is it not?

Yes, Comcast has owned Sky now for several years—five or six years, I cannot remember how long—but actually the Sky leadership is very much ensconced in the UK broadcasting ecosystem. You can see that with Sky News, for example. Sky News is an incredibly powerful news organisation. There was always a fear that Murdoch was going to lessen its output, but that has not happened under Comcast either.

There is a huge amount of investment going into the UK from Comcast in Sky, and actually if it were to be able to acquire ITV, you would have a very strong player there. I mentioned before that you are likely to have one or two strong local players in each market. ITV and Sky together could become the second one behind the BBC because Sky can put that investment in tech. It has the tech already from Comcast that can give it the scale to be able to compete and to negotiate with th e likes of Samsung and LG in terms of getting on to the TV sets and getting good deals in terms of visibility, which ITV as a smaller company is less able to do. There are benefits for public service broadcasting in there as well.

Q13 Lord Tarassenko : I would like to switch tracks slightly to R&D. I am a professor of engineering at a university, and our top graduates used to compete to join the BBC R&D department s . They are prestigious jobs, but of course technology, R&D and innovation were removed last time round. I know that the British Broadcasting Challenge is very keen that they should be reinstated. I looked on the web and there are 200 R&D staff currently in the BBC in North Lab and South Lab . What difference would reinstating it as one of the six now in the charter make to R&D, compared with what the BBC is already doing now in the current charter?

The public purpose that was in the previous charter gave the BBC a responsibility to make available to the British public the benefits of new emerging digital technologies. At the time, that was part of the requirement for the BBC to lead the analogue switch-off: the switch from analogue broadcasting to digital broadcasting. It also slightly gave the BBC the opportunity to build iPlayer. At the time, it sat under that public purpose and allowed the BBC to do more things. The BBC is and always has been an engineering organisation, something that builds things with public interest at the heart. The patents on the things it has invented have been shared and have also provided a stream of income for the BBC.
