The bigger point that you are alluding to is what is really changing. Quite apart from the noise and the son et lumière of President Trump’s Administration, globalisation is being rewritten. The shift from a focus on a global order that makes global supply chains as cheap, easy and efficient as they can be has been replaced. That started accelerating during Covid, with a vision of secure and resilient supply chains. The idea of cheapest production wherever you can do it is being replaced by a sovereign concern for jobs at home. These messages are not just in the United States; they are across Europe and most of the world. That has been presaged by reports that show us that, in so many countries, people have lost the belief that if they work really hard their children’s lives will be better than theirs. I remember McKinsey Global Institute did a report more than a decade ago, Poorer Than Their Parents? , highlighting that this would be a lightning rod for politics around the world.

We are seeing a rise of not just economic security but also industrial policy in a world that needs to build anew an infrastructure that can deliver cheap, abundant energy, and a realisation in western democracies that the 1980s forward trend of just leaving it all to the market is not going to work. You need serious planning and continuity to rise to some of these challenges. The deeper trend is that rewriting of globalisation, but it does not mean we are heading into a completely uncertain world. Let us not forget that the post-world order to which Dr Slaughter referred was an order of embedded liberalism. It was one in which there was a lot of sovereign control over currencies and economic planning in this country and others, and in which the international economic interactions were relatively controlled. What I see in a lot of the world is a yearning for not a return to that order but the possibility that Governments can do more to protect jobs, their citizens and the safety of products, and the renewability and abundance of their energy. That is what we are seeing re-emerge. It will redraw what we think of as global order.

Yes, it is absolutely possible to have an effective global order without the United States leading it, for the reasons that have been outlined and because you have the opportunity now for the so-called, self-styled middle powers to work together. If they work together, you will see a more effective global order. The idea of middle powers working together might be seen as very novel, but it is not, because you had these visions of the middle powers working together since at least the 1950s. If you think of the non-aligned movement, it was not simply about countries not aligning with the power blocks; it was about countries that work together to provide an alternative order. Those visions are now coming to fruition. To go back to an earlier question, it is for Britain to identify where it stands and how it works with the emerging power configuration. My answer is that it is very much possible to think about an effective global order without the United States leading it or as the hegemon, as has been said.
Thank you. Those were brilliantly thoughtful answers.

Q5 Professor Roy, you just talked about the United States not playing necessarily the lead role, but we have in the last few days even seen China playing an increasingly lead role. What do you think China’s vision is for the multilateral order, whether it is working through international organisations, pressing its influence at the UN and WTO, or establishing new organisations such as the Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank? What is China’s vision? Does it want to assume the leadership of whatever new global arrangement, if we do not want to use the word “order”? How do you think it sees things?

That is such a fascinating question, partly because it is China and partly because of the size of the country. In some ways, what China wants is often de-linked with what happens irrespective of what China wants, simply because of its size. It is a big country with a very strong civilisational identity. Some would talk about China not as a rising power but as a resurgent power. There is the idea that China is now finally overcoming, has overcome or is about to overcome what is commonly called within Chinese circles the “century of humiliation”. Historically, China has had ideas of how it is the Middle Kingdom, and there is no reason to believe that those historical memories have disappeared.

That said, there is some exaggeration about China’s vision, because even though it is a one-party state there are several competing visions within the Chinese Communist Party. It is possible that the present head of state may be able to push his views over that of the others, but there has historically been a great deal of competition within the Chinese Communist Party. A lot of academic work suggests that all these large infrastructure projects, such as the belt and road initiative, which are often exemplified as evidence of China’s “great game” or grand strategy, are in effect retrospectively cobbled together on the basis of what local bureaucrats did or could not do. They are often portrayed as blundering individuals who just have their own interests and no such grand vision. We need to recognise that ideas of Chinese great powerfulness exist, but what is more important is that whatever China does has an effect on the world whether or not others like it.

That does not mean that other countries should be paralysed by fear or feel that they are about to be taken over. Of course, there are limits to China’s ability to extend in so far as it may have any hegemonic vision, and the fact that its hegemonic vision is not necessarily shared by countries in its immediate neighbourhood. Vietnam, the Philippines, South Korea, Japan and India have long-standing contradictions with China’s vision of itself. Whether China has a vision—there surely is a vision in some circles of China of a grand strategy and of China resurging—do we need to be worried about it? I do not think so. Should we take that seriously? Yes, of course, as you would take the visions articulated by any large power, and work with them in a way that is realistic and reasonable.
Dr Slaughter, what do you think?

I agree with Professor Roy’s diagnosis. I do not think we need to worry about China replacing the role of the United States as hegemon or its own vision. There are a couple of differences in the way China sees the world. The biggest one is it wants an international order based on absolute sovereignty. It has absolutely no interest in the parallel evolution of the human rights regime alongside the original concept of the United Nations. As Professor Woods said, that original conception was much more based on sovereignty, and that is what China wants.

Secondly, I do not think China has any desire to take over any kind of global policeman role. Indeed, it pushed back on the idea that it is going to replace the United States. It is too expensive and it has too much to do at home.

Finally, watching China in Africa and Latin America, as we might have watched the United States in the 1950s and earlier, the Chinese often generate their own antibodies on the ground. Where they are very active, often national Governments push back. That is to be expected. You see that when it is too assertive with a particular view of what the international order should be. It is a resurgent power, in my view. It demands respect and a role, but I do not think it is planning to replace the United States. I do not think anybody will, in that 20th century role.

As with all its policies, China sets out very clearly what its vision and goals are. In 2025, Xi Jinping set out his global governance initiative, which quite clearly outlines for us what his goal and the goal of China is in reshaping global governance. That is important to look at. It is the culmination of a decade of thinking in China as it has increasingly competed for the headships of organisations, and increased its funding and the earmarking of its funding. It is using exactly the same mechanisms other Governments have used to try to gain more influence over international organisations.

I agree very much with both Professor Roy and Dr Slaughter on the role that other coalitions can play, but at the same time we have to be realistic that there are three very important powers that both China and the United States have. The first is the control of access to resources and markets that really matter for other countries. Most countries are very dependent on one or the other for trade and investment. Secondly, there is its control of dominant technologies for not just the economy but for military use. Thirdly, there is its influence over the rules of the game. I am not saying China controls it. I agree with Dr Slaughter that this has always been a competition, and other countries play a role in that competition, but China’s role on those three things is indisputably dominant. That does not mean we have a totally bipolar system, but we have to be realistic about its competition for control of those things, and the role that multilateral organisations can play in moderating, restraining and shaping that. My view is that the United Kingdom working together with other parts of Europe can work to increase the extent to which each of these multilateral organisations provide an ecosystem for Britain and other countries to succeed. That is the important way to see it.

I will add one small thing to Lord Ahmad’s point about UN agencies. I want to underscore, in case there was any doubt about this, that, starting in the 1980s, many UN agencies had their core budgets cut and began to rely more and more on earmarked funding—on voluntary contributions. Most UN specialised agencies today rely for more than 90% of their funding on earmarked contributions. That has the unfortunate effect that they become guns for hire. They start looking for funding and do whatever people are willing to fund them to do. That means we have—I know people are uncomfortable voicing this—international organisations doing things that we do not need UN agencies to do. They do it because it is the only way they have been able to fill their coffers. This is a good moment for us to really think about what they are doing that they do not need to do and what it is that the world needs them uniquely to do because they are multilateral organisations, and then commit to funding that rather than using the begging-bowl model of funding whichever activities any particular individual country or small group of countries want to fund them to do.

Forgive me, but can we momentarily go out of order, because we are going to lose Dr Slaughter at 10 o’clock? If Baroness Fraser could ask her question to Dr Slaughter, who is the lead responder, we will come back to you next.

Q6 Thank you. This follows on nicely from the point that Professor Woods just made. There has been much talk and much written about the need to reform multilateral institutions, but this morning you all emphasised the opportunities for international relations and co-operation with newer flexible groupings, alliances and multiplexes rather than necessarily institutions. In this context and specifically following on from your point about restricted funding pots, can there be any meaningful reform of institutions? If so, given conditions such as the scepticism of the US, how? Will it require a catalysing event potentially such as a massive energy crisis, cyberattacks on critical national infrastructure or a health crisis such as Ebola?

To start, I very much agree with Professor Woods’s analysis of the US and Chinese control of markets, technology and the rules of the game. On the rules of the game maybe I agree a little less so, but the first two are important points. We really have not talked about technology enough. That goes directly to your question. There are 80 think tanks, universities and others creating a network of thinkers, scholars and practitioners coming up with a blueprint for reform of a lot of these institutions. There will have to be a major crisis—one hopes not a global war but an AI crisis or another pandemic that is worse, but something really major—to create the amount of political will necessary to reform the formal institutions. It is important, as the UK did starting in 1942, to think through what that reform could look like, and to try to build support. You have that plan on the shelf, as you do domestically, for when the moment is right. It probably will not be just one big crisis, but we will have that kind of crisis to change political will.

In the interim, you can work through some institutions. Professor Woods’s point about financing is important, but there are also institutions. You would not work on refugee issues without the UNHCR. The UNHCR and the humanitarian machinery also depend critically on the eight big humanitarian NGOs and various other kinds of non-state organisations. You might see a situation in which the General Assembly will be re-engineered to replace the Security Council. It does not have the same status of international law that Security Council resolutions do, but I am not sure that that is the binding constraint. You could imagine regional institutions and different global institutions being repurposed or used by a group of key states, and then those states working with many important non-state actors: again, with multinational corporations, philanthropists, NGOs and universities.

This is a very messy process and I do not think that we can begin to see the outcomes, but you can work, as I said, on two tracks and imagine real reform and new institutions, although a new international order will have to be more flexible than the one created. It will have to allow much more room for work with non-state actors. At the same time, depending on what the issues of the day are, you pull together the states and non-state actors that you need. Here again, I strongly endorse the role of the UK.

Since my time is limited, I will leave you with an image. In the Financial Times , I wrote about an armadillo order of many overlapping groups. Perhaps, moving from Texas to Britain, the original international order was more like a French garden: quite formal and clear about all the divisions and boundaries. What we are seeing is much closer to an English garden, with an enormous number of things growing and quite wild in some ways and very hard to see exactly what the final product will look like, but something to cultivate and engage. The United Kingdom has an important and special role to play.
Thank you very much. I know that you have a hard stop, so thank you very much for being here with us this morning.
My pleasure.
Professor Woods, would you like to comment?

My experience is that three things change international organisations for the better. The first is obviously crisis, where it can change existing organisations and lead to new ones. Think about the G7, born out of the collapse of the Bretton Woods system—a new crisis committee for the world. Then think about the way that was expanded after the e ast Asian financial crisis into the G20—again, a committee. People then say, “Well, we should institutionalise it, build a secretariat”. No, actually. What the world needed was a crisis committee, and those crisis committees, I think, function quite well.

The second thing that changes international organisations is competition. I say this having spent over a decade trying to persuade the IMF and World Bank on behalf of developing countries and emerging economies to begin to change their governance. The progress was glacial. During the e ast Asian financial crisis, when a Japanese official murmured that they thought it might be time to produce an Asian monetary fund to compete with the IMF, that was an electric lightning rod for reform. Suddenly, the G20 was formed and there was a far more active pursuit of how we open up the organisation and change its governance to be more inclusive of other countries.

Likewise, what we see today in things like China’s credit lines to countries is competition for both US credit lines and things like the IMF. Think about the way the Argentinian president campaigned on getting China out of Argentina but then quickly realised once he was elected that China’s $18 billion credit line to Argentina is vital and used, and that China is Argentina’s third-largest trade partner. Therefore, an immediate cut-off was not wise. Most countries have found that they cannot afford to choose between the United States and China; they need both. The question is how to use both, and international organisations can help them.

The third thing about international organisations is that leadership is really important. At the moment, countries compete to try to get their national to be the head of an organisation. The minute that person is installed, all countries get on with competing over who will get the headship of another organisation, and far too little attention is paid to how you hold that person to account. That is important because good leaders of international organisations can really bring about change. Think about the way the Secretary-General of the United Nations several decades ago, using his own special offices, created peacekeeping operations, which at the time played a critical role. That was the invention of a leader. I have seen heads of international organisations do their job extraordinarily well and quietly behind the scenes help countries come together to make their case collectively so that the organisation can be more responsive. Sadly, I could also give you a list of heads of international organisations who have been forced out because of corruption, terrible behaviour, incompetence and so on. If we want international organisations to work, we should pay more attention to their leadership. I can send the committee a report that we did with a scorecard of leaders across international organisations and a very simple list of seven things that countries should think about when they start nominating candidates. That is important because the world is heading towards selecting a new Secretary-General.
We have three and a half questions, 13 minutes, and only two witnesses.

Q7 I have a very long question. Much has been made of the political paralysis of larger international institutions, for instance the UN and the WTO, and we hear talk of smaller new institutions appearing. People refer to BRICS. BRICS, of course, was a wonderful journalistic acronym invented by a Member of this House. I am not sure to what extent it actually is an organisation and has become institutionalised or has common objectives, although I know they hold regular meetings together. We are obviously going to have opportunistic regional groupings and people getting together on specific issues, but do you see new institutions that could seriously challenge the architecture of the so-called rules-based system? Could they really seriously challenge the architecture as opposed to just being ad hoc opportunistic groupings?

Let me give three examples of where BRICS+ has acted. First, let us note that BRICS has quite rapidly expanded. A number of countries say they want to be part of it, presumably because they see some advantage. The BRICS has created its own contingent credit lines, which are important, otherwise countries rely on swap lines from either the US or China. The BRICS has created its own development bank, the New Development Bank, that sits in Shanghai and is lending. In the wake of the US tariffs over the last year, the BRICS very rapidly moved to redirect agricultural exports to China in a co-ordinated way that gave it some leverage. It is not just an acronym. It is actually an example of a coalition of countries moving together.

Another thing is that we have learnt in the last 18 months how difficult it is for countries to hold together in a coalition if there is any defection risk. The particular way in which the White House is unfolding foreign policy makes countries very aware of the defection risk because, for example, they can be individually singled out for increased tariffs. That is why we see that it took much more than just tariffs against the countries of Europe and the United Kingdom to get a collective response. It took literally the rumour of a threat of force to take Greenland to get European countries to come together using some of the mechanisms of the Anti-Coercion Instrument to put a huge retaliatory package together, which changed the US’s statements and at least short-term intent. That is important. It tells us two things about coalitions. It says that for them to get over the defection risk they have to share a truly imminent threat and an equal perception of the intensity of that threat. Secondly, they need some pre-existing mechanism to collectivise their action. To your comment about BRICS, Lord Lamont, it has some apparatus now for taking collective action, and so does wider Europe—the European Union, with the United Kingdom, Norway, Switzerland and others. Having the institutions and then being able to face down an imminent threat is going to be pretty important.

The BRICS is an incredibly useful example of a group that seemed to be going nowhere when it started out and yet it has not only cohered but expanded. It is also a good example of what countries can do as a coalition, but not in a military alignment or alliance. Remember, the BRICS is made up of countries that are otherwise at each other’s throat—China and India, for instance. Even as they are fighting, and their troops face off against each other, they have agreements and discussions at the BRICS summits. Iran and the UAE both recently joined the expanded BRICS. They are also not on the best of terms ; l ikewise, Egypt and Ethiopia. It is a very good example of an interest-based coalition that may look opportunistic, and indeed some people have called it a coalition of convenience or something. The point remains that it is interest based, and it is heavily so. It may not be principles based or values based, although there can be questions on that as well. Some would say it is values based because it is pushing back against a unipolar dominant order. The point remains that it is a coalition of countries that is trying to set up alternative institutions.

When I say alternative institutions, these are not necessarily competing or seeking to undermine existing institutions. In fact, if you look at the language of the New Development Bank that the BRICS countries put together, a lot of their guidance and justifications for supporting projects are drawn from the UN. In some ways, you could say the BRICS paradoxically strengthens the UN because it is a group outside the UN that still pushes for UN-supported ideas.

A third misconception is that there is a tendency to think of the BRICS as an extension of China’s outreach policy. Nothing can be further from the truth. If you look at how the BRICS came into being, it was preceded by a trilateral agreement between India, Brazil and South Africa—what used to be called IBSA—and then they realised that bringing in China and Russia would get them more attention, which, of course, it did. It is therefore important to think about the internal dynamics within the BRICS. To go back to the question that was asked, “What can the UK do?”, instead of being suspicious of the BRICS and thinking of it as a China-led intervention, it is useful to recognise the internal dynamics within the BRICS and work with it rather than against it. The BRICS is not a military alliance, and it does not intend to be for the reasons I mentioned. It is here to stay, but not in a way that is easily recognisable as coherent to others.

Q8 Quite a bit of this material on the global South you have talked about already. If I can put it in this context, I think Professor Woods mentioned early on about the numbers of states that there are now—190-odd. if you look at the broad picture, that is a colossal difference from the 50-odd that set up the UN in the first place. If you were taking a view, that is a terrific change. To me, it speaks to the enduring strength and popularity of the nation state, despite all the criticisms that I know are made about it, and a contrast to the received wisdom. I do not know how long this goes back, but the received wisdom has always been that globalism is inevitable. Tony Blair once said that moaning about it is a bit like moaning about winter coming or something; it will happen whether you like it or not. It seems to me that the reality on the ground is quite the reverse. There are lots of separatist movements around to point towards even more nation states.

I racked my brain to think of this. It is very difficult to think of any state mergers since the Second World War. I am talking about Tanganyika and Zanzibar, or Canada and Newfoundland. I think they tried one between Egypt and Syria. The trend is towards more and more nation states. What implication does that have for the subject of our inquiry—multilateralism? Does it make it more difficult or easier? To what extent does the word say anything useful any longer? As I say, the reality is different from the perception in many cases. I would like your thoughts on that. It is a bit broad, but it is relevant to our inquiry.

The number of states in the international system has increased. You see many of these increases in the global South. It is tempting to think of the global South as somewhat of a homogeneous entity. That is to be guarded against. There is a great deal of divergence within the global South. There is what a lot of us would call the poor South and the power South, as in southern countries that have rapidly increased their economic and technological advances, and others that have not done so as quickly. There are a lot of dynamics and contentions within the global South between the poor South and the power South. That makes multilateral co-operation that involves the global South as an entity a little tricky, and it is therefore tempting to say, “Oh, well, let’s just stick to the existing arrangements”. As I said, the fact that you have many more entities and many more sorts of tensions within and between the global South is actually an opportunity for learning from global South countries on how to work best together.

The BRICS is, again, a great example. You have opposing entities or, in examples that you could give, states that may have fought secessionist wars and emerged independently as independent nations, but they still have to work together. They have to be brought to the table. They could have their domestic or border issues or quarrels, as indeed China and India do, even though they did not emerge from the same system but you get the point, or as India and Pakistan, or other neighbouring countries with problems do. But that does not mean that they cannot be brought to the table. There is a lot of learning to be done from those countries that are in conflict with one another along certain issues but are willing to talk to each other and collaborate along other issues. Taking an issue-based approach is how these examples would really help us, and—as the point has been made—get us to not think about the world order as if it is organised in a way that it is not. That is how I would respond.
Were you going to add something, Professor Woods?
Yes, but did you have a further question?

Q9 Yes. I wonder if you can help us with our inquiry on the issue of definition. Most Select Committee inquiries end up mushrooming and getting wider and wider, and less and less focused, basically. Given that there are an awful lot of international organisations, for the reason I said in the earlier question that there are likely to be more and more of them, can you give us other categories of these organisations that are talked about in academic circles? Are there, say, four main types? I am trying to anticipate what we might do and how we might focus our inquiry now. It would be greatly helpful if we could think in terms of, “These are the four categories we are looking at, and these are their distinctive characteristics”. I am asking you to write the report, basically.

One of the first things that I would do if I were in your shoes is uncover the multilateral effectiveness reviews that were done by DfiD, because they do exactly that. They set out all the major international organisations. They say which ones are vital for the United Kingdom, how well they do, why, how and what. That work is done. It was done by what was then DfiD. It is worth dusting off that work. That would give you a good grounding on that.

Your question is a very deep one about sovereignty, why sovereignty matters, and how states use their sovereignty and strengthen it. Often, people think there is sovereignty and then there is international relations. Actually, the international relations of Governments can reinforce and strengthen their sovereignty. This is something this committee needs to look at, or could look at, when it thinks about the United Kingdom and multilaterals. One big surprise when I was doing the global impact review of the FCDO was how much foreign policy has mushroomed across every department of the British Government. It was a surprise to discover that there were some 600 people in the Cabinet Office doing foreign policy, that there was a whole unit in the Home Office doing foreign policy, and that there are many different parts of the UK doing foreign policy. Whether you are a small poor country, as Indrajit said, or a powerful country, your ability to influence multilaterals comes very much from how cohesively and in a unified way you push your case. One reason why Britain was always seen to punch above its weight in the past was that other countries saw it working very cohesively. They knew that, if one part of the British Government showed up at this organisation with this policy, it would be reinforced by other parts of the same British Government in other organisations and in heads of government meetings. It did not always feel like that in London, I am sure. But that was the perception and what was felt by other countries, and it saddens me that that has disappeared to some degree.

It is important for the G20 leadership by the United Kingdom Government to find a way to knit g overnment back together. It is partly because it has been a, let us say, dynamic time politically. Over a period of four years in the last decade, there were 34 different Ministers in the Cabinet Office. We are on our eighth or ninth Foreign Secretary in just as many years. There has also been huge change among our civil servants on foreign policy. The Brexit debate led to a huge increase in staff; Covid led to another. All these things have to be worked through. A powerful push from your committee about what it will take to bat as one team and to do that powerfully across the multilateral organisations would be very useful.

Can I stress test the witnesses? Lord Grocott’s question took seven of the available five minutes. Are you still all right for a few more minutes? Are you both all right to stay maybe as long as half past, and then we can get to the final two? That is very kind. Lord Bruce, you had a supplementary on this.

Q10 First, this has been a fantastic session and really helpful to the committee. I want to focus on the UK’s convening role in this changing world. What Dr Woods said about cross-government participation on foreign policy was very interesting. We are in the process of cutting one-third of the staff of our Foreign Office. In other words, we are dismantling our diplomatic capacity. We have slashed our aid budget. My concern is how the UK uses its influence across the world as a convenor to make things happen in a different, much more dynamic way when we have destroyed most of the levers that we previously used. A comment we had from the State Department, when on our previous inquiry we were in Washington, was that the UK’s imperial legacy meant that we had influence and reach across the world in ways and places that the United States did not always appreciate, and it valued our participation. How can we use our convening power? What role should we have in engaging particularly with African countries rather than just the bigger powers? They are the ones that tend to think that this debate is all about the big guys discussing their influence and they are just sitting on the outside looking in. How can we best use our convening power to change these things?

It is tragic that so many colleagues who knew the dynamics of a post-colonial world and studied or worked with colleagues in Africa, Asia and elsewhere are part of this reshuffling and rejigging that you mentioned. There is a great loss of institutional knowledge that you will suffer from. I do not think talking about imperial legacies helps anyone, to be honest, and to put that up front and bluntly. What helps is to re-emphasise the way in which Britain really wants to learn from as well as contribute to a changing world order. Britain should think of itself perhaps not as a legate of an imperial power but as an emerging middle power that has at heart the best interests of—you do not want to say former colonies—the countries that you have had historical relations with, at the very least.

Obviously, I cannot comment on the way in which the Government have restructured themselves, but what Britain does or could benefit from is the network of alumni that you have who emerged from British universities and have gone back to their own countries and taken up professional roles there. Perhaps this committee or others could convene some sort of input workshop or something that is able to reach out to policymakers from those countries with a specific view on how Britain might leverage its role in the G20. I do not think speaking about imperial legacies will help. What will help is to recognise and be up front about Britain being an emerging middle power and doing what it can to work with others—superpowers, middle powers and do not forget, as we have been saying, the ones that are neither superpowers or middle powers, the so-called poorer countries of the world as well. The G20 is a more limited forum, but you could use that to highlight Britain’s global role. Sorry, I hope that answers your question at least partially.
Sorry, the point about the imperial thing was not me; it was a comment that was made—
No, I know. I realised.

In the course of my global impact review interviewing a lot of Britain’s potential partners abroad, as Indrajit said, there was not a huge nostalgia for an imperial Britain, I have to say. The serious point that I found was that there was some perplexity felt by other countries as to what Britain actually wants. In the words of one Foreign Minister, “We know that Britain always wants to lead, to convene and to hold the pen, but we honestly don’t know why. We don’t know what Britain wants”. This leads countries to project on to Britain all kinds of different motives.

I think the case is that the United Kingdom today does not always know what it wants, so we need to ask the question: what does it take to know what you want in your international relations? It takes a carefully orchestrated and planned consultation, and the voice of your businesses and other interests across the country. It takes cohesion across government and a genuine plan. There is space for development, as we say when we teach, for the UK on that. It has not been helped by the merger of the FCO and DfiD. All mergers take very careful planning. When you bring two companies or agencies together, to get the best of each instead of defaulting to the worst of each takes real planning, organisation and serious change management. The FCO and DfiD were simply slammed together.

Finally, you mentioned the shedding of 30% of the workforce. It is worth understanding that, if you took the full staff of the FCO and the full staff of DfiD when they were merged, the staffing today of the FCDO is 30% more than the total staff of both. I do not think there is a single person in the FCDO who thinks that they have become 30% more effective, efficient and focused. So there is a job to be done. That is not the fault of the people who work in the FCDO, but it is a serious task to ensure Britain’s apparatus for taking forward its foreign policy, for defining what Britain wants and needs, and taking that forward needs very serious attention. Although it is certainly the FDCO it is not just the FCDO, but it also the other parts of government that have not exploded but greatly increased their foreign policy capabilities as well, but there is not a lot that is bringing them all together.

That is brilliant. Some of it answers Baroness Blackstone’s question. Restate the question, and then we would like some pithy instructions to the committee about how we go forward and structure our review.

Q11 Thank you very much. It does indeed partly answer the question that I want to put. In fact, what you both said in the last one and a half hours touches on this question. What should this committee tell the Government to do in terms of their involvement in multilateral organisations around the world? I absolutely endorse what Professor Woods just said on the need to bring together different government departments. The advice that you would give would not just be to the Foreign Secretary, it has to be to a number of senior Ministers, nearly all of whom have quite a lot of work to do in relation to the wider world and multilateral organisations. Could you both succinctly give us some bullet points beyond your last bit of advice to Government, which was to get organised on how you determine what your foreign policy is across government because many departments are involved in it? What are the four or five key things that the UK Government should do?

It is hard not to fall into the usual things: get Government working together, clarify the strategic and operational goals of Britain foreign policy, look again at the multilateral effectiveness reviews, and define which ones Britain really both wants and can shape, because those are slightly can ned recommendations. The question for Government is always how to do that, when there are so many different competing priorities and the Government themselves are in a state of some uncertainty and flux.

First, I would use the opportunity of leading the G20 to do two things. One is internal: get the British Government working as one together; secondly, use the preparatory process to reach out to other future partners, other countries, and engage them in the process as a way of strengthening Britain’s partnerships with other countries. Britain has not entirely shed its imperial legacy. It goes to other countries with a sense of, “This is what we’re going to offer you”, and not always a sense of, “This is actually what you could be offering us”. It needs in that sense to be more focused on practical, mutual partnerships and less on leadership and offering something to the rest of the world. So use the G20 to do those two things.

Secondly, take the issue of energy as an example of a high priority. We are heading towards what Fatih Birol [1] called the greatest energy crisis of all time. Britain has its own energy problem, which is a much higher energy price for industry than competitors. There is a need for cheap and abundant and renewable energy in this country, and several different government departments each have something to say about that. That is an example of where that needs to come together and you need a plan.

Planning is something that since the 1980s western democracies stopped doing. Governments became the facilitators of markets, and as a result there are very few planning muscles left. When I talked to the CEOs who got engaged in various attempts in the last decade of industrial strategy, they felt that huge amounts of their time were wasted on a process that was then casually dropped by whichever politician was in charge, and then the next would announce another. That use of the extremely scarce and valuable time of Britain’s business leaders is not good. But they do need to be engaged, as do other groups in Britain, in a serious strategy that is both economic and international for the country.

So, I think focusing on a couple of the issues, we have talked today about energy, technology and global health. Those are three areas that could really serve to illuminate some of what this country needs to do both internally and externally, and which multilateral organisations could help in that.

Thirdly, I cannot stress enough how important this is for a Britain that the rest of the world sees has defined the countries that it does not want close partnerships with post Brexit and so on, with the changing relationship with China, and now the need to be managing the relationship with the United States. It is not seen as a country that has clearly defined which countries it wants to be close to and partner with, and to what end. I think it is beginning to do that. Britain’s accession into the CPTPP, the trans-pacific trade partnership, although it is geographically a little perplexing to be part of the Pacific, and the Japan-Italy-UK defence agreement, are important steps, as are other partnerships that the FCDO and other parts of government are taking forward. It is to really start thinking what the mutuality is in this. What do we need? Do we need to learn better flood management from Pakistan? Probably, yes. What is it that Pakistan wants from us and what does that look like? Where is it that we need to work with our European partners? Other countries primarily want two things—security and access to markets and investment. How is it that we work with our European partners, perhaps to extend the umbrella of an expanded anti-coercion instrument so that there is a competitive offering to that from China and the United States? How do we work with them to get a bonanza kind of market and investment access that is predictable and reliable, and slightly less tough than some of the alternatives? Those are the things that I would focus on, but start with the multilateral effectiveness review. There are things on the nuts and bolts side where Britain could help improve international organisations and therefore international co-operation. Thank you all.

There is a great deal of room to recognise the opportunities rather than only focus on the crisis element. There is room for cautious optimism, and that has to reflect in the vocabulary and language we use.

Secondly, Britain needs to be willing to talk to its potential and actual partners in terms of what they are looking at in reforming the multilateral system. You have to talk to the Indias, the Turkeys, the Brazils, the Indonesias, and other countries that you are interested in developing your partnerships with. Be willing to build alliances beyond your traditional ones in the North Atlantic. Look out for alignments and work with a variety of different actors. There has been a lot of talk about the Indo-Pacific, but the Indo-Pacific strategy tends to latch on to what the US does rather than what Britain itself might bring to the table. I have to say this as a member of the university. Perhaps think about investing in higher education that generates the sort of knowledge that will ultimately feed back to you. See that as not a drain on resources but an investment that will help answer some of these questions. I am sorry I could not beat what Anne-Marie said, so I thought it would be useful to close on that. Thank you very much for this opportunity.

Thank you very much. I wrote down for myself that it is a delight to be inspired by the prospect of a review rather than be thrown into a sense of imminent and prolonged despair, and this is what our witnesses today have absolutely done. I often say to some of my friends that the pleasure and the privilege of serving on this committee is that it is like a slow-moving MPhil in international relations and I come away much wiser. We can now embark on this with the prospect of a hugely enjoyable and informative review that we hope, thanks to you, will have the right impact on the recommendations that we subsequently make. In closing this particular session, we thank you very much indeed and wish you well.
[1] Executive director of the International Energy Agency

sessions.iT: Convention establishing an International Claims Commission for Ukraine
sessions.w: Markiyan Kliuchkovskyi (Register of Damage Caused by the Aggression of the Russian Federation against Ukraine); Maria Tymofiienko (British Institute of International and Comparative Law); Tetyana Nesterchuk (Fountain Chambers)

segs.tx: International Agreements Committee
C orrected oral evidence: Convention establishing an international claims comm ission for Ukraine
Tuesday 19 May 2026
Watch the meeting

Members present: Lord Johnson of Lainston (The Chair); Lord Anderson of Swansea; Baroness Anelay of St Johns; Baroness Blower ; Lord Boateng; Lord German; Lord Hannay of Chiswick; Baroness Lawlor; Lord Stevenson of Balmacara .
Evidence Session No. 1 Heard in Public Questions 1 – 10
Witness es

I : Markiyan Kliuchkovskyi , Executive Director, Register of Damage Caused by the Aggression of the Russian Federation against Ukraine; Maria Tymofiienko, Head of Projects, Ukraine International Law Response, British Institute of International and Comparative Law ; Tetyana Nesterchuk, Barrister, Fountain Court Chambers .
Examination of witness es
Markiyan Kliuchkovskyi , Maria Tymofiienko and Tetyana Nesterchuk .

Q1 Welcome, everyone, and thank you for very much indeed for coming together to discuss the Ukrainian claims commission. This is a public evidence session, and we are extremely grateful that we have three contributors today : Markiyan Kliuchkovskyi , the executive director of the register of damage, which is the precursor to the claims commission—we look forward to hearing more details about how that will function; Maria Tymofiienko, who is head of projects for the Ukraine international law response at the British Institute of International and Comparative Law; and Tetyana Nesterchuk, who is a barrister at Fountain Court Chambers and has worked on this issue for a number of years. We are very grateful to you three for coming to contribute to this.

We are also grateful to the Government for giving us a slight extension of the CR a G process, which will allow us to give this some proper scrutiny. We are able to hold two, maybe even three , evidence sessions over the next few weeks , so I hope that we can produce a powerful and useful scrutiny report on the back of that.

I normally ask the first question, but I am quite keen to ask a question a bit later, given some of the developments that have taken place over the last few days. We will start with Baroness Lawlor, if she can ask her question first , then I will come in towards the end.

What is the scope of the claims commission? In particular, who has standing to bring a claim before the c ommission , what types of loss are within scope , and when and where must these losses have been suffered?

Markiyan Kliuchkovskyi : Thank you very much for the opportunity to speak to the committee and give evidence on this important matter. As far as the claims commission is concerned , in accordance with the convention that was signed in December in The Hague , the c ommission will in many respects follow the approaches and guidelines that have been established thus far in the register of damage, because it is meant not only to succeed but to continue the work of the register of damage.

The types of claimants who can submit claims can broadly be grouped in three ways : claims by individuals, claims by legal entities — businesses, essentially —and claims by the state of Ukraine in the broad sense of its Government, g overnmental authorities, enterprises, communities, local authorities and so on.

The variety of claims is quite broad . The c onvention on the claims commission does not stipulate the exact list of categories, but the r egister does . T here are 43 distinct categories , which are again broken down along the same lines as the three groups of claimants. They cover various kinds of pecuniary and non-pecuniary damage, and everything from loss of life, missing persons, injuries, consequences of torture and sexual violence, deportation of children and adults, displacement, loss of residential and non-residential property, loss of enterprise, loss of gainful employment, loss of education and similar things.

When it comes to legal entities, they are predominantly asset - focused, with more of an economic , business angle on the consequences of the war, including the loss of access to assets that remain in the territories that are currently under temporary occupation and traditional categories of claims, such as loss of cultural and historic heritage, as well as damage to the environment.

In our work, the r egister has tried specifically to reference every category of damage that is compensable under international law , to eliminate all the gaps that could exist. As I mentioned, the claims commission will have to make its own decision on which categories to pursue, but every indication is that it will be along the guidelines, if not exactly continuing the approach , adopted by the r egister.

I have a slight point of clarification. A trade union is not a legal entity, but it has another incorporated position within this. In your view, might a trade union that has lost a significant amount of property and suffered other kinds of damage be an entity with standing in this ?

Markiyan Kliuchkovskyi : Certainly. A legal entity as a concept, especially in the Ukrainian context, is broad and not limited to corporations and LLC s . It is all kinds of formations of legal entities , including co - operatives , unions and certainly trade unions . In so far as they have a legal personality under either Ukrainian law or any other applicable legal regime, they would be in a position to submit a claim.
Briefly, if anyone has any interests to declare—I should have said this before the first question —maybe you could declare it before your question or note that post the meeting. Thank you very much.

Q2 Will the principles of compensation in our civil law be applicable ? For example, will future earnings be taken into account for the widow of an astrophysicist compared to the widow of a carpenter ? W ould the amount be the same or does it depend on matters like future earnings?

Markiyan Kliuchkovskyi : It is yet to be determined . It is for the future claims commission to determine approaches to compensation in each category . In all likelihood , the approaches will be different from one category to another. There are two elements of this . First, as a matter of concept , f uture earnings are a factor to the extent that the register is already collecting those claims . We have collected more than 150,000 claims at this point. We are inviting information from claimants about what that could be. The s ame applies to claims from businesses or legal entities. They have the opportunity to claim for not only the loss of assets but the loss of future earnings.

That being said, the commission in the future, as a matter of its approach and then its review of individual cases, will have to determine what approach to take. The experience of previous claims commissions suggests that , sometimes, in the interest of the efficiency of the entire mass process , commissions can adopt principles of generalisation and standardisation in their approach. It may be less of an individual assessment, rather than a lump sum arrangement or something fairly standard . Then again, I am looking into the future and trying to understand how the future c ommission will make those decisions.

Regarding the UK’s role , once the UK has ratified the convention , it would hopefully be part of the c ouncil that consists of nine member states and would be able to inform the rules and procedure for evaluating the damage done. That is why it is so important that the UK is part of the council that will be formed and that it can inform and set up those proceedings.

Q3 The international claims commission for Ukraine would, on the face of it, appear to have to negotiate and find a way through several complex challenges regarding its relationship with the International Criminal Court and with other accountability mechanisms . In relation to complementarity as opposed to duplication , for instance, how do you prevent double - dipping where a claimant seeks to obtain reparations through the ICC while simultaneously pursuing financial compensation via the ICC U ? Then there are other issues that I anticipate the ICC U will face around prosecutorial confidentiality , information sharing and evidence sharing. This question is really to all three of you : how do you see these complex relationships being negotiated?

I can give a general overview. The compensation claims commission is probably the only show in town when it comes to compensation. Neither the ICC —the International Criminal Court —nor the Special Tribunal for the Crime of Aggression against Ukraine has any right to award or make an order for compensation, whether on behalf of a state or on behalf of individuals whom they find guilty. The only court that could award compensation is the European Court of Human Rights.

T here will be a small overlap between any possible just satisfaction award ed by the European Court of Human Rights. You recall that, in July last year , there was a huge decision on the merits, where the European Court of Human Rights found that Russia was responsible for all the acts of aggression in Ukraine from , I believe , May —I cannot quite recall the date —or April 2014 [1] all the way up to 16 September 2022, which is when Russia left the European Convention on Human Rights and the Council of Europe. No decision as to just satisfaction has been made by the European Court of Human Rights. In fact, what it said on that award of compensation is , to paraphrase, “We know that a register has been established whose aim is to record all the losses, so we will postpone the decision on just satisfaction and we will see how that mechanism evolves”. [2] So there will have to be a conversation between the C laims C ommission, the R egister, the Council of Europe and the European Court of Human Rights to ensure that there is no double recovery, but I cannot imagine that being a very difficult process given that they are all bodies within the same international institution.

There are also decisions — I say that this is the only show in town with a caveat — because there are also decisions by Ukrainian national courts and there might be decisions by other foreign national courts to determine compensation claims against the Russian Federation. Those decisions will be very few and far between. The reason is that, while there are a lot of decisions, certainly in the Ukrainian courts, none of those ha ve been enforced against the Russian Federation. When it comes to the enforcement of a national court judgment, not an international one, there is a principle of sovereign immunity against enforcement that applies to the Russian Federation’s assets.

So in the very few circumstances where there might have been enforcement—I am not aware of a single case where there has been successful enforcement against the Russian Federation in claims for damages—information should be supplied by the national authorities. I would expect some sort of mechanism where the national courts supply the information to the C laims C ommission and the R egister to ensure that there is no double counting. In terms of the viable options for individuals to get compensation, they could go to national courts, but they could not very well enforce any awards that they get from them due to the fact that the majority of Russian state assets will be covered by immunity from enforcement.

Markiyan Kliuchkovskyi : If I could complement that with two short points, first, the c onvention on the c laims c ommission in A rticle 19 .3 establishes a positive obligation on the c ommission and its bodies to communicate with other mechanisms specifically with the purpose of co - ordination and avoidance of double compensation for the same damage. T h at is something that the drafters and negotiating parties have thought of.

Secondly, for one of the instruments that is being established —the Special Tribunal for the C rime of A ggression against Ukraine—A rticle 37 of its statute foresees that , if there are any assets to be confiscated from the defendants prosecuted by that tribunal , they are to be handed over to the c laims c ommission for distribution among its victims.

F inally, I can speak to the other aspect of your question from my experience of having engaged with the ICC and other bodies, especially th ose that prosecute criminal acts , with respect to exchange of evidence. Y ou have metaphorically hit the nail right on the head in saying that prosecutorial confidentiality put s severe restrictions on the ability of those bodies to share evidence with us. W e have to think how to do it thoughtfully, legally and , most importantly, without subjecting those proceedings to harm from those disclosures.

Q4 Thank you for that. Could you help me with this issue ? I understand that t he ICC has territorial and temporal jurisdiction over core international crimes in Ukraine since 2014 b ut , in contrast, the ICC U’s current temporal jurisdiction is limited to damage and injuries incurred on or after the full - scale invasion on 24 February 2022. T hat would leave a jurisdictional gap, would it not , r egarding losses suffered during the initial 2014 annexation of the Crimea and Donbas ? How will that be dealt with?

Markiyan Kliuchkovskyi : There is indeed a limitation in the mandate of the c ommission to address the acts that started on 24 February 2022. The reason is that it addresses the full - scale invasion of the Russian Federation into Ukraine , which has been qualified, including by the United Nations General Assembly, as an act of aggression. I t follows that logic. That being said, the provisions of the convention allow the possibility for expansion of the temporal scope of the c laims c ommission to include the events that started in 2014. States would have to make a positive decision about it and make an amendment to the convention, but that possibility has been specifically referenced in the text of the convention.

I am sorry if I did not understand this correctly but, when talking about the conflict between domestic cases in other countries, maybe the UK , and this separate claims commission , would assets confiscated in the UK go into the compensation pot , as it were, or would a separate claim have to be made on those assets in relation to the claims ?

Markiyan Kliuchkovskyi : In so far as the architecture of this claims mechanism is concerned, t he next phase after the establishment of the c laims c ommission is the establishment of the c ompensation f und t hat is meant to facilitate payments of the awards of the c ommission . T hose decisions have not been made yet b ut , conceivably , whatever assets are available for that purpose — whether it is assets immobilised in various jurisdictions or otherwise — they would be made available to that fund and become the source for those claims.
And are we signing up to that?
Markiyan Kliuchkovskyi : That would be the singular process. The claimants would not be required to make any additional steps or claims.

Right now, you are not signing up to that. The only thing you are signing up for now is the establishment of the C laims C ommission . H ow the compensation fund will be established and where its funds will come from y ou are not signing up for right now . T hat will be a separate decision.

Q5 Baroness Anelay of St Johns: Following up on the same theme, it has been clear in discussions in both the House of Commons and the House of Lords that there is very strong support here for ensuring that there should be compensation to Ukraine for the illegal activities carried out by Russia against human beings and businesses. W hat you have described is really a three -p art system. T he first is the register of damage and the variety of people and businesses that can register damage — including , I understand , UK businesses. S econdly, we have heard about the i nternational c laims c ommission, but , as the C hair mentioned, it is then the compensation fund itself.

W e have discussed at length, not in this c ommittee but certainly in the European Affairs Committee , h ow we can ensure that someone like Mr Abramovich can have his ill - gotten gains used for compensation . I understand that there is a case going on in Guernsey, so I will not say more. What kind of processes can happen at the moment to start to give confidence to the people of Ukraine that there will be a compensation fund — not just for the administrative costs being born e at the moment but as a reality, and not just in several generations ’ time but so that they can see something happening ?

In terms of process , you mentioned Abramovich’s funds . W e know that there is also about £ 2 billion from the sale of Chelsea languishing somewhere in the banks here in London. But there is more. A bout £ 300 billion of state assets, from the C entral Bank of the Russia n Federation, have been frozen around the world. A bout £ 200 billion is in Euroclear and , as I understand it, about £ 9 billion is here in the UK. Both the US and Canada have legislation that authorises the ir Government s , by an order , to make those funds available to a future C ompensation F und. So t here is already legislation in Canada and the US. I would certainly urge this Government to introduce similar legislation authorising — not ordering it right now — the Government , by an order , to make the transfer of those immobilised assets to the C ompensation F und once it is established, because that legislative authorisation will send a signal that this country will support the establishment of a compensation mechanism that will work for Ukrain e .

Baroness Anelay of St Johns: I have a follow-up question. When David Cameron was our Foreign Secretary , having been Prime Minister, he seemed to think that there was going to be an agreement between the European Union and the UK that there could be a method by which those assets could be obtained. Is that still the case ?

That is still on the table . As I understand it, efforts are now being made. Back in December, we were led by Germany , which floated a slightly different idea . It wanted to use those assets to borrow against and lend the money to Ukraine. As I understand it, right now the Netherlands is leading on an initiative to start again the discussion about using those immobilised assets as , in effect, a down payment on Russia’s obligation to compensate Ukraine.

This convention recognises that the responsibility for compensation lies with Russia . U ntil Russia joins the C onvention by consent , t he only way of ensuring that Russia’s obligations are complied with and compensation is paid is by using the immobilised assets as a prepayment of the already recognised obligation for reparations. The general position in international law is that the obligation to pay compensation or reparations , whatever you call it, arises immediately upon the breach of international law. We know that the breach here is fundamental : it concerns A rticle 2.4 of the UN C harter .

Upon that breach, two obligations ar i se . The first is to cease the breach , which, as we know, has not happened. The second is to compensate for all loss caused. That has been established. The only thing international law does not give you is a mechanism . So this C onvention provides the implementation mechanism for the payment , enabling Russia to pay compensation. Again, under international law, the consent of the aggressor state to the payment of reparations is not needed because there are other mechanisms, such as a doctrine of countermeasures , that enable states to ensure the aggressor state ’s compliance with international norms. This mechanism has been used by the US and Canada—perhaps the time has come for the UK to join in . This does not mean that you have to use it , but at least you have i t in place so that it can be used once an agreement is reached in Europe.

T here is a very good report outlin ing the possible legal avenues for dealing with the transferral of the frozen assets into the future fund ; perhaps I can submit that as evidence for the committee to consider the possible legal mechanisms. Of course, there is already a precedent. The UK has contributed £2.26 billion to the G7’s extraordinary revenue acceleration loan s mode l, which is made up of t he windfall profits generated from immobilised assets. So this has already been done. This question needs to be considered to create a law to enable the transfer of all assets into the future f und .

Lord Hannay has a good segue here but, i n terms of the treaties that we are scrutinising , the compensation fund would be a separate treaty over which we would have additional scrutiny. O bviously , there will be further discussions around that —this is specifically for the claims commissio n—s o there is a n argument to be had there later.

Q6 Before I put my question, I should make a declaration : I was the British ambassador on the UN Security Council when the Kuwait compensation commission was set up. I voted for it , on the instruction of my Government , and I was there for all of the follow-up, which was pretty detailed and , as I am sure you are aware, resulted in complete 100% payment for the damage incurred by Saddam Hussein’s aggression against Kuwait. So I have a little experience of this matter.

The claims commission is being established on the basis that , under the laws of state responsibility, Russia is responsible for all damage caused by its internationally illegal or wrongful—however one likes to characterise them— acts . However, the c ommission is being established in the context of a war of ongoing hostilities. Is engagement with Russia , as the aggressor , a necessary step in order to make the claims commission and the compensation fund effective ? Or are you basically envisaging making it effective without Russian co-operation—that is, without Russia being willing to discuss this and pay from its own funds ?

Markiyan Kliuchkovskyi : As we have discussed, Russia’s duty to make reparations is not conditional on its consent to or acceptance of the duty; that is just part of customary international law. From that perspective, the participation of Russia in this mechanism is not, strictly speaking, required.

That said, I think everyone agrees that Russia’s participation is quite desirable . There are provisions in the Convention E stablishing an International Claims Commission for Ukraine that speak to that effect and say that Russia is welcome to join this claims commission at any time on the condition that it accepts responsibility for its wrongful acts against Ukraine and commits to paying the awards issued by the commission. Russia can then be a participant in the process.

However, this mechanism was designed so as not to make it a hostage of Russia’s willingness or unwillingness to join . W e come back to the starting point : it has a duty to make reparation s, regardless of whether or not it wants to do so. T hrough access to various resources , including the vast volumes of sovereign funds of the Russian Federation that ha ve been immobilised by various countries in Europe and elsewhere , the states signatory to this convention have in their hands , at least in principle, the tools to make this mechanism work without Russia’s participation. So, in essence, it will work both ways: with or without Russia’s participation .

U nlike the situation in the case of Kuwait , where the legal basis was provided by UN Security Council resolutions that were adopted under Chapter 7 and therefore had the force of international law on both Iraq and everyone else, you do not have an instrument like that at your disposal here. So it is a rather different proposition, although no doubt the jurisprudence and procedures that were gone through in the case of Kuwait —and operated very successfully —are important to the way in which you a re handling things.

Markiyan Kliuchkovskyi : That is exactly right. If I can speak freely, the only reason why the convention was drafted and the register was established in the way they were is that the Security Council is not capable of dealing with this matter because of Russia’s veto rights. Hence in 2022 the matter ended up with the UN General Assembly , which first acknowledged and deplored the act of aggression . It then issued a resolution in November 2022 stating that Russia has a duty to make reparation s and is to be held responsible for its aggression against Ukraine. It was then up to the able and willing states in the international community at large to establish this mechanism , as guided by the General Assembly . Otherwise—again, if I can speak freely—I am sure that it would have been much easier to have done it through the Security Council and the powers of Chapter 7 of the UN charter.

I should also add that , in many ways, the register and the claims commission were modelled on and inspired by the lessons of the UN CC, including with respect to the establishment of a compensation fund . The concept that the fund could hypothetically be filled with a share of Russia’s future oil revenue, as was done in the case of Iraq, i s also on the table and should be considered a viable option.

I have looked into th is precedent, because it remains one of the few precedents that we have. Very importantly, the resolution that declar ed Iraq liable to pay compensation under international law said that it reaffirms that Iraq is liable. I t did not declare Iraq liable. T here was no mechanism for declaring Iraq liable ; t here is already a recognised law that Iraq is liable. T he resolution was simply needed to reaffirm that, and then to establish the mechanism for the implementation of the liability to compensate.

T his is precisely what happened here in the case of Ukraine . B ecause the UN Security Council was blocked by Russia , on 27 February — a few days after the full - scale invasion — the General Assembly scheduled an unscheduled meeting to deal with the situation in Ukraine. T he special resolution, the “U niting for P eace ” resolution — you probably know about it — requires that the General Assembly will consider the matter of peace and security immediately , if the Security Council is unable to do so . I t was under that same procedure that there were unscheduled meetings in which there was a resolution , first , condemning the invasion . A lso , and importantly, the resolution passed in November 2022 recognised that t he Russian Federation must be held to account for violations of international law and must bear the legal consequences of its internationally wrongful act. T hat was supported by 94 states . U nder the C laims C ommission C onvention , they can join t his mechanism.
Has Russia given any explanations as to how it was able to vote for the Kuwait c ommission but was threatening to veto this one ?

It did not threaten to do so—it actually did veto. An emergency meeting was convened, and Russia vetoed. The draft resolution was tabled on 25 February, calling for the withdrawal of Russian troops. Russia vetoed that Security Council resolution, after which there was the UNGA meeting.

I want to add the importance of the commission to establish the scale of damage and to quantify that damage . O bviously, your question relates to Russia joining the c ommission, which would require a process under A rticle 28 of the c ommission to be followed . But as we do not have the willingness of Russia to do so, a nd as the war is continuing , it is very important that the c ommission functions now in the absence of Russia agreeing to this process . I t is important for both questions , in terms of the Ukrainian public, that there is an established, quantified measure of d amage that can be used to deter Russia and encourage Russia to come to the negotiating table and seek peace eventually.

A t the moment , while Russia is not part of the process, we are looking at the frozen assets. W e know already from the initial assessment of the damage that it goes way beyond those figures. T he damage is already quantified at $ 500 billion or $600 billion. It is so important for the commission to function so that those figures can be substantiated.

So you are saying that the sheer process of this is important in, hopefully , driving to a good conclusion , because it is visible and recorded, even if we have not got to the compensation mechanism itself.
Lord Stevenson is online. I will hand over to him to ask his question.

Q7 Lord Stevenson of Balmacara : It would helpful if you could give us a little more background about how much the UK has been involved in these negotiations and in the development of the convention. Has it been an active one , or is it more of a second order? C ould you also expand on what you think we should do here to help with the development of this ? You said already that the United States and Canada have legislated. Are there other legislative opportunities that you think we should take ?

Markiyan Kliuchkovskyi : With respect to the UK’s participation in this entire process , I should start by saying that the UK has been a steadfast supporter of this mechanism every step of the way — from the r egister to the preparation and negotiation of a claims commission convention . T he UK Permanent Representative to the Council of Europe , A mbassador Sandy Moss , is the chair of the Conference of Participants, and we have had the pleasure of working together with him for the past almost three years, advancing the cause of the register at the forefront of the mechanism . W e are very grateful for that .

H aving served as the secretary of the negotiations process, I can say that the United Kingdom delegation was among the most active , and indeed probably the biggest in number of participants. I ts participation was absolutely vital , because not only is the UK a powerful and respectable member of the negotiating community —if I can put it this way , other delegations listened to what the UK has had to say —i t was also quite important that the UK kept focus both on the goals and targets of this process and where we want to end up, and on the viability of this mechanism, including from a point of view of financing , budget and sustainability, so that it did not become an unbearable burden for those states that are willing to support the process. A ll in all, it was an incredibly efficient participation in an overall very fast and efficient negotiation process. W e are quite happy and pleased, but also not surprised , that the UK bec a me one of the signatories of the convention on the day it was adopted.

I will just add to that. W e have submitted a report from BIICL for this c ommittee ’s attention. T he recommendation for this c ommittee is to advise the Government first to join the c ommission, to ratify the process and then to e ncourage the expansion of the scope of the claims commission to cover the period from 2014, so that we do not have that gap in the period in which the claims c ommission is considering the claims. I t is important, as we discussed, to adopt legislation for transferring the frozen assets and set up of the future compensation fund. A ll of th ese are critical and important steps that UK should lead on.

I will just add to what Markiyan said about the UK ’s delegations involvement. I sit on the Bar Council’s International C ommittee , and particularly in our public international law group, and I know that we currently have a lawyer from the UK involved in every single case before the International Court of Justice. W e have the expertise here in the UK on issues of public international law. I am not surprised that it was the biggest delegation by size, because there is a lot of learning here. I think that all members of the Bar Council would be very happy to share that learning and welcome the implementation of the C laims C ommission.

Q8 If Britain were to withdraw from the convention, would this have any effect on the matters we are talking about , including the role it could play ? C ould you tell us what your view s on those questions are ?

Markiyan Kliuchkovskyi : Frankly, we have not given much thought to the consequences of withdrawal from the convention , as it has not yet entered into force . W hat I will say is that , under the terms of the convention and in the context of the Council of Europe, the United Kingdom has a status of what we call “ major contributor ” , which means that its role, including financial contribution to the budget and financing of the commission, is considerable. A withdrawal from the convention would have difficult consequences , even from that perspective, let alone from the point of view of the political signal that it would send.

F rankly , we are in quite a n optimistic mindset, if I can put it that way. W e are working towards t his convention coming into force. As you may know, coming into force requires ratification by at least 25 states, including three major contributors , s o speedy ratification by the United Kingdom is absolutely vital in that sense.
Would the same considerations apply if the UK were to withdraw from the European Convention on Human Rights?

Markiyan Kliuchkovskyi : I am sure that it would be an equally difficult proposition. I am not an expert on the European Convention on Human Rights, so I should caveat my response, but I can imagine that, as accountability in struments have a considerable history and considerable effort is being put into their establishment and authority, they are to be safeguarded in the current world, to the extent possible.

I am happy to comment. Withdrawing from the C laims C ommission C onvention would have a lot of practical consequences. The UK would not be able to participate in the establishment and setting up of all the rules, such as on how the evidence will be treated. It would not be able to nominate people to serve as commissioners ; it is supposed to work on the determination of different c ommissioners . Of course, it would send a huge signal about the UK’s commitment to Ukraine and, I should say, to international law and upholding international law.

The European Convention on Human Rights is a completely separate issue. The only thing I would say is that withdrawing from the European Convention on Human Rights would probably have similar political consequences to withdrawing from the EU , in terms of the voice of the UK internationally. The European Convention on Human Rights was intended as a peace project . W ithdrawing from it at a time when peace is so fragile would probably be quite disastrous.
