Again, it is not rocket science , all these things are quite straightforward , but it is about treating young people with respect and almost how you might ask a consultant team whether they were happy with the process. It was the same principle applied to how we were working with young people.

There are various ways that we then go on to improve future youth engagement exercises. One example that we took from the youth forum was ensuring that we were hearing from a really diverse mix of young adults. We were probably still hearing from people who were slightly higher on the socioeconomic background. We needed to do a bit more to make sure that we were hearing from a more representative group. The young people had lots of suggestions about ways we might make the programme a bit more engaging , such as different food we could offer. They were not holding back on different ideas and suggestions , but again it was about treating them with respect and being open to the feedback that they might have too.

That was quite a select group of people you used. Across the board with children and young people, perhaps Teres a has more to say about the breadth and existence of skills among young people to be able to contribute in this way, other than through being involved in a big project such as Nicola described.

We have always gone to work with young people assuming that they will have sufficient skills to start the ball rolling. It was never a requirement of, “ This is what we need from the young people who we are going to be meeting ” . They would be on that journey with us and the students, and this cross-co-learning that is taking place is a fantastic thing to see. The skills are a really nice output , and teachers and youth workers can see those developing as the programme continues.

There are really clear outputs that I am keen to share with you in terms of the effectiveness of that engagement in a planning process. It is quite difficult at the more strategic level but one is the tool of using a neighbourhood plan . We have seen that bringing a young person’s voice and the skills that they have demonstrated in sharing that voice into policy .

One case in particular is Wool er , which is a very rural town in the depths of Northumberland. A group of students who wanted to do some engagement with young people were called in to try to elevate and help the young people to have confidence in what their views were and to contribute to the discussion within the neighbourhood plan framework.

The steering committee of the neighbourhood plan had a real vision for the future of the town , where these young people would work and live . They wanted to have the young people say that for themselves so that they could evidence that as part of that planning process, which we helped them to do. It was not in the same written format ; i t was through presentations , doing a guided tour and identifying sites that they would like some investment in. They wanted to be attached to that and to be able to feel they could come back to that town to live, work and support their families after they had left to go to university .

In terms of demonstrating effectiveness, there is now a policy document that has triggered development on the back of these young people’s evidence. The skills that they used as part of that process were very varied. It was done within the school environment , with some additional walkabout tours as well.

Also on measuring effectiveness , and to come back to this whole idea about democracy and young people having a say and feeling they have a right to express their views and contribute to decisions made in their local area , in time perhaps we will see increased numbers voting in local elections, possibly in general elections. If the voting age is reduced , we might see those impacts even sooner.

We will also see them going into built environment careers. I know the Royal Town Planning Institute is doing a lot of work with schools to share education about the environment and say, “ If you ’ re interested and want to have a say, you can work as a town planner. The UK is desperately short of planners , so everybody benefits ” . There are different ways of measuring that effectiveness.

Just briefly, if your question is around whether young people have the skills to be involved, the short answer would be : absolutely yes . Is our current education system encouraging or teasing those skills out of them? That comes back to a lot of what was talked about in last week’s session , so I will not reiterate all those. Some fundamental ones are that of course they have the skills in the sense that they have the lived experience and that is why you want to engage them . You want to hear about their experience, which is unique and invaluable to placemakers in understand ing that day-to-day experience.

In terms of knowing what they could be advocating for, possibly our current education system is not fully enabling that. Last week w e heard about the number of young people who have not visited the religious building , museum or theatre in their own town. A lot of young people — when we work with them — maybe do not know the possibilities of what is there with design. We are not talking about expensive design , but they have seen such a limited lens of what is possible .

There is a huge amount of work that could just be happening in the background that would enable young people to have more of that knowledge of what they could be advocating for. You could argue that for democracy to work best, it needs to be armed with knowledge to know what you can be asking for.

So I would say absolutely, yes , they do. Maybe we are letting them down in that we are not giving them enough of those tangible , physical experiences. That is where — in any of these ways of engaging young people in the built environment —first-hand lived experience is important, taking young people out to see what is possible , to meet people , to use their hands and to think in three dimensions. For a lot of young people, this will be very new to them , so that can be something that they build as skills going through these engagement processes . It also makes it a much more transparent process in terms of what a placemaker is trying to understand and learn.
Would you say that it does not have to be a very expensive process to get young people to be able to participate — particularly at their own local level —i n these sorts of exercises you have done?

Not at all. I t often comes back to the simplest things and that is about seeing, experiencing, and feeling. They do not need to be mini-planners, mini-architects or mini-engineers. It is great if they develop a thirst or a passion for that —super— but it is really just about giving them an opportunity to experience the world and start to form opinions and be told , “ You ’ re allowed to have an opinion. It ’ s not right or wrong ; it is your experience and what works for you, and that ’ s what you ’ re advocating for ” .

Q16 I am interested in the use of digital technology and digital resources in educating young people. Last week I mentioned a program called SimCity, which is a game in which players plan an urban environment. I also proposed that architects’ computer-aided design programme should be readily accessible to children.

Beyond that , I would like to offer a contention for your appraisal. I believe that the rules of perspective are easily taught to young children and that with this facility children would be keen to draw pictures of buildings with the same enthusiasm that affected Renaissance artists. Can you comment on that after your experience with the use of digital resources ?

I will kick off. I might not have as much in-depth use of a broad range of technology , but one of the most useful tools that young people see their environment through is actually a camera lens. We have worked with young people — 60 at a time — where they just took out disposable cameras .

You mentioned perspective. We asked them to take a photograph of a place that was important to them . We had some architecture students demonstrate how to frame a shot and how to construct the view within the viewfinder. That was incredibly helpful as an exercise for those young people to come back and say, “ This place is important to me and I wanted to set it in its importance and how I see it ” . Perhaps they would critique the photograph that was produced and say, “Well, it doesn ’ t really look as I would see it , necessarily ” .

That was a useful first step : starting to assess their local environment in terms of technology and how others might see it as well. Taking those photographs was a skill that we were able to encourage them to use and then we developed discussions about why those places were important to them. At a base level that was a good introduction to use of technology. I know that digital technology has taken things in a lot of different directions and I will let somebody else comment on that.

No doubt digital plays a really important part and is something that appeals to a huge number of young people. Next week’s focus will be more on the digital. We have yet to find a young person who is not playing Minecraft, which is often one of their first ways into thinking about the potential to shape their built environment.

I feel there is potentially a missed opportunity there if young people feel they can impact the world only in the digital sphere. If we are going to use digital tools with young people, we need to be showing them that they are tools that can be applied to the physical world. In an engagement process, you may use something such as SketchUp or a simple computer-aided design program to enable young people to design , alongside drawing by hand.

We often find that physical 3D model-making is one of the most transparent processes to enable young people to take the ideas in their imagination and demonstrate them to another audience. There is huge potential in the digital, possibly as a hook to entice young people in, but in our experience it cannot be the sole way to engage with young people. It has the potential to remove the transparency.

Talking from my own experience within architecture, architecture schools are struggling right now with the use of AI. A lot of students are producing incredibly professional-looking drawings and thinking that their tutors will think they have designed a beautiful building. They are creating beautiful Escher drawings and t he walls and the floors are not lining up. If you were physically doing a carpentry course, you would never imagine that you could float a piece of timber on something else , but t hey are producing drawings and not even noticing that that is what the drawing is showing. The digital is all well and good — i t is brilliant , it is a tool — but you have to have the critical faculties alongside to understand whether what you are creating in the digital actually makes sense and holds up.
Nicola, have you had experience of teaching the rules of perspective to young people?

Using and leveraging technology throughout the process is something that we always routinely try to do , sometimes as a hook of getting people engaged in the first instance. That speaks to some of the principles of going to where young people are , b e that trying to engage them in a school or youth club or trying to get them to engage within your consultation programme by having some sort of post on TikTok of all things .

TikTok is not normally the space that property companies feel comfortable in or have a presence on but needing to get out there into these youth spaces to speak the language of young people and make sure that they are hearing about the opportunities that you have available to them is something that we try to do more of. All that said, we would maybe work on that with a youth partner that would have the skills and expertise of how to make a TikTok ad look good and engaging.

I agree particularly with what Fiona was saying around needing to use and leverage digital tools , with that caveat and acknowledgement that you still need the tangible and physical alongside it. We have used a number of digital platforms , such as Commonplace, which has a really helpful neighbourhood mapping tool . We would go out with young people and tour their neighbourhoods, find out places that they liked and did not like, and then tag them on the map as we were walking through the urban sphere with them.

That is a really nice example of how you can translate something physical into something digital without losing sight of how beneficial these analogue engagement methods are. Whether that is 3D modelling, getting out and sketching buildings or encouraging young people to use their hands in other ways of placemaking, i t is so valuable and often slightly more novel these days to young people , who spend so much of their time online.
That was a good warm-up act for next week, as you said, Fiona. Next , we are moving on to current engagement, which is led by Baroness Griffin and Lord Bailey.

Q17 Fiona has answered this question but I want to dig a bit deeper. Does current policy sufficiently encourage robust and meaningful engagement with children and young people? I think n ot. What policies or guidance could be changed to create greater impact? Fiona has talked already about the social value matrix , but can we do more? What are the other examples that we can hold from there? Do you have international examples of good practice ?

From a T h eresa to a Teresa, you talked about neighbourhood plans and engaging with social services and schools. This was partially covered last week but there is an issue of resource and time, especially in our challenged schools. Teachers do not have the time . How do we do that? How do we engage hard-to-reach and disabled young people and children meaningfully? I have spoken about c lean and green , but how do we scale this up?

What was great about last week was hearing the fabulous examples of good practice and y ou are talking about really good examples of good practice . C ampaigning across the country, I am aware of where it does not happen at all. How do we take, advocate and influence your sectors to reach further geographically and to our children and young people?

If I may end on an example, I am dealing with two pieces of casework —y es, Chair, I probably should not pick up casework —where I am working with the relevant local councillors and MPs on a housing development that is three years old and has no safe crossing to the local primary school. That is in the Midlands, not the north-west.

I have another one in the Midlands at the moment that is an older school , and w e will solve this but there is no safe crossing from where c hildren live to go to their primary schools. I do not mean to be doom and gloom. What I am really interested in is how we take what is good and scale it up , who we have to influence in terms of policy, guidance and law , and who we have to resource. Teresa.

Thank you, Theresa. I will look at the policy side. I do not necessarily have the international examples but in terms of a statutory duty to include young people and children in the planning process, there is no such statutory requirement in England. Scotland ha s that statutory requirement ; i t was introduced in 2019. I am sure the evidence will probably come into this committee , but it will be interesting to see how that has been working in Scotland as part of that process and whether that has made a difference. It would certainly help to have that national requirement.

As we have seen , there is excellent engagement going on despite there not being that requirement at a national level. I have been able to trace back how English planning policy has dealt with community and young people’s engagement over the last 50 or 60 years. To be honest , it has found it very difficult to come to terms with what it needs to do. It has never made it through into legislation and is just starting to emerge at local authority level.

I spoke earlier about the lack of incorporation of the children’s rights into English legislation. The closest we got in terms of planning policy in England was in 2020 . We were talking about digital engagement previously , and t he White Paper — Planning for the Future — actually heralded the digital age as being the way that young people would be involved. We were looking to see how that would then develop into legislation or policy , and i t did not. All we have in our National Planning Policy Framework now is a requirement for effective, proportionate and early engagement. It does not specifically require any particular members of the community to be involved.

At local authority level, councils are required — under their statements of community involvement — to set out how they think consultation and engagement will take place across their communities. This varies from one council to the next. Even when it is spelled out in terms of placing young people or different minority groups as a priority, quite often it does not actually deliver tangible work on the ground. It is relying on other organisations such as Planning Aid England to deliver that engagement.

There is a willingness among the 13 local authorities that we studied in the north-east : 10 had very strong priorities towards involving young people and children in the planning process. As I said , the resources were just not there to deliver it. In that context, I wonder whether having it at a national level will actually create the resources to deliver it at a local level. It is a constant fact of life that that is going to be a challenge.

Coming back to the last point we were talking about, all engagement is valuable and it can be very cheaply done. Given the local authority’s priority, i f there are ways of working out how it can deliver an across-the-board way of getting young people’s views on a particular development proposal or the local community and visions for that area, it could be done quite easily. I suppose people will say, “ Is that effective ?” So we are between a rock and a hard place . The resources are very restricting in terms of people to do the engagements , and the policy could be better.
Nicola, how do you scale up the good work that you are doing right across the Grosvenor estate , including the north?

There are a number of different policy examples and processes that Teresa reflected on that can be bolstered to make sure that this is something that we see more consistently across the nation. We heard about the statement of community involvement processes needing to talk to how consultations have been meaningful and appropriately early . What is missing there is how representative they have been . T hat also pick s up your point around how we can ensure that young adults from different backgrounds or with different abilities are also given the chance to share their views.

Requiring an inclusive engagement statement within S C Is is one way that we can see this get some teeth and requirements. I have talked to some frameworks and processes that we have developed and used , but mandating those existing frameworks such as Voice , Opportunity , Power and requiring schemes to follow that process is one way that we can really make sure that this gives some teeth to the process.

Another point that would just be quite an interesting and leading - by - example exercise is involving young people in the actual development and rollout of this bolstered policy process. There are some fantastic youth councils out there that no doubt will have some brilliant ideas on how we can see this come to fruition. Actually involving them in the rollout of this is just testament to how we can lead by example and make sure that young people are part of the solution.
Fiona, how do we achieve not having “No ball games” signs on estates that have families on them?

It seems that if your example of the safe crossings had been explored and a young person had been consulted on what was proposed , they would have spotted that in the first five seconds. In terms of expenditure, that could have been good expenditure — if that had happened — in terms of then preventing what has happened further down the line.

It comes back to how we value this work and thinking about long-term custodians of place. It is not a coincidence that some of the most powerful and impactful pieces of youth engagement that are happening right now are coming from developers such as Grosvenor, housing association developer wings such as Latimer , or developers that have a long-term stake in that community where they really see that if they do not get it right, they will be the ones paying the price in five, 10 or 20 years , as opposed to developers working in different modes. Having a policy that demands more from developers could help to rectify that.

It does not need to cost developers more. Looking at those frameworks, there could be funds that are already put aside for social value that could go towards this , so it would not increase the bottom line for developers. It would just mean re-proportioning where their expenditure goes, which is a really important point. We have been told about how the London Borough of Newham has a requirement for statements of social value . That could be another requirement that would be put in that would take things beyond the current situation with statements of community involvement , where this youth engagement often just sits as an appendix. It should not be an appendix ; i t needs to be front and centre.

Q18 Thank you for coming this morning. I am going to be slightly more contentious than many of my colleagues just because I feel that way. Let me start with the idea that it will have very little to no cost. That means there is something that a developer is paying for now from wh ich that money will have to be taken away. Will that loss not be keenly felt by that project or work that is no longer being funded? Is that not a tension here if you include some work that you are talking about now?

That is a really good point. I cannot and would not talk about developers’ particular budgets ; I do not have that oversight. We work very closely with some construction skills centres and there is a huge amount of levy payments that contractors are paying that are not being used. I do not know the details of why they are not being used but it has to do with Section 106 payments that are required to be made . There is then no uptake on using that fund , so t hose funds are going back into the system. There are definitely areas where there are funds sitting but they are not currently accessible to the work.

Nicola, let me come to you. The comment was made earlier that some developers develop and leave so they do not have the same sort of motivation, let us say, that you might have to consult with a community. You are a unique developer , if only because of the size and financial muscle that you have. How do developers that do not have that financial muscle do the same sort of work that you are doing?

There are a number of points there. First , I would say that we are seeing the model of placemaking change in that there are many more developers taking that more estate-wide neighbourhood approach, whether that is the likes of Argent, wh ich developed King ’ s Cross and now Brent Cross, or Delancey. There are many more that are not seeing development a t an individual building or portfolio scale and are thinking more about that placemaking.

There is a trend that we are seeing more and more people moving into the model that Gr osvenor has been in for hundreds of years. There are obviously still individual developers and people who are changing places at a much smaller scale . It is important to acknowledge that there is a requirement for even those smaller-scale developments to consult with communities .

Why should it be that those young people within those communities do not fall into that requirement? This is where that policy argument comes in so importantly we need to ensure that the requirements and what is asked of developers are totally watertight and that they cannot not consult. It is something that is required of them to develop , even at the smallest scales.

I guess it is also about cost and smaller developers that might not necessarily have an engagement team , as Grosvenor do es. We are seeing more and more skillsets and capabilities around consultation being something that architects are increasingly up skilled in. This does not necessarily need to be something that people see as an engagement or a consultation expertise job. This is something that is going to become more and more routine and that we will see architects, surveyors and maybe planners becoming more and more skilled in . It will not be a separate , dedicated cost but something that is woven into the life cycle of a development project.

I am going to say something that is slightly complicated and may be perceived as slightly mean , but would this development model not suit the likes of you and Argent? It would then mean that you have an additional supposed social good to gain extra sites because other people would not be able to do it given that they do not have a development team as you do . One of the biggest problems we have in development across the piece is that we have only a few large developers and that is a very poor economic situation for us as a country . H ow do we avoid the tension of making things even easier for you as large developers but also raising the quality of what those smaller developers are bringing along?

It highlight s the benefits of placemaking at a neighbourhood scale when you can take that long-term approach . We should not shy away from that ; it is a benefit that is highlighted here . Through the availability of open-source tools and frameworks — such as the toolkit that I mentioned, which is making this available for free for developers of any scale — there is no excuse . It is being able to be really clear about what the expectations and requirements are from a policy point of view and ensuring that those frameworks, guidance, tools and resources are available to people so that they can deliver it at a smaller cost.

Teresa, let me come to you now . I am not sure that you made this comment but lived experience is not a skill ; it is an experience. I am a youth worker of some 35 years ’ standing and I come from a very poor community . If we harp on too much about people’s lived experience, we then deny that community to develop saleable skills that they can then build careers and jobs from . That is my little starting point.

How do we then use this whole conversation in proportion ? I am a school governor and have been for years . To my mind , we are having a conversation that largely you could ask schools to deliver . How much of this work should be delivered by developers , bearing in mind their social good is to provide homes ? Anything that gets in the way of that — homes and places — should be frowned upon .

If we are honest with ourselves , we probably would all have different motivations for our engagements and that is the world, I am afraid. If you have to get the resources to run that engagement, you have to tick boxes —including schools in the curriculum—to say that you are meeting the aims and objectives and that this is going to meet the requirements of the organisation you are working with . If it means that developers get a slightly smoother ride through the planning process as a result of that engagement with young people , so be it .

All engagement around the environment is good, skill development is good, and if we are encouraging young people to look at potential careers in the built environment professions, that longer-term benefit is one that we should perhaps be focusing on as much as anything . When young people realise that they can influence a decision — say , in a mock planning inquiry that we have run — and they say, “ Wow, I contributed to that discussion ; the outcome of that decision did actually take my views on board” , they start to feel that they have some buy-in to decision-making . They might have been nurturing an interest there in how their local area looks and the design that might go into it .

Even if we are cynical about the motivations , we must n o t underestimate the potential for young people to emerge with really useful professions and trades, and we should support the Government’s apprenticeship schemes through all engagement . I tend to just take th e view that it is all good and the more contact that young people have with professionals around places that are important to them, it can be only for their longer-term good as well.

I happen to agree and I am just asking you difficult questions because this is a cost . There is no other way of wrapping it up ; it is a cost and therefore you have to be able to justify that cost . There is a tension there because there is always some good place that money can be spent.

Could I just come back ? It is really important that we do not pit developers against young people or communities ; our experience is that this is not what is happening at all. We have work ed with small developers that want to do this work . They often see that it can support what they are trying to achieve because young people tend to be more open to forward-thinking or progressive modes of thinking about community and place, low-car neighbourhoods and higher - density living . Those are things that perhaps certain older audiences will just automatically say no to because it is a change from what they are used to .

Actually , it is where the industry wants to be going . We have examples of developers reaching out to us that recognise that those young people are going to be supporting a lot of the change that they are trying to make and that makes the community and the world a better place . It can often be blocked by those demographics that most typically turn up at our current consultation events.

Actually , if we are trying to achieve a better built environment, it is cost-effective to involve young people who are thinking about the fact that they will be inheriting climate change and issues around social justice . They tend to be talking from a very different perspective — coming back to that point of seeing the built environment in its truest terms as place and space and not property.

I accept what you are saying but it strays in to a territory of using young people to justify other professionals ’ views of the world, which I see happen quite a lot. My last question is about scale . Ultimately , I am very interested in the idea of the development of tools that smaller developers can use. I agree ; I happen to be a smaller developer , and we are very interested in using other people’s tools to lower our costs and the like. Nicola, y ou said quite explicit ly that Grosvenor has developed these tools and is pushing them out. Do you push them out just among community groups or is it something you provide to the industry and other developers?

Definitely the latter. That said, the tool that I mentioned — Voice , Opportunity , Power — is an open-source tool that is designed for developers, planners, design teams and sports professionals, given that it was produced also with Sport England support. It is for anyone who wants to involve young people in placemaking and managing but does not really know where to begin. I would encourage people across the board to look at it.

Q19 This is a social good that you are describing and it often seems that the planning processes are an obstacle course for developers and development. How do we avoid what is obviously a social good falling into that mindset and way of thinking? How much can best practice play a part in overcoming some of those obstacles so that it does not feel like an obstacle course for planners and developers?

Reflecting on the successes is a really good way to build that advocacy and buy-in for this type of work . That is something that we continue to do — working with others who are here on the panel today — to really highlight where this goes well and what we can learn from past engagement exercises that we have carried out.

One method that we have found really effective —unsurprisingly— is having the young people who were part of that process be part of that reflection and almost communication and promotion of the process. I have mentioned the Mayfair Youth Forum with which we worked on the redesign of Grosvenor Square. We have built some really strong working relationships with that group . When we were speaking with them about the project, they were from 14 to 19 years old ; many are now in their early 20s and are joining me on panel events like this one to talk about how important the youth voice is in placemaking and managing.

That is just one example of how we can really raise the profile of how beneficial this is . It should not just be developers speaking about it themselves but young people who have gone through this process and can speak from that lived experience of being involved meaningfully.

There is o ne small question I forgot to ask : w hat do you ask young people that differ s from what you ask the oldies? What is it you say that makes it age-appropriate or do you not need to change the content of your questions?

With any exercise that I have been involved in with whatever age , the first question is asking about what the place means to them and what is most important. It is n ot necessarily focusing on the negative but just trying to tease out this relationship that they have with their place and open space . Then you can start—in a building block form— focusing on common issues but very much being led by the young people t alking about how they experience their local area.

We did a lot of work with hot food takeaways as an engagement exercise and because every young person— everybody — likes a takeaway, it was relevant. It was another way of looking at the local area and the impact it was having on the community. This came out of a conversation with the young people about the litter that was gathering around the local hot food takeaways in the shopping street.

From that, it was quite a natural development of, “ Okay, if we had a community strategy around trying to control and understand what the issues a re, how would we do that? ” Just from discussion, you soon pull young people’s perspectives out about how they feel : that ther e is a lack of investment because there is a lot of litter and that must mean that they are not worthy of having that investment . There are all sorts of layers of how they perceive their local area. I am not trying to pursue a consultation around a particular development , but it is about trying to nurture something that is quite organic from where those young people already are.

I n the latter half of the 19th century much of London’s domestic architecture was built in reference to pattern books at a time when there was an enduring aesthetic consensus. What I would like to know is to what extent you see your role as stimulating a debate about architectural aesthetics.
Who are you going to on that one?
Whoever.
Come on, Fiona.

Tha t is a fantastic question. I get delighted when young people are talking about the built environment as something that they can have an opinion on because it is within the realm of something they can actually change and have a say in rather than something that is happening to them. Combining both your point and Lord Bailey’s in terms of what you are engaging young people in, it comes back to the aims of it.

We can decouple it from planning . I t is not just young people being asked what they think in terms of planning ; i t can be in the broader sense of what they think generally about their neighbourhoods and neighbourhood plans , through to very specific co-design exercises. We have created a youth engagement overlay to the R IBA Plan of Work, which shows that young people can be involved at every single stage , whether their neighbourhood is going through no change whatever through to whether there is something happening and that is at the earliest stage of visioning, brief, design or even physically building that space.

A really important part of that —it comes back to an earlier point — is about first encouraging young people to look at the world and recognise that there are different styles and different types of buildings and to start to form an opinion : “ How does it make me feel? What do I like? ” If we are in the visioning stage of working with a placemaker that is thinking about what these buildings should feel like, we put examples in front of the young people to get a sense of what it is that they like . This is only in instances where the placemaker is in a position where they are going to be able to listen to those young people’s responses.

A cross the board here, everybody understands that the number one thing is to be managing the expectations of young people and never going into a room saying , “ You can have any of this ” , when in fact you can only have this. It is doing real due diligence — whether you are a local authority , placemaker , developer or planner — to understand what agenc y we are willing to give over to the young people, framing the conversations through that and ensuring that they appeal to that wide range of learners. You are going out, seeing buildings and getting the opportunity to draw and make . You start to understand that everything in this room and in any room that you are in has been designed , made and thought about, and that opinions and decisions have gone into that that then have an impact and knock-on effects.

It is not necessarily a pattern book but it is about showing young people the range of possibilities of what is there, and arguably for all people being consulted with on built environment. Maybe we need to be moving the conversation from statutory consultation to participation and enabling people to not just respond yes or no to a question or even just to have information shared with them . We need to respect that they have opinions and knowledge that are worthy of being considered alongside that professional expertise and that will actually have value in the built environment that is ultimately created.
That is a good tee-up to the next area, the final area of question ing , which is led by Lord Ravensdale and Baroness Andrews.

Q20 We have already touched on this idea of a statutory duty but I wanted to dig into that in a bit more detail . You can view the story of our planning system over the past decades almost as l ots of well-intentioned changes that have gone into the system and it ha s built up and up. Now we are in a situation where it is actually very difficult to get things built in this country. We have some really aggressive targets , such as t he 1.2 million homes, the huge infrastructure pipeline , and of course there is a lot of thought going into the planning system as to how that can work more effectively.

I am interested in whether a statutory duty would create further delays in the planning system , in your view . If so , how could some issues with that be thought about and mitigated? Maybe through that you could think about whether there is any experience you can bring to bear on how this has worked in other jurisdictions ; I think Scotland was mentioned. Teresa, you mentioned this before . Perhaps you could start us off on that , please.

It has to be a multi-pronged approach . It would be wonderful to finally get that statutory duty into planning legislation and policy but , as you say , it is a challenging time to be a planner . I know the Royal Town Planning Institute is constantly making th e case that we are thousands of planners short.

In terms of processing planning applications, there are not enough people in place to do this , and we then add that extra layer of the engagement that is required . It depends on whether you are looking at it as being an advantageous layer or one that is going to be a hindrance and time -consuming and costly . There should perhaps be some kind of guidance as to what that a cross the board layer of engagement should be with children and young people.

We need to have a really positive rhetoric about the planning system and what planners are trying to do and doing very well. I have personally been in planning for 40 years . F irst , I was not encouraged to go into planning because I was a woman, which is really hard to believe but that is going back to the early 19 80s . Now the planners are damned if they do not hurry up with their planning decisions, but if they do they are still damned because they are not doing consultation properly. So we need a much more positive narrative.

It is not just about policy ; it is about resources , having people to do it and bringing the next generation along. Particularly if an additional statutory duty is introduced , w e might not see those changes immediately . We have to think about the next generation , bringing more planners through the apprenticeship scheme and making conditions such that they do not want to leave the workforce. Some 20% of current planners are thinking that they will leave the profession in the next three years , according to a survey done by the RTPI . We are not even replacing that number ; t he situation could potentially just get worse from what you have described there.

I cannot really speak with authority in terms of what Scotland has done to overcome that and how it feels that that is emerging. I understand that the RTPI is looking at the impact of that on resourcing a nd that might come out through written evidence.
Very briefly , you talked about a multi-pronged approach. Do you still think a statutory duty is part of that?

We need to catch up with other countries. Basically , a lot of other countries worldwide have done so much more , not only in planning but planning being regarded as part of that engagement with young people . There is a much more integrated approach to involving young people in the decisions that are made locally in Sweden, Italy, New Zealand, Australia, the United States —the list is endless . We could look at examples , although I do not have a case study in detail that I could share with you .

Because it has been integrated much earl ier since the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child, service provision has been much more joined - up in those other countries. Now what we are trying to do is play catch-up and make it cost-effective and efficient at the same time. It is important but we also have to resource the people who are going to do that.
Nicola, what are your views on this from running a property portfolio?

In principle, a statutory duty could be very effective ; i t is important that it is framed and positioned appropriately. We do not want this to become something that is just tick-boxy; i t needs to be accompanied by really clear expectations around what good looks like , what is expected of developers and what we touched on earlier around how local authorities are handling that at their different levels .

That might be around ensuring that inclusive engagement is also picked up as engagement that is early and meaningful. To the point that I have raised throughout this conversation, also linking it with resources and standards that are available to people to help them on the way is going to be really key to ensuring that this is actually delivered and that it is seen as something that leads to better outcomes rather than a hurdle that people have to overcome.

I agree with everything that has already been said. I wonder whether the statutory duty should apply to schemes at a certain scale and , alongside that , could become proportionate to the scale and the scope of developments and how much impact it is likely to have on young people , s o a slightly more nuanced approach. I completely appreciate how challenging it is to get things built right now but our experience with the developers we have worked with is that the youth engagement process has not slowed it down.

If anything, it has kept it to its targets and helped to bridge those relationships with the community. We need to stress t he importance of that guidance and break down that it is not rocket science ; i t is really straightforward . It is not something for developers to fear doing and the gains that can be made are huge on all sides — for the young people, the place and those organisations.

It seems that there is a real challenge around joined-up thinking across the board when we are talking about the built environment , coming to those pipelines of talent and people coming in and understanding what it means to work in construction or the built environment. Mart y n Evans , c reative d irector at Landsec , made a salient point that I am sure everyone in this room is familiar with : the built environment has no single voice in g overnment and that makes it extremely challenging to ever join up strategy.

Martyn Evans said : “ Architecture is filed under ‘ creative industries ’ , construction under ‘ infrastructure ’ , engineering under ‘ manufacturing ’, and property under ‘ real estate and finance ’ . But , w hen you step back, it is clear that all these activities are part of one continuous chain , from conception to completion to operation, united by a single purpose ” . I would argue that if you are trying to introduce children and young people in the next generation, you are bringing in the Department for Education and it gets even more complex.

Re-establishing something like the Commission for Architecture and the Built Environment would really support that. That was around in the early days of my career and felt like it was part of a more joined-up approach to thinking about the built environment and to connecting voices and showing that actually a lot of people are looking at the same challenges but in silos. I do not know w hether that is something that you all in this room would have the potential to look at: both top - down as well as what is happening at the grass - roots scale at the moment.
To pick up on your initial point, you mentioned development size. If there were a statutory duty, would you be concerned about the impact on SMEs, for example, rather than larger developers ?

Yes, but we find that smaller developers engage in these processes. Bywater Properties is one of those. In fact, they are not engaging at planning stage . It is completely decoupled ; t hey are engaging with young people wherever they are proposing to develop , from that social value perspective where they have very high environmental targets . They also see those social targets as being part and parcel of what they do.

Coming back to that point around the relatively short lifespan of a lot of our buildings, if we are doing this big push in building it feels incredibly important that we get it right. There are cases now that we have all heard of — not just in the UK but internationally — where a building is being demolished before anyone ha s even stepped foot in it because it is no longer relevant to the ways that people are living. This should all be seen as constant research - gathering and information that can support the industry as a whole.

Just very briefly, I completely agree with you about CABE ; w e should definitely bring it back. There is a bit of tension here, is there not ? If you take the Scottish example and look at the way children are involved in those specific developments that involve play or space for children, there would be an argument for saying that in those situations there should be a statutory duty to have children involved.

In a way , what you have also been saying is that there is one conversation . Many of the issues that young people raise are exactly the same as would be raised across the board because everyone wants safe spaces, green spaces and so on. I ask this specifically of Fiona because she ha s developed this . Would you suggest that we go for a limited model along the lines of the Scottish proposals or that we put it into the N PPF as a specific requirement — without it being in the highest statutory provision — for children to have an explicit role in every development? What do you think would work best?

Definitely the latter. We all in this room have a huge amount of respect for children and young people and we know that their opinions go beyond just play or spaces that are seen for children. In our work w e see that w hat they offer to thinking about long-term housing, education, transport and environment is impactful across the board.

Exactly to Nicola’s point, my main worry with it becoming statutory is whether it becomes a tick box where it is consultation at best, information - sharing at worst, and no agency is given to young people . Actually , taking more of a policy framework that offers guidance and shows a myriad of different ways of doing it at different stages could be much more potent.

Could you provide some international examples? Teresa mentioned the international examples in the context of the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child and the way European countries have gone further than us . I wonder whether you could think of any international examples where children have been incorporated in the statutory process of consultation and the impact that that may have had on the nature of the quality of place . You also spoke about the way young people can contribute to a vision of the quality of place because they live in the place and are not making judgments about who owns what. That would be very useful , as well as anything else that you have on the metrics.

It would also be good to have examples of not just where it has gone well internationally but where it has gone badly. Anything you have o n that that you could provide in written evidence after this would be good. We touched on it a little last week but i f there is anything you have about the role that parents and the wider family or carers can have in this process and how it can be brought together , that would also be helpful .

The third and final thing — just channelling my inner Lord Bailey —is from a developer’s point of view, obviously Grosvenor has the assets and we talked about the rights of a child and the longevity of a site . If there is anything you have that would demonstrate the tangible, immediate uplift for a site commercially , that would be useful. We can all agree that this is good and worth while but are there any examples or case studies of where this has gone well from a financial point of view ? If a developer i s strapped for cash or ha s a lot of other pressures on it , we can say this is good but is there some financial uplift in the immediate vicinity?

With that, that is the end of this session. I am very grateful to everyone from the committee who took part, but especially to our witnesses for your time and your experience that you shared with us. Yet again t his has been a very interesting and vital debate , and I am very grateful to you for giving up your time. Please write to us with anything else you have and stay in touch with us . Thank you very much.

C orrected oral evidence: Young p eople and the built environment
Tuesday 14 April 2026
Watch the meeting

Members present: Lord Gascoigne (The Chair); Baroness Andrews; Lord Bailey of Paddington; Lord Bassam of Brighton ; Lord Cameron of Dillington ; Baroness Griffin of Princethorpe ; Viscount Hanworth; Baroness Janke ; Baroness Miller of Chilthorne Domer; Lord Porter of Spalding; Lord Ravensdale ; Viscount Younger of Leckie .
Evidence Session No. 1 Heard in Public Questions 1 - 11
Witnesses
I : Terry Watts, CEO, Built Environment School s Trust; Dr Jenny Russell, Director of Education and Learning, RIBA; Neil Pinder, Head of Architecture , Graveney School .
USE OF THE TRANSCRIPT
This is a corrected transcript of evidence taken in public and webcast on www.parliamentlive.tv
Examination of w itness es
Terry Watts, Dr Jenny Russell and Neil Pinder .

Q1 The Chair : Good morning and welcome to the House of Lords Built Environment Select Committee. As everybody knows, we have focused a lot over the p ast year or so on the new towns programme . We are taking a slight pause from that today to start an entirely new inquiry — a short one — into something that I personally find very interesting and which has come u p quite a lot in the new town s work that we have already done : younger people and their interaction with , interest in and engagement with the built environment sector. Today , we will focus on the education side of that —that is, the national curriculum, careers and skills. We have some distinguished guests and witnesses before us to talk us through things . Can you briefly introduce yourselves to the team ?
I am the CEO of the Built Environment Schools Trust. We are a charity aimed at improving young people ’s knowledge of careers and opportunities to work in the built environment.

Good morning, everyone. I am the d irector of education and learning at the Royal Institute of British Architects. I have a PhD in children’s perceptions of architectural space and schools. C hildren and the built environment , including how they engage with it , is a subject that is very close to my heart.

I am a secondary school teacher . I am passionate about architecture and changing the narrative around the built environment. I have been given an honorary fellowship by RIBA and an honorary professorship by the Bartlett School of Architecture for some of my work. I am honoured to be here today.

Q2 The Chair : The honour is ours. Thank you very much for coming before us today. As you know, we have a series of questions to go through. As I have said, if you do not know the answer, please do not feel obliged to fill the time ; w e are push ed for time, as are you . A ll I ask is for everyone in this room, u s included, to keep questions and answers as short and concise as possible.

First , we are going to talk about the national curriculum. My colleague , Baroness Andrews , and I will ask you a few questions. B efore we go into that in great detail, can you briefly give us your analysis or stocktake of where we are more generally on this , perhaps in comparison to other countries ? Do they do anything that we could or should learn from?

On the national curricul um, there was a review last year. There are lots of priorities that people will argue s hould feature on the national curriculum ; I love history so I would say that history should be in there. I am s orry to play devil’s advocate but d oes having any element of the built environment matter ? I f so, why?
There are lots of questions in there.
The Chair: S orry.

You have done five in one, I think. We are not in a very good state , in that people do not really engage with the built environment in schools. There are some exceptionally good programmes — I am sure that we will hear about them as today goes on — where organisations take good - quality activities into schools and generate interest around the built environment , but they are patchy and unco - ordinated. They tend to be focused on London and the south - east or where the building is being done.

I live in a place called Abingdon . N o one apart from me has visited the three average secondar ies in Abingdon. They are good schools, actually — I will get told off if I say “average” — but they are normal schools . T he only person from the built environment sector who has visited them in the p ast 10 years is me , as far as I know, because there is no big construction work going on there. It is vital to link knowledge of the sector into the curricul um, and it is very easily done. That is what we do : w e provide teachers with materials to teach geography at every stage in the national curriculum from the age of eight to 18 — key stage s 2 to 5, for those who know th e jargon.

A ll young people can do that . T hey all talk about urban environments, depending on how old they are. That is the built environment. They skip over it and talk about the urban environment in a geography context . W e say , “This is why that ’s important , and these are the people who do the work to create our environments ” . I t is quite easy to do . I t is really important because it gives a context to the young people for their study. It also opens up a whole world to teachers , who do not know about the built environment either . I t puts the whole sector into context.

There is so much to say on this. I cannot answer quickly but , going forward, it should be about places . There was a section in your last report about your work with some children . Y ou saw exactly the same enthusiasm that they have for the built environment. They care about it at least as much as we do. They care about the environment and the impact of the 42% of CO 2 that comes from the built environment at least as much as we do , because they will have to live in that world when we are all long gone . T hey care about sustainability and the impact on communities .

We can bring all of this out. We focus on geography. We would love to expand that to physics, maths and other subjects. In fact, one of our schools up in Brighouse in Yorkshire has managed to include English, history, geography, the sciences and design technology in using our schools programme, which , again , is free, to try to get the whole school involved. There is a little video that I can send around , if you like , with the youngsters telling us what they thought . I t really does work. They have a natural passion for the built environment.

It is not difficult to inspire young people once you get into a school. As a sector, we do not get into that many schools. We are the biggest schools programme in the sector — in the country , probably ; I would like to stake that claim. Just this year, we have engaged 242 more geography teachers in more than 200 schools. They have brought with them 34,500 young people in schools across the country who I know are looking at the built environment as a career destination through our My Environment My Future programme, which is free . That is great, except we have reached only around 500 schools so far . We primarily target secondary schools at the moment , but w e are moving into junior schools now. There are 4,178 secondary schools. The sector employs 12% of the workforce and is responsible for 15% of GDP. As a sector, those 500 schools are probably the maximum number of schools that we reach in a year. We are not reaching most schools .

W e go in as particular professions or trades, and we are up against industries. I do not want to pick on anyone because everybody does some really good stuff . W e go in as surveyors , engineers or architects . R oofers go in and do a schools programme, which is great. Other sectors go in as the healthcare sector, financial services or retail , then people understand the specialisms. We are trying to sell individual careers in a sector that people do not know exists. We need to go in—this is what we do — as the built environment sector.

If Jenny were to go in with My Environment My Future and help us with the competition, she would instinctively give that presentation an architectural bias , fragrance or direction. If someone from RICS were to do it, there would be a surveying context. They are still promoting the built environment. Those children who are not interested in those particular professions will get the knowledge that other professions are available . W e can make the whole sector more visible .

We went to a meeting up in the north - west in November . It was organised by Unifrog, which provides careers information in schools , and 150 careers leads from the north - west were there. We had to pay to go to that. It was n ot much —t hey gave us a big discount , which was helpful, because they want to work with u s— but we had to pay for that. We were the only people representing the built environment because we are not co - ordinated. We do not punch above our weight . W e need to do better by w orking together.
The Chair : Dr Russell , can you give your own perspective , as well as RIBA’s ? T he two may be the same.
I will start by zooming out a little from what T erry has been talking about and talk about engagement with schools . I will talk about our schools programme more as the morning goes on , I am sure.

When we think of the national curriculum and what it is doing, there is a lot in it. There is a lot of learning that has to take place for children and young people. The built environment is a three-dimensional space, and we need to experience that. F or me, the word “ experience ” is really important. Some thing that comes out when RIBA does its schools programme — we get this time and again in our feedback — is that it is inclusive. A ny child or young person in the room can engage with it. W e are building models and working as teams . I t draw s out all the young people and get s them to work and engage with subjects in different ways than just learning. That process of learning is important. The built environment , being three-dimensional , is a great example of a subject that draws together lots of the threads.

Perhaps I can give some personal experience . A s an academic who has taught students studying architecture at university , when students come into their first year, often , you are trying to encourage them to think and problem - solve because so much of the national curriculum is them learning and coming up with an immediate answer. I n university, you are trying to get them to go through a process and understand what “ process ” means ; f rom our perspective in architecture, that is the design process. It means thinking about construction and the experience of people in a space, which is essentially what we do: w e creat e spaces for people. I n some ways, we are trying to unpick a bit of that and give students the opportunity to think.

Sometimes , we do not give children and young people the opportunity to get it wrong and to learn from th at opportunity. We have so much assessment and learning by rote. I have a daughter going through her GCSEs at the minute . She is learning essays ; I am not sure that I see the point of that . When young people go into any employment , particular ly in the built environment, they need to be able to problem - solve and think through issues.

I realise that I have completely zoomed out from what Terry talk ed about, but it may give you a broader understanding of the relationship between the built environment , the way in which young people are learning and the way in which we need them to be learning.
The Chair : It is not just what is on the national curricul um; it is how you teach it and how you engage.

Yes . It is also about t he support that teachers have to do that. At RIBA , we have put together lots of resources for teachers. We have a national schools programme. However, teachers need time to go through those resources and think about how to deliver them. We take architects into schools. Architects are really keen to go into schools and engage with children and young people, but there needs to be space in the curriculum to do that.

You spend a lot of time on literacy and numeracy , so all the other subjects get squashed in terms of time . T hat is where all of the built environment comes in. You are trying to tie together all the threads from the other subject areas to equate to learning about the built environment , but t eachers need time to work out how to do that.
The Chair : Neil, you were nodding a bit.
Yes . T here were quite a few bits there with which I really agree.

I am going to come at it from a different perspective. By rights, people may say that I should not be here today , because I come from a council estate that is two miles down the road as the crow flies , opposite Battersea Power Station. My secondary school was a bit further down as the crow flies —around three kilometres in total. T he most inspirational people for me, apart from my parents, were my art teacher and my music teacher. I would bet that anybody in this room had a teacher who made them think ; that teacher is the one who changed your life.

The national curricul um can be augmented to suit different ways of teaching. I teach in one of the best schools in England : Graveney School. Its inspirational head, Graham Stapleton, g ave me the freedom to experiment with the built environment and architecture. F rom there, I integrated it into design and technology . I turned design and technology into a subject that students wanted to know about.

A s Jenny said , the curriculum is now quite constrained with Progress 8 . Her daughter will have gone through the tests . B efore that, in primary school, children have a test in year 6 via the Fi sc her Family Trust . T hat determines , in an academic way , the ir GC SE or A- level outcome prediction s . If we rewind on that to make the tests creative and let young people think outside the box, I honestly think that the matrix may be a bit different.

E very one of you will have been on a beach and seen a young person digging a hole or playing with sand. T hat is construction. That is learning about the density of material s . H ow do you sell that? Trojan horses. I have invented Trojan horses to deliver my teaching. They come in as one thing but then they teach young people about the density of material s , construction, structures or aesthetics . Y ou link those things in . Y ou cannot just say, “ I ’ m going to teach you about construction ” . You have to slowly wind it into them so that they love the subject. Once they get a passion, you can change the narrative and get them to think about what profession they would like to be in.

We are facing, at this precise moment, a skill s shortage. Young people — I see them all the time — cannot make. I f any of you guys here wanted a plumber, a carpenter, an electrician or somebody to design something, the first thing that they would do is pull out a pad and do a really good drawing. You would say to them, “Now make that ” . There we have problems. T he national curriculum is quite constrained at the moment, as has been said . Creativity is the tool that gives everybody access. If we can get young people to understand that their creativity is a gift, we can broaden the national curriculum to accept that.

There are things that we can implement right now . T he GCSE in my subject, product design , went from 60% NEA, which is the making and the project work, to 50 % —that is, from 60:40 to 50:50 . T hat 10% deduction may seem small but it throws a lot of young people off doing the subject , because it is taken up by a bit of maths and a bit more theory when , really , we should be asking and enthusing them to design, be creative, think outside the box, problem - solve and context ualise . A ll these things need to be implemented. If you have a daughter or a son right now and you see them playing, rather than being on a computer , it is such a relief.
The Chair : Yes, totally. Baroness Andrews, there is lots to go at here.

Q3 My question is enormous . I n relation to what you have just said, it is also very difficult , because you have set out such a brilliant and comprehensive diagnosis of the challenges and needs in terms of creativity, problem - solv ing and all the things that can be incorporated in good teaching and yet have a particular resonance in relation to what you have described as the elements of the built environment — architecture, design, CDT and understanding place. First, what can you, as professionals, do to present a more integrated vocabulary and offer to schools ? H ow can the new curricul um, which we know has put bigger emphasis on PSHE and elements of creativity, take up a better offer?

Secondly, you have all talked about how extremely concerned you are about the skills market and jobs for young people . T he different elements, whether it is construction , architecture or design, all have a different application in different bits of the curriculum. Are you looking for teachers and curriculum - setters to be more aware of how you can put the built environment and use the vocabularies you are all using in things such as the science curricul um — obviously , it fits in with the engineering bits of the science curricul um —or, as Terry raised, s hould we be thinking about adding a new element to the curricul um, however difficult that may be , in terms of how young people and everybody else fit into place ? You could then bring together sustainability, demographic change, social behaviours , designing out crime and all the other social and environmental elements. Th ere are two slightly different approaches , are the re not? I ask Jenny to start and give RIBA’s point of view .

I n some ways , you have already answered the question that you asked. It is really encouraging to hear you talk about place in the wholeness of the curriculum. W hen I was going through the questions , the first point I wrote down was that, when we are asked to look at the national curricul um, t he difficulty is that so much of the built environment is tying threads between all the different subject areas.
It gets lost, does it not?

It does. It gets diluted down to learning stuff about the built environment. A s I was thinking through these questions, I brought it completely down to the word “ value ” . What do we value? We value young people . W e value children . W e value the built environment and the place in which they exist. D rawing those threads together within the curricul um would , in many ways , answer the question with which we are struggling .

T eaching creativity and design is not a key part of the PGCE. We need to be supporting teachers to do that. C reativity as part of place - making is really important. We need t hree - dimensional thinking. A rchitecture is , at its most fundamental , three - dimensional problem - solv ing. It is about how you deal with people in the spaces they are in. We are struggling because we do not do that three - dimensional problem - solving.

That is how children work and learn. I do not know about you but , when my young children were little, we would go into shops and I would say, “ Don’t touch ” . T hey were dragging their hands along everything and I was hoping that they did not break something. We all know what that means. We have all built dens out of the cushions on the sofa . T hat is them exploring space.

We have all these amazing children in our schools, but they are not all designed to be academic. They are not all there to be academic s . Some of them are going to be plumbers and builders. Going back to that word , “ value ” , we need to value those young people , as a part of the built environment education system, as much as we do those who will become engineers , architects or specialists in their own area s .

We are talking about slightly different topics , really . T he curriculum has been set ; it has been designed. It will not chang e for eight years. I have tried in various jobs for the p ast 25 years to change the curriculum but I have not been very successful. T hat is not something I will be able to do ; y ou may be able to influence that , but I cannot.

I recognise that more creativity in the curriculum would be good , but we have got what we have got . We work alongside the existing curriculum and the awarding bodies. Thinking about the My Environment My Future programme , in GCSE and A- level g eography, they talk about urban environments at GCSE and places at A- level . We say, “You need to teach this module”. There are six lessons. We look at the curriculum specification and the awarding body specification. We write lesson plans for teachers ; t hey have lesson plans for every lesson now. We say, “ These are the learning outcomes , these are the stretch exercises and these are the things you need to cover. Here is a presentation that does all of that for you ” .

Embedded in that presentation are links to videos from RIBA and RICS with case studies of young people who have worked in the sector and are now environmental surveyors , engineers or architects. Y ou can see real people , and they are presented by the teachers using those materials in the classroom. All of that is free . T hey can edit them, too; t hey can take them out and use their own presentations. We are not saying , “Y ou have to use our resources ”. They can just use those resources as a starting point.

We are using what exist s already and making it work for teachers. You are talking to two people who have been teachers . T here are some brilliant teachers around the country ; I am not saying that there are not. Some of them are spending the extra time they have as social workers . They are running food banks . T hey are trying to help children cop e with drug issues, problems at home and absenteeism. The pressure on teachers these days is absolutely monumental.

We work very closely with the Geographical Association and the Royal Geographical Society. M ost geography teachers are members of th e Geographical Association . We have to persuade them that we are trying to make their li ves easier : “ Just spend 15 minutes looking at this . Y ou need no training because it ’ s about teaching the curriculum you already teach . It just adds to it, enriches it and makes it easier to do , and you can introduce the built environment ” .

From our polls — we have thousands of students — we know that 94% of students do not want to work in construction when we meet them. As Jenny said, everybody slips into thinking that this is about plumbing and electricity. That is a very important part of it , but that is to the built environment what coding is to the tech sector.

I used to work for IBM. I did not want to join the IT sector when I was young b ecause it was boring . I t was nerdy. It was the people who lived in their grandparents’ basement and ate pizza. That was the stereotype. They ha d n o friends and no girlfriend . N o one wants that , but t hat was the situation 20, 30 or 40 years ago — I am that old. Now , the tech sector gets the people who have rejected financial services. I t ell you what , guys : it is the same jobs. They do the same things. I ended up working at IBM . I did do some programming, but I also ran a business unit. I did marketing . I presented at various committees , conferences and all sorts of things. I had a really exciting job. It was n othing to do with coding . M ost of the people in the tech sector do not do coding, but it is vital.

A lot of people in the built environment work in the trades, but most of them do not. There are around 500,000 professionals, not all of whom are architects, in the built environment sector. The y are engineers, environmentalists and waste management professionals . A ll those sorts of people work in the sector . They do not know that those jobs exist , and s ome of them are really quite exciting. We need to make more of them.

I argue that we should stop talking about construction completely. People know whether they want to be come a bricklayer or a plumber ; t hey will find that out very quickly. I work with CBEE — I do not know whether you know it—which is Construction & Built Environment Education . They are the people who used to be advis e rs to what were the sector skills council s in universities, colleges, training providers, employers and schools . They care about the built environment and careers in the sector. We still meet to try to influence things.

I chair a little subgroup there to look at the case for a built environment GCSE. W e want something that is more academic. W e need to make people realise that this is not just a trade route. Why can you not have a version of business studies for the built environment? E verything you cover in business studies , you can cover in the built environment. There are careers linked to it. They say that teachers cannot teach the built environment. How many teachers have been in business? They teach business studies. T here is a case for doing that , and we are working on it ; I will be happy to share our statement with you when we finish it soon.
The Chair: P lease do.
It is not in the timescale for this inquiry , I do not think .
The Chair: You can share a nything you want.

We are trying to use the system as it is. I would like to see new GCSEs and a curriculum change , but we need to work alongside teachers to see whether we can help them do their jobs better or give more relevance and more of a careers slant to what they are teaching , because Gatsby requires them to do that now anyway. We do that by working within the existing qualifications framework and the curriculum that is there.
Neil, do you see any scope in the new curriculum for you?

Yes, there is scope. I would not like another curriculum change . I have seen so many changes in the curriculum , and they seem to be running to stand still. A s a teacher , I have to interpret another curricul um, which is based off another curricul um, et cetera . W hat I say to students is , “C reativity changes lives ” . Y ou can begin from that premise . I say to them, “M aths, English, geography and all these other subjects are absolutely brilliant . T hey can underpin everything that you want to be in the built environment ” .

Instead of looking at it from the academic side downwards, we look at those subjects as underpinning what we want to do. We want to be engineers . H ow do we go about it? We want to work in construction — sorry for using that word . H ow do we go about it? It still involves maths, English and science . W e need to look at it from that angle , not necessarily thinking that the academic subjects are the be-all and end - all. If we look at the curriculum from a creative angle and say , “A ll these other subjects underpin creativity” , we are looking at it as a glass that is half full as opposed to half empty.

Young people are literally asking for creative subjects. They are asking to learn about what they can do to change their environment : “ We want more of a say in where I live, design, sleep and go to school. How do we do that? ” When we are delivering the curriculum as it is now, we need to make sure that we incorporate all the elements that we want them to learn about in terms of their specific environment. A ll these things are going to take us from the past and stay with us in the present . W e are building capacity , which is the main thing , for future generations to come so that they have value for their society.

Q4 I have a very quick and specific question for Terry. You said that you live in and around the Abingdon area, although I note that you cover other areas of the country. You said that there is not too much going on there. A s I understand it, there is a huge plan for a massive reservoir in that area. T o what extent have schools been, and should be, involved in looking at all the aspects relating to that in terms of the built environment ?

I happen to live in Abingdon but t he Built Environment Schools Trust covers the whole of the UK . S chools in Nigeria, Dubai, New Zealand, Australia and Cape Verde have picked up the materials and used them because they are free for anyone to use.
